text: The State of Greece from the earliest Times to the Commencement of the Peloponnesian War Thucydides, an Athenian, wrote the history of the war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians, beginning at the moment that it broke out, and believing that it would be a great war and more worthy of relation than any that had preceded it.
text_raw:
The State of Greece from the earliest Times to the Commencement of the Peloponnesian
War
Thucydides, an Athenian, wrote the history of the war between the Peloponnesians and
the Athenians, beginning at the moment that it broke out, and believing that it would be a
great war and more worthy of relation than any that had preceded it.

text: This belief was not without its grounds.
text_raw:
This belief was not
without its grounds.

text: The preparations of both the combatants were in every department in the last state of perfection; and he could see the rest of the Hellenic race taking sides in the quarrel; those who delayed doing so at once having it in contemplation.

the last state of perfection; and he could see the rest of the Hellenic race taking sides in the
quarrel; those who delayed doing so at once having it in contemplation.

text: Indeed this was the greatest movement yet known in history, not only of the Hellenes, but of a large part of the barbarian world—I had almost said of mankind.
text_raw:
Indeed this was
the greatest movement yet known in history, not only of the Hellenes, but of a large part of
the barbarian world—I had almost said of mankind.

text: For though the events of remote antiquity, and even those that more immediately preceded the war, could not from lapse of time be clearly ascertained, yet the evidences which an inquiry carried as far back as was practicable leads me to trust, all point to the conclusion that there was nothing on a great scale, either in war or in other matters.
text_raw:
For though the events of remote
antiquity, and even those that more immediately preceded the war, could not from lapse of
time be clearly ascertained, yet the evidences which an inquiry carried as far back as was
practicable leads me to trust, all point to the conclusion that there was nothing on a great
scale, either in war or in other matters.

text: For instance, it is evident that the country now called Hellas had in ancient times no settled population; on the contrary, migrations were of frequent occurrence, the several tribes readily abandoning their homes under the pressure of superior numbers.
text_raw:
For instance, it is evident that the country now called Hellas had in ancient times no
settled population; on the contrary, migrations were of frequent occurrence, the several
tribes readily abandoning their homes under the pressure of superior numbers.

text: Without commerce, without freedom of communication either by land or sea, cultivating no more of their territory than the exigencies of life required, destitute of capital, never planting their land (for they could not tell when an invader might not come and take it all away, and when he did come they had no walls to stop him), thinking that the necessities of daily sustenance could be supplied at one place as well as another, they cared little for shifting their habitation, and consequently neither built large cities nor attained to any other form of greatness.
text_raw:
Without
commerce, without freedom of communication either by land or sea, cultivating no more
of their territory than the exigencies of life required, destitute of capital, never planting
their land (for they could not tell when an invader might not come and take it all away, and
when he did come they had no walls to stop him), thinking that the necessities of daily
sustenance could be supplied at one place as well as another, they cared little for shifting
their habitation, and consequently neither built large cities nor attained to any other form
of greatness.

text: The most powerful victims of war or faction from the rest of Hellas took refuge with the Athenians as a safe retreat; and at an early period, becoming naturalized, swelled the already large population of the city to such a height that Attica became at last too small to hold them, and they had to send out colonies to Ionia.

text: Before the Trojan war there is no indication of any common action in Hellas, nor indeed of the universal prevalence of the name; on the contrary, before the time of Hellen, son of Deucalion, no such appellation existed, but the country went by the names of the different tribes, in particular of the Pelasgian.

text: Hellen and his sons grew strong in Phthiotis, and were invited as allies into the other cities, that one by one they gradually acquired from the connection the name of Hellenes; though a long time elapsed before that name could fasten itself upon all.

text: Born long after the Trojan War, he nowhere calls all of them by that name, nor indeed any of them except the followers of Achilles from Phthiotis, who were the original Hellenes: in his poems they are called Danaans, Argives, and Achaeans.

text: He does not even use the term barbarian, probably because the Hellenes had not yet been marked off from the rest of the world by one distinctive appellation.

text: It appears therefore that the several Hellenic communities, comprising not only those who first acquired the name, city by city, as they came to understand each other, but also those who assumed it afterwards as the name of the whole people, were before the Trojan war prevented by their want of strength and the absence of mutual intercourse from displaying any collective action.

text: He made himself master of what is now called the Hellenic sea, and ruled over the Cyclades, into most of which he sent the first colonies, expelling the Carians and appointing his own sons governors; and thus did his best to put down piracy in those waters, a necessary step to secure the revenues for his own use.

text: For in early times the Hellenes and the barbarians of the coast and islands, as communication by sea became more common, were tempted to turn pirates, under the conduct of their most powerful men; the motives being to serve their own cupidity and to support the needy.

For in early times the Hellenes and the barbarians of the coast and islands, as
communication by sea became more common, were tempted to turn pirates, under the
conduct of their most powerful men; the motives being to serve their own cupidity and to
support the needy.

text: They would fall upon a town unprotected by walls, and consisting of a mere collection of villages, and would plunder it; indeed, this came to be the main source of their livelihood, no disgrace being yet attached to such an achievement, but even some glory.

text: So the Epidamnians went to Corinth and delivered over the colony in obedience to the commands of the oracle.
text_raw:
So the Epidamnians went to Corinth and delivered over the
colony in obedience to the commands of the oracle.

text: They showed that their founder came from Corinth, and revealed the answer of the god; and they begged them not to allow them to perish, but to assist them.
text_raw:
They showed that their founder came
from Corinth, and revealed the answer of the god; and they begged them not to allow them

text: This the Corinthians consented to do.
text_raw: This the Corinthians consented to do.

text: Believing the colony to belong as much to themselves as to the Corcyraeans, they felt it to be a kind of duty to undertake their protection.
text_raw:
Believing the colony to
belong as much to themselves as to the Corcyraeans, they felt it to be a kind of duty to
undertake their protection.

text: Besides, they hated the Corcyraeans for their contempt of the mother country.
text_raw:
Besides, they hated the Corcyraeans for their contempt of the
mother country.

text: Instead of meeting with the usual honours accorded to the parent city by every other colony at public assemblies, such as precedence at sacrifices, Corinth found herself treated with contempt by a power which in point of wealth could stand comparison with any even of the richest communities in Hellas, which possessed great military strength, and which sometimes could not repress a pride in the high naval position of an island whose nautical renown dated from the days of its old inhabitants, the Phaeacians.
text_raw:
Instead of meeting with the usual honours accorded to the parent city by
every other colony at public assemblies, such as precedence at sacrifices, Corinth found
herself treated with contempt by a power which in point of wealth could stand comparison
with any even of the richest communities in Hellas, which possessed great military
strength, and which sometimes could not repress a pride in the high naval position of an
island whose nautical renown dated from the days of its old inhabitants, the Phaeacians.

text: This was one reason of the care that they lavished on their fleet, which became very efficient; indeed they began the war with a force of a hundred and twenty galleys.
text_raw:
This was one reason of the care that they lavished on their fleet, which became very

text: All these grievances made Corinth eager to send the promised aid to Epidamnus.
text_raw: All these grievances made Corinth eager to send the promised aid to Epidamnus.

text: Advertisement was made for volunteer settlers, and a force of Ambraciots, Leucadians, and Corinthians was dispatched.
text_raw:
Advertisement was made for volunteer settlers, and a force of Ambraciots, Leucadians,

text: They marched by land to Apollonia, a Corinthian colony, the route by sea being avoided from fear of Corcyraean interruption.
text_raw:
They marched by land to Apollonia, a Corinthian colony,
the route by sea being avoided from fear of Corcyraean interruption.

text: When the Corcyraeans heard of the arrival of the settlers and troops in Epidamnus, and the surrender
text_raw:
When the

text_raw: of the colony to Corinth, they took fire.

text: Instantly putting to sea with five-and-twenty ships, which were quickly followed by others, they insolently commanded the Epidamnians to receive back the banished nobles—(it must be premised that the Epidamnian exiles had come to Corcyra and, pointing to the sepulchres of their ancestors, had appealed to their kindred to restore them)—and to dismiss the Corinthian garrison and settlers.
text_raw:
Instantly putting to sea with five-and-twenty ships,

text: But to all this the Epidamnians turned a deaf ear.
text_raw:
But to all

text: Upon this the Corcyraeans commenced operations against them with a fleet of forty sail.
text_raw:
Upon this the Corcyraeans commenced operations

text_raw:
They took with them the exiles, with a view to their

text: Sitting down before the city, they issued a proclamation to the effect that any of the natives that chose, and the foreigners, might depart unharmed, with the alternative of being treated as enemies.
text_raw:
Sitting down before the city, they

text: On their refusal the Corcyraeans proceeded to besiege the city, which stands on an isthmus; and the Corinthians, receiving intelligence of the investment of Epidamnus, got together an armament and proclaimed a colony to Epidamnus, perfect political equality being guaranteed to all who chose to go.
text_raw:
On their refusal
the Corcyraeans proceeded to besiege the city, which stands on an isthmus; and the
Corinthians, receiving intelligence of the investment of Epidamnus, got together an
armament and proclaimed a colony to Epidamnus, perfect political equality being
guaranteed to all who chose to go.

text: Any who were not prepared to sail at once might, by paying down the sum of fifty Corinthian drachmae, have a share in the colony without leaving Corinth.
text_raw:
Any who were not prepared to sail at once might, by
paying down the sum of fifty Corinthian drachmae, have a share in the colony without

text: Great numbers took advantage of this proclamation, some being ready to start directly, others paying the requisite forfeit.
text_raw:
Great numbers took advantage of this proclamation, some being ready to
start directly, others paying the requisite forfeit.

text: In case of their passage being disputed by the Corcyraeans, several cities were asked to lend them a convoy.
text_raw:
In case of their passage being disputed by

text: Megara prepared to accompany them with eight ships, Pale in Cephallonia with four;
text_raw:
Megara prepared to
accompany them with eight ships, Pale in Cephallonia with four;

text: Epidaurus furnished five, Hermione one, Troezen two, Leucas ten, and Ambracia eight.
text_raw:
Epidaurus furnished five,

text: The Thebans and Phliasians were asked for money, the Eleans for hulls as well; while Corinth herself furnished thirty ships and three thousand heavy infantry.
text_raw:
The Thebans and Phliasians
were asked for money, the Eleans for hulls as well; while Corinth herself furnished thirty

text: When the Corcyraeans heard of their preparations they came to Corinth with envoys from Lacedaemon and Sicyon, whom they persuaded to accompany them, and bade her recall the garrison and settlers, as she had nothing to do with Epidamnus.

When the Corcyraeans heard of their preparations they came to Corinth with envoys

text: If, however, she had any claims to make, they were willing to submit the matter to the arbitration of such of the cities in Peloponnese as should be chosen by mutual agreement, and that the colony should remain with the city to whom the arbitrators might assign it.
text_raw:
If, however, she
had any claims to make, they were willing to submit the matter to the arbitration of such

text: They were also willing to refer the matter to the oracle at Delphi.
text_raw:
They were also
willing to refer the matter to the oracle at Delphi.

text: If, in defiance of their protestations, war was appealed to, they should be themselves compelled by this violence to seek friends in quarters where they had no desire to seek them, and to make even old ties give way to the necessity of assistance.
text_raw:
If, in defiance of their protestations, war
was appealed to, they should be themselves compelled by this violence to seek friends in

text: The answer they got from Corinth was that, if they would withdraw their fleet and the barbarians from Epidamnus, negotiation might be possible; but, while the town was still being besieged, going before arbitrators was out of the question.
text_raw:
The answer they got from Corinth was that, if they would
withdraw their fleet and the barbarians from Epidamnus, negotiation might be possible;

text: The Corcyraeans retorted that if Corinth would withdraw her troops from Epidamnus they would withdraw theirs, or they were ready to let both parties remain in statu quo, an armistice being concluded till judgment could be given.
text_raw:
The Corcyraeans retorted that if Corinth would withdraw her troops from

text: Turning a deaf ear to all these proposals, when their ships were manned and their allies had come in, the Corinthians sent a herald before them to declare war and, getting under way with seventy-five ships and two thousand heavy infantry, sailed for Epidamnus to give battle to the Corcyraeans.
text_raw:
Turning a deaf ear to all these proposals, when their ships were manned and their allies
had come in, the Corinthians sent a herald before them to declare war and, getting under
way with seventy-five ships and two thousand heavy infantry, sailed for Epidamnus to
give battle to the Corcyraeans.

text: The fleet was under the command of Aristeus, son of Pellichas, Callicrates, son of Callias, and Timanor, son of Timanthes; the troops under that of Archetimus, son of Eurytimus, and Isarchidas, son of Isarchus.
text_raw:
The fleet was under the command of Aristeus, son of
Pellichas, Callicrates, son of Callias, and Timanor, son of Timanthes; the troops under that

text: When they had reached Actium in the territory of Anactorium, at the mouth of the mouth of the Gulf of Ambracia,
text_raw:
When they had reached
Actium in the territory of Anactorium, at the mouth of the mouth of the Gulf of Ambracia,

text: where the temple of Apollo stands, the Corcyraeans sent on a herald in a light boat to warn them not to sail against them.
text_raw:
where the temple of Apollo stands, the Corcyraeans sent on a herald in a light boat to warn

text: Meanwhile they proceeded to man their ships, all of which had been equipped for action, the old vessels being undergirded to make them seaworthy.
text_raw:
Meanwhile they proceeded to man their ships, all of which
had been equipped for action, the old vessels being undergirded to make them seaworthy.

text: On the return of the herald without any peaceful answer from the Corinthians, their ships being now manned, they put out to sea to meet the enemy with a fleet of eighty sail (forty were engaged in the siege of Epidamnus), formed line, and went into action, and gained a decisive victory, and destroyed fifteen of the Corinthian vessels.
text_raw:
On the return of the herald without any peaceful answer from the Corinthians, their ships
being now manned, they put out to sea to meet the enemy with a fleet of eighty sail (forty
were engaged in the siege of Epidamnus), formed line, and went into action, and gained a
decisive victory, and destroyed fifteen of the Corinthian vessels.

text: The same day had seen Epidamnus compelled by its besiegers to capitulate; the conditions being that the foreigners should be sold, and the Corinthians kept as prisoners of war, till their fate should be otherwise decided.
text_raw:
The same day had seen
Epidamnus compelled by its besiegers to capitulate; the conditions being that the
foreigners should be sold, and the Corinthians kept as prisoners of war, till their fate
should be otherwise decided.

text: After the engagement the Corcyraeans set up a trophy on Leukimme, a headland of Corcyra, and slew all their captives except the Corinthians, whom they kept as prisoners of war.
text_raw:
After the engagement the Corcyraeans set up a trophy on Leukimme, a headland of
Corcyra, and slew all their captives except the Corinthians, whom they kept as prisoners
of war.

text: Defeated at sea, the Corinthians and their allies repaired home, and left the Corcyraeans masters of all the sea about those parts.
text_raw:
Defeated at sea, the Corinthians and their allies repaired home, and left the
Corcyraeans masters of all the sea about those parts.

text: Sailing to Leucas, a Corinthian colony, they ravaged their territory, and burnt Cyllene, the harbour of the Eleans, because they had furnished ships and money to Corinth.
text_raw:
Sailing to Leucas, a Corinthian
colony, they ravaged their territory, and burnt Cyllene, the harbour of the Eleans, because
they had furnished ships and money to Corinth.

text: For almost the whole of the period that followed the battle they remained masters of the sea, and the allies of Corinth were harassed by Corcyraean cruisers.
text_raw:
For almost the whole of the period that
followed the battle they remained masters of the sea, and the allies of Corinth were
harassed by Corcyraean cruisers.

text: At last Corinth, roused by the sufferings of her allies, sent out ships and troops in the fall of the summer, who formed an encampment at Actium and about Chimerium, in Thesprotis, for the protection of Leucas and the rest of the friendly cities.
text_raw:
At last Corinth, roused by the sufferings of her allies,
sent out ships and troops in the fall of the summer, who formed an encampment at Actium
and about Chimerium, in Thesprotis, for the protection of Leucas and the rest of the
friendly cities.

text: The Corcyraeans on their part formed a similar station on Leukimme.
text_raw: The Corcyraeans on their part formed a similar station on Leukimme.

text: Neither party made any movement, but they remained confronting each other till the end of the summer, and winter was at hand before either of them returned home.
text_raw:
Neither party made any movement, but they remained confronting each other till the end
of the summer, and winter was at hand before either of them returned home.

text: Corinth, exasperated by the war with the Corcyraeans, spent the whole of the year after the engagement and that succeeding it in building ships, and in straining every nerve to form an efficient fleet; rowers being drawn from Peloponnese and the rest of Hellas by the inducement of large bounties.
text_raw:
Corinth, exasperated by the war with the Corcyraeans, spent the whole of the year after
the engagement and that succeeding it in building ships, and in straining every nerve to
form an efficient fleet; rowers being drawn from Peloponnese and the rest of Hellas by the
inducement of large bounties.

text: The Corcyraeans, alarmed at the news of their preparations, being without a single ally in Hellas (for they had not enrolled themselves either in the Athenian or in the Lacedaemonian confederacy), decided to repair to Athens in order to enter into alliance and to endeavour to procure support from her.
text_raw:
The Corcyraeans, alarmed at the news of their preparations,
being without a single ally in Hellas (for they had not enrolled themselves either in the
Athenian or in the Lacedaemonian confederacy), decided to repair to Athens in order to
enter into alliance and to endeavour to procure support from her.

text: Corinth also, hearing of their intentions, sent an embassy to Athens to prevent the Corcyraean navy being joined by the Athenian, and her prospect of ordering the war according to her wishes being thus impeded.
text_raw:
Corinth also, hearing of
their intentions, sent an embassy to Athens to prevent the Corcyraean navy being joined
by the Athenian, and her prospect of ordering the war according to her wishes being thus
impeded.

text: An assembly was convoked, and the rival advocates appeared: the Corcyraeans spoke as follows: “Athenians! when a people that have not rendered any important service or support to their neighbours in times past, for which they might claim to be repaid, appear before them as we now appear before you to solicit their assistance, they may fairly be required to satisfy certain preliminary conditions.
text_raw:
An assembly was convoked, and the rival advocates appeared: the Corcyraeans
spoke as follows:
“Athenians! when a people that have not rendered any important service or support to
their neighbours in times past, for which they might claim to be repaid, appear before
them as we now appear before you to solicit their assistance, they may fairly be required
to satisfy certain preliminary conditions.

text: They should show, first, that it is expedient or at least safe to grant their request; next, that they will retain a lasting sense of the kindness.
text_raw:
They should show, first, that it is expedient or at
least safe to grant their request; next, that they will retain a lasting sense of the kindness.

text: But if they cannot clearly establish any of these points, they must not be annoyed if they meet with a rebuff.
text_raw:
But if they cannot clearly establish any of these points, they must not be annoyed if they
meet with a rebuff.

text: Now the Corcyraeans believe that with their petition for assistance they can also give you a satisfactory answer on these points, and they have therefore dispatched us hither.
text_raw:
Now the Corcyraeans believe that with their petition for assistance
they can also give you a satisfactory answer on these points, and they have therefore
dispatched us hither.

text: It has so happened that our policy as regards you with respect to this
text_raw: It has so happened that our policy as regards you with respect to this

text: request, turns out to be inconsistent, and as regards our interests, to be at the present crisis inexpedient.
text_raw:
request, turns out to be inconsistent, and as regards our interests, to be at the present crisis
inexpedient.

text: We say inconsistent, because a power which has never in the whole of her past history been willing to ally herself with any of her neighbours, is now found asking them to ally themselves with her.
text_raw:
We say inconsistent, because a power which has never in the whole of her
past history been willing to ally herself with any of her neighbours, is now found asking
them to ally themselves with her.

text: And we say inexpedient, because in our present war with Corinth it has left us in a position of entire isolation, and what once seemed the wise precaution of refusing to involve ourselves in alliances with other powers, lest we should also involve ourselves in risks of their choosing, has now proved to be folly and weakness.
text_raw:
And we say inexpedient, because in our present war with
Corinth it has left us in a position of entire isolation, and what once seemed the wise
precaution of refusing to involve ourselves in alliances with other powers, lest we should
also involve ourselves in risks of their choosing, has now proved to be folly and weakness.

text: It is true that in the late naval engagement we drove back the Corinthians from our shores single-handed.
text_raw:
It is true that in the late naval engagement we drove back the Corinthians from our shores
single-handed.

text: But they have now got together a still larger armament from Peloponnese and the rest of Hellas; and we, seeing our utter inability to cope with them without foreign aid, and the magnitude of the danger which subjection to them implies, find it necessary to ask help from you and from every other power.
text_raw:
But they have now got together a still larger armament from Peloponnese
and the rest of Hellas; and we, seeing our utter inability to cope with them without foreign
aid, and the magnitude of the danger which subjection to them implies, find it necessary to
ask help from you and from every other power.

text: And we hope to be excused if we forswear our old principle of complete political isolation, a principle which was not adopted with any sinister intention, but was rather the consequence of an error in judgment. “Now there are many reasons why in the event of your compliance you will congratulate yourselves on this request having been made to you.
text_raw:
And we hope to be excused if we forswear
our old principle of complete political isolation, a principle which was not adopted with
any sinister intention, but was rather the consequence of an error in judgment.
“Now there are many reasons why in the event of your compliance you will congratulate
yourselves on this request having been made to you.

text: First, because your assistance will be rendered to a power which, herself inoffensive, is a victim to the injustice of others.
text_raw:
First, because your assistance will be
rendered to a power which, herself inoffensive, is a victim to the injustice of others.

text: Secondly, because all that we most value is at stake in the present contest, and your welcome of us under these circumstances will be a proof of goodwill which will ever keep alive the gratitude you will lay up in our hearts.
text_raw:
Secondly, because all that we most value is at stake in the present contest, and your
welcome of us under these circumstances will be a proof of goodwill which will ever keep
alive the gratitude you will lay up in our hearts.

text: Thirdly, yourselves excepted, we are the greatest naval power in Hellas.
text_raw:
Thirdly, yourselves excepted, we are the
greatest naval power in Hellas.

text: Moreover, can you conceive a stroke of good fortune more rare in itself, or more disheartening to your enemies, than that the power whose adhesion you would have valued above much material and moral strength should present herself self-invited, should deliver herself into your hands without danger and without expense, and should lastly put you in the way of gaining a high character in the eyes of the world, the gratitude of those whom you shall assist, and a great accession of strength for yourselves?
text_raw:
Moreover, can you conceive a stroke of good fortune more
rare in itself, or more disheartening to your enemies, than that the power whose adhesion
you would have valued above much material and moral strength should present herself
self-invited, should deliver herself into your hands without danger and without expense,
and should lastly put you in the way of gaining a high character in the eyes of the world,
the gratitude of those whom you shall assist, and a great accession of strength for
yourselves?

text: You may search all history without finding many instances of a people gaining all these advantages at once, or many instances of a power that comes in quest of assistance being in a position to give to the people whose alliance she solicits as much safety and honour as she will receive.
text_raw:
You may search all history without finding many instances of a people
gaining all these advantages at once, or many instances of a power that comes in quest of
assistance being in a position to give to the people whose alliance she solicits as much
safety and honour as she will receive.

text: But it will be urged that it is only in the case of a war that we shall be found useful.
text_raw:
But it will be urged that it is only in the case of a
war that we shall be found useful.

text: To this we answer that if any of you imagine that that war is far off, he is grievously mistaken, and is blind to the fact that Lacedaemon regards you with jealousy and desires war, and that Corinth is powerful there—the same, remember, that is your enemy, and is even now trying to subdue us as a preliminary to attacking you.
text_raw:
To this we answer that if any of you imagine that that
war is far off, he is grievously mistaken, and is blind to the fact that Lacedaemon regards
you with jealousy and desires war, and that Corinth is powerful there—the same,
remember, that is your enemy, and is even now trying to subdue us as a preliminary to
attacking you.

text: And this she does to prevent our becoming united by a common enmity, and her having us both on her hands, and also to ensure getting the start of you in one of two ways, either by crippling our power or by making its strength her own.
text_raw:

and her having us both on her hands, and also to ensure getting the start of you in one of

text: Now it is our policy to be beforehand with her—that is, for Corcyra to make an offer of alliance and for you to accept it; in fact, we ought to form plans against her instead of waiting to defeat the plans she forms against us. “If she asserts that for you to receive a colony of hers into alliance is not right, let her know that every colony that is well treated honours its parent state, but becomes estranged from it by injustice.
text_raw:
Now it is our
policy to be beforehand with her—that is, for Corcyra to make an offer of alliance and for
you to accept it; in fact, we ought to form plans against her instead of waiting to defeat the

text: For colonists are not sent forth on the understanding that they are to be the slaves of those that remain behind, but that they are to be their equals.
text_raw:
For colonists are not sent forth on the understanding that they are to

text: And that
text_raw: And that

text: Corinth was injuring us is clear.
text_raw: Corinth was injuring us is clear.

text: Invited to refer the dispute about Epidamnus to arbitration, they chose to prosecute their complaints war rather than by a fair trial.
text_raw:
Invited to refer the dispute about Epidamnus to
arbitration, they chose to prosecute their complaints war rather than by a fair trial.

text: And let their conduct towards us who are their kindred be a warning to you not to be misled by their deceit, nor to yield to their direct requests; concessions to adversaries only end in self-reproach, and the more strictly they are avoided the greater will be the chance of security. “If it be urged that your reception of us will be a breach of the treaty existing between you and Lacedaemon, the answer is that we are a neutral state, and that one of the express provisions of that treaty is that it shall be competent for any Hellenic state that is neutral to join whichever side it pleases.
text_raw:
And let
their conduct towards us who are their kindred be a warning to you not to be misled by
their deceit, nor to yield to their direct requests; concessions to adversaries only end in
self-reproach, and the more strictly they are avoided the greater will be the chance of

text: And it is intolerable for Corinth to be allowed to obtain men for her navy not only from her allies, but also from the rest of Hellas, no small number being furnished by your own subjects; while we are to be excluded both from the alliance left open to us by treaty, and from any assistance that we might get from other quarters, and you are to be accused of political immorality if you comply with our request.
text_raw:
And it is intolerable for Corinth to be allowed to obtain men
for her navy not only from her allies, but also from the rest of Hellas, no small number
being furnished by your own subjects; while we are to be excluded both from the alliance
left open to us by treaty, and from any assistance that we might get from other quarters,

text: On the other hand, we shall have much greater cause to complain of you, if you do not comply with it; if we, who are in peril and are no enemies of yours, meet with a repulse at your hands, while Corinth, who is the aggressor and your enemy, not only meets with no hindrance from you, but is even allowed to draw material for war from your dependencies.
text_raw:
On the
other hand, we shall have much greater cause to complain of you, if you do not comply
with it; if we, who are in peril and are no enemies of yours, meet with a repulse at your
hands, while Corinth, who is the aggressor and your enemy, not only meets with no

text: This ought not to be, but you should either forbid her enlisting men in your dominions, or you should lend us too what help you may think advisable. “But your real policy is to afford us avowed countenance and support.
text_raw:

text: The advantages of this course, as we premised in the beginning of our speech, are many.

The advantages of
this course, as we premised in the beginning of our speech, are many.

text: We mention one that is perhaps the chief.
text_raw:
We mention one that
is perhaps the chief.

text: Could there be a clearer guarantee of our good faith than is offered by the fact that the power which is at enmity with you is also at enmity with us, and that that power is fully able to punish defection?
text_raw:
Could there be a clearer guarantee of our good faith than is offered by

text: And there is a wide difference between declining the alliance of an inland and of a maritime power.
text_raw:
And there is a wide difference between declining

text: For your first endeavour should be to prevent, if possible, the existence of any naval power except your own; failing this, to secure the friendship of the strongest that does exist.
text_raw:
For your first endeavour should be to
prevent, if possible, the existence of any naval power except your own; failing this, to
