text: And if any of you believe that what we urge is expedient, but fear to act upon this belief, lest it should lead to a breach of the treaty, you must remember that on the one hand, whatever your fears, your strength will be formidable to your antagonists; on the other, whatever the confidence you derive from refusing to receive us, your weakness will have no terrors for a strong enemy.
text_raw:
And if any of you believe that what
we urge is expedient, but fear to act upon this belief, lest it should lead to a breach of the
treaty, you must remember that on the one hand, whatever your fears, your strength will be
formidable to your antagonists; on the other, whatever the confidence you derive from
refusing to receive us, your weakness will have no terrors for a strong enemy.

text: You must also remember that your decision is for Athens no less than Corcyra, and that you are not making the best provision for her interests, if at a time when you are anxiously scanning the horizon that you may be in readiness for the breaking out of the war which is all but upon you, you hesitate to attach to your side a place whose adhesion or estrangement is alike pregnant with the most vital consequences.
text_raw:
You must
also remember that your decision is for Athens no less than Corcyra, and that you are not
making the best provision for her interests, if at a time when you are anxiously scanning
the horizon that you may be in readiness for the breaking out of the war which is all but
upon you, you hesitate to attach to your side a place whose adhesion or estrangement is
alike pregnant with the most vital consequences.

text: For it lies conveniently for the coast- navigation in the direction of Italy and Sicily, being able to bar the passage of naval reinforcements from thence to Peloponnese, and from Peloponnese thither; and it is in other respects a most desirable station.
text_raw:
For it lies conveniently for the coast-
navigation in the direction of Italy and Sicily, being able to bar the passage of naval
reinforcements from thence to Peloponnese, and from Peloponnese thither; and it is in
other respects a most desirable station.

text: To sum up as shortly as possible, embracing both general and particular considerations, let this show you the folly of sacrificing us.
text_raw:
To sum up as shortly as possible, embracing both
general and particular considerations, let this show you the folly of sacrificing us.

text: Remember that there are but three considerable naval powers in Hellas—Athens, Corcyra, and Corinth—and that if you allow two of these three to become one, and Corinth to secure us for herself, you will have to hold the sea against the united fleets of Corcyra and
text_raw:
Remember that there are but three considerable naval powers in Hellas—Athens, Corcyra,
and Corinth—and that if you allow two of these three to become one, and Corinth to
secure us for herself, you will have to hold the sea against the united fleets of Corcyra and

text: Peloponnese.
text_raw: Peloponnese.

text: But if you receive us, you will have our ships to reinforce you in the struggle.” Such were the words of the Corcyraeans.
text_raw:
But if you receive us, you will have our ships to reinforce you in the
struggle.”
Such were the words of the Corcyraeans.

text: After they had finished, the Corinthians spoke as follows: “These Corcyraeans in the speech we have just heard do not confine themselves to the question of their reception into your alliance.
text_raw:
After they had finished, the Corinthians spoke
as follows:
“These Corcyraeans in the speech we have just heard do not confine themselves to the
question of their reception into your alliance.

text: They also talk of our being guilty of injustice, and their being the victims of an unjustifiable war.
text_raw:
They also talk of our being guilty of
injustice, and their being the victims of an unjustifiable war.

text: It becomes necessary for us to touch upon both these points before we proceed to the rest of what we have to say, that you may have a more correct idea of the grounds of our claim, and have good cause to reject their petition.
text_raw:
It becomes necessary for us to
touch upon both these points before we proceed to the rest of what we have to say, that
you may have a more correct idea of the grounds of our claim, and have good cause to
reject their petition.

text: According to them, their old policy of refusing all offers of alliance was a policy of moderation.
text_raw:
According to them, their old policy of refusing all offers of alliance
was a policy of moderation.

text: It was in fact adopted for bad ends, not for good; indeed their conduct is such as to make them by no means desirous of having allies present to witness it, or of having the shame of asking their concurrence.
text_raw:
It was in fact adopted for bad ends, not for good; indeed their
conduct is such as to make them by no means desirous of having allies present to witness
it, or of having the shame of asking their concurrence.

text: Besides, their geographical situation makes them independent of others, and consequently the decision in cases where they injure any lies not with judges appointed by mutual agreement, but with themselves, because, while they seldom make voyages to their neighbours, they are constantly being visited by foreign vessels which are compelled to put in to Corcyra.
text_raw:
Besides, their geographical
situation makes them independent of others, and consequently the decision in cases where
they injure any lies not with judges appointed by mutual agreement, but with themselves,
because, while they seldom make voyages to their neighbours, they are constantly being
visited by foreign vessels which are compelled to put in to Corcyra.

text: In short, the object that they propose to themselves, in their specious policy of complete isolation, is not to avoid sharing in the crimes of others, but to secure monopoly of crime to themselves—the licence of outrage wherever they can compel, of fraud wherever they can elude, and the enjoyment of their gains without shame.
text_raw:
In short, the object
that they propose to themselves, in their specious policy of complete isolation, is not to
avoid sharing in the crimes of others, but to secure monopoly of crime to themselves—the
licence of outrage wherever they can compel, of fraud wherever they can elude, and the
enjoyment of their gains without shame.

text: And yet if they were the honest men they pretend to be, the less hold that others had upon them, the stronger would be the light in which they might have put their honesty by giving and taking what was just. “But such has not been their conduct either towards others or towards us.
text_raw:
And yet if they were the honest men they pretend
to be, the less hold that others had upon them, the stronger would be the light in which
they might have put their honesty by giving and taking what was just.
“But such has not been their conduct either towards others or towards us.

text: The attitude of our colony towards us has always been one of estrangement and is now one of hostility; for, say they: ‘We were not sent out to be ill-treated.’ We rejoin that we did not found the colony to be insulted by them, but to be their head and to be regarded with a proper respect.
text_raw:
The attitude of
our colony towards us has always been one of estrangement and is now one of hostility;
for, say they: ‘We were not sent out to be ill-treated.’ We rejoin that we did not found the
colony to be insulted by them, but to be their head and to be regarded with a proper
respect.

text: At any rate our other colonies honour us, and we are much beloved by our colonists; and clearly, if the majority are satisfied with us, these can have no good reason for a dissatisfaction in which they stand alone, and we are not acting improperly in making war against them, nor are we making war against them without having received signal provocation.
text_raw:
At any rate our other colonies honour us, and we are much beloved by our
colonists; and clearly, if the majority are satisfied with us, these can have no good reason
for a dissatisfaction in which they stand alone, and we are not acting improperly in making
war against them, nor are we making war against them without having received signal
provocation.

text: Besides, if we were in the wrong, it would be honourable in them to give way to our wishes, and disgraceful for us to trample on their moderation; but in the pride and licence of wealth they have sinned again and again against us, and never more deeply than when Epidamnus, our dependency, which they took no steps to claim in its distress upon our coming to relieve it, was by them seized, and is now held by force of arms. “As to their allegation that they wished the question to be first submitted to arbitration, it is obvious that a challenge coming from the party who is safe in a commanding position cannot gain the credit due only to him who, before appealing to arms, in deeds as well as words, places himself on a level with his adversary.
text_raw:
Besides, if we were in the wrong, it would be honourable in them to give way
to our wishes, and disgraceful for us to trample on their moderation; but in the pride and
licence of wealth they have sinned again and again against us, and never more deeply than
when Epidamnus, our dependency, which they took no steps to claim in its distress upon
our coming to relieve it, was by them seized, and is now held by force of arms.
“As to their allegation that they wished the question to be first submitted to arbitration, it
is obvious that a challenge coming from the party who is safe in a commanding position
cannot gain the credit due only to him who, before appealing to arms, in deeds as well as
words, places himself on a level with his adversary.

text: In their case, it was not before they laid siege to the place, but after they at length understood that we should not tamely suffer it, that they thought of the specious word arbitration.
text_raw:
In their case, it was not before they
laid siege to the place, but after they at length understood that we should not tamely suffer
it, that they thought of the specious word arbitration.

text: And not satisfied with their own misconduct there, they appear here now requiring you to join with them not in alliance but
text_raw:
And not satisfied with their own
misconduct there, they appear here now requiring you to join with them not in alliance but

text: in crime, and to receive them in spite of their being at enmity with us.
text_raw: in crime, and to receive them in spite of their being at enmity with us.

text: But it was when they stood firmest that they should have made overtures to you, and not at a time when we have been wronged and they are in peril; nor yet at a time when you will be admitting to a share in your protection those who never admitted you to a share in their power, and will be incurring an equal amount of blame from us with those in whose offences you had no hand.
text_raw:
But it was when
they stood firmest that they should have made overtures to you, and not at a time when we
have been wronged and they are in peril; nor yet at a time when you will be admitting to a
share in your protection those who never admitted you to a share in their power, and will
be incurring an equal amount of blame from us with those in whose offences you had no
hand.

text: No, they should have shared their power with you before they asked you to share your fortunes with them. “So then the reality of the grievances we come to complain of, and the violence and rapacity of our opponents, have both been proved.
text_raw:
No, they should have shared their power with you before they asked you to share
your fortunes with them.
“So then the reality of the grievances we come to complain of, and the violence and
rapacity of our opponents, have both been proved.

text: But that you cannot equitably receive them, this you have still to learn.
text_raw:
But that you cannot equitably receive
them, this you have still to learn.

text: It may be true that one of the provisions of the treaty is that it shall be competent for any state, whose name was not down on the list, to join whichever side it pleases.
text_raw:
It may be true that one of the provisions of the treaty is
that it shall be competent for any state, whose name was not down on the list, to join
whichever side it pleases.

text: But this agreement is not meant for those whose object in joining is the injury of other powers, but for those whose need of support does not arise from the fact of defection, and whose adhesion will not bring to the power that is mad enough to receive them war instead of peace; which will be the case with you, if you refuse to listen to us.
text_raw:
But this agreement is not meant for those whose object in
joining is the injury of other powers, but for those whose need of support does not arise
from the fact of defection, and whose adhesion will not bring to the power that is mad
enough to receive them war instead of peace; which will be the case with you, if you
refuse to listen to us.

text: For you cannot become their auxiliary and remain our friend; if you join in their attack, you must share the punishment which the defenders inflict on them.
text_raw:
For you cannot become their auxiliary and remain our friend; if you
join in their attack, you must share the punishment which the defenders inflict on them.

text: And yet you have the best possible right to be neutral, or, failing this, you should on the contrary join us against them.
text_raw:
And yet you have the best possible right to be neutral, or, failing this, you should on the
contrary join us against them.

text: Corinth is at least in treaty with you; with Corcyra you were never even in truce.
text_raw:
Corinth is at least in treaty with you; with Corcyra you were
never even in truce.

text: But do not lay down the principle that defection is to be patronized.
text_raw: But do not lay down the principle that defection is to be patronized.

text: Did we on the defection of the Samians record our vote against you, when the rest of the Peloponnesian powers were equally divided on the question whether they should assist them?
text_raw:
Did we on the defection of the Samians record our vote against you, when the rest of the
Peloponnesian powers were equally divided on the question whether they should assist
them?

text: No, we told them to their face that every power has a right to punish its own allies.
text_raw: No, we told them to their face that every power has a right to punish its own allies.

text: Why, if you make it your policy to receive and assist all offenders, you will find that just as many of your dependencies will come over to us, and the principle that you establish will press less heavily on us than on yourselves. “This then is what Hellenic law entitles us to demand as a right.
text_raw:
Why, if you make it your policy to receive and assist all offenders, you will find that just
as many of your dependencies will come over to us, and the principle that you establish
will press less heavily on us than on yourselves.
“This then is what Hellenic law entitles us to demand as a right.

text: But we have also advice to offer and claims on your gratitude, which, since there is no danger of our injuring you, as we are not enemies, and since our friendship does not amount to very frequent intercourse, we say ought to be liquidated at the present juncture.
text_raw:
But we have also advice
to offer and claims on your gratitude, which, since there is no danger of our injuring you,
as we are not enemies, and since our friendship does not amount to very frequent
intercourse, we say ought to be liquidated at the present juncture.

text: When you were in want of ships of war for the war against the Aeginetans, before the Persian invasion, Corinth supplied you with twenty vessels.
text_raw:
When you were in want
of ships of war for the war against the Aeginetans, before the Persian invasion, Corinth
supplied you with twenty vessels.

text: That good turn, and the line we took on the Samian question, when we were the cause of the Peloponnesians refusing to assist them, enabled you to conquer Aegina and to punish Samos.
text_raw:
That good turn, and the line we took on the Samian
question, when we were the cause of the Peloponnesians refusing to assist them, enabled
you to conquer Aegina and to punish Samos.

text: And we acted thus at crises when, if ever, men are wont in their efforts against their enemies to forget everything for the sake of victory, regarding him who assists them then as a friend, even if thus far he has been a foe, and him who opposes them then as a foe, even if he has thus far been a friend; indeed they allow their real interests to suffer from their absorbing preoccupation in the struggle. “Weigh well these considerations, and let your youth learn what they are from their elders, and let them determine to do unto us as we have done unto you.
text_raw:
And we acted thus at crises when, if ever,
men are wont in their efforts against their enemies to forget everything for the sake of
victory, regarding him who assists them then as a friend, even if thus far he has been a foe,
and him who opposes them then as a foe, even if he has thus far been a friend; indeed they
allow their real interests to suffer from their absorbing preoccupation in the struggle.
“Weigh well these considerations, and let your youth learn what they are from their
elders, and let them determine to do unto us as we have done unto you.

text: And let them not acknowledge the justice of what we say, but dispute its wisdom in the contingency of war.
text_raw:
And let them not
acknowledge the justice of what we say, but dispute its wisdom in the contingency of war.

text: Not only is the straightest path generally speaking the wisest; but the coming of the war, which the Corcyraeans have used as a bugbear to persuade you to do wrong, is still
text_raw:
Not only is the straightest path generally speaking the wisest; but the coming of the war,
which the Corcyraeans have used as a bugbear to persuade you to do wrong, is still

text: uncertain, and it is not worth while to be carried away by it into gaining the instant and declared enmity of Corinth.
text_raw:
uncertain, and it is not worth while to be carried away by it into gaining the instant and
declared enmity of Corinth.

text: It were, rather, wise to try and counteract the unfavourable impression which your conduct to Megara has created.
text_raw:
It were, rather, wise to try and counteract the unfavourable
impression which your conduct to Megara has created.

text: For kindness opportunely shown has a greater power of removing old grievances than the facts of the case may warrant.
text_raw:
For kindness opportunely shown
has a greater power of removing old grievances than the facts of the case may warrant.

text: And do not be seduced by the prospect of a great naval alliance.
text_raw: And do not be seduced by the prospect of a great naval alliance.

text: Abstinence from all injustice to other first-rate powers is a greater tower of strength than anything that can be gained by the sacrifice of permanent tranquillity for an apparent temporary advantage.
text_raw:
Abstinence from all
injustice to other first-rate powers is a greater tower of strength than anything that can be
gained by the sacrifice of permanent tranquillity for an apparent temporary advantage.

text: It is now our turn to benefit by the principle that we laid down at Lacedaemon, that every power has a right to punish her own allies.
text_raw:
It is
now our turn to benefit by the principle that we laid down at Lacedaemon, that every
power has a right to punish her own allies.

text: We now claim to receive the same from you, and protest against your rewarding us for benefiting you by our vote by injuring us by yours.
text_raw:
We now claim to receive the same from you,
and protest against your rewarding us for benefiting you by our vote by injuring us by
yours.

text: On the contrary, return us like for like, remembering that this is that very crisis in which he who lends aid is most a friend, and he who opposes is most a foe.
text_raw:
On the contrary, return us like for like, remembering that this is that very crisis in
which he who lends aid is most a friend, and he who opposes is most a foe.

text: And for these Corcyraeans—neither receive them into alliance in our despite, nor be their abettors in crime.
text_raw:
And for these
Corcyraeans—neither receive them into alliance in our despite, nor be their abettors in
crime.

text: So do, and you will act as we have a right to expect of you, and at the same time best consult your own interests.” Such were the words of the Corinthians.
text_raw:
So do, and you will act as we have a right to expect of you, and at the same time
best consult your own interests.”
Such were the words of the Corinthians.

text: When the Athenians had heard both out, two assemblies were held.
text_raw: When the Athenians had heard both out, two assemblies were held.

text: In the first there was a manifest disposition to listen to the representations of Corinth; in the second, public feeling had changed and an alliance with Corcyra was decided on, with certain reservations.
text_raw:
In the first there was
a manifest disposition to listen to the representations of Corinth; in the second, public
feeling had changed and an alliance with Corcyra was decided on, with certain
reservations.

text: It was to be a defensive, not an offensive alliance.
text_raw: It was to be a defensive, not an offensive alliance.

text: It did not involve a breach of the treaty with Peloponnese:
text_raw:
It did not involve a breach
of the treaty with Peloponnese:

text: Athens could not be required to join Corcyra in any attack upon Corinth.
text_raw:
Athens could not be required to join Corcyra in any attack
upon Corinth.

text: But each of the contracting parties had a right to the other’s assistance against invasion, whether of his own territory or that of an ally.
text_raw:
But each of the contracting parties had a right to the other’s assistance
against invasion, whether of his own territory or that of an ally.

text: For it began now to be felt that the coming of the Peloponnesian war was only a question of time, and no one was willing to see a naval power of such magnitude as Corcyra sacrificed to Corinth; though if they could let them weaken each other by mutual conflict, it would be no bad preparation for the struggle which Athens might one day have to wage with Corinth and the other naval powers.
text_raw:
For it began now to be felt
that the coming of the Peloponnesian war was only a question of time, and no one was
willing to see a naval power of such magnitude as Corcyra sacrificed to Corinth; though if
they could let them weaken each other by mutual conflict, it would be no bad preparation
for the struggle which Athens might one day have to wage with Corinth and the other
naval powers.

text: At the same time the island seemed to lie conveniently on the coasting passage to Italy and Sicily.
text_raw:
At the same time the island seemed to lie conveniently on the coasting
passage to Italy and Sicily.

text: With these views, Athens received Corcyra into alliance and, on the departure of the Corinthians not long afterwards, sent ten ships to their assistance.
text_raw:
With these views, Athens received Corcyra into alliance and,
on the departure of the Corinthians not long afterwards, sent ten ships to their assistance.

text: They were commanded by Lacedaemonius, the son of Cimon, Diotimus, the son of Strombichus, and Proteas, the son of Epicles.
text_raw:
They were commanded by Lacedaemonius, the son of Cimon, Diotimus, the son of
Strombichus, and Proteas, the son of Epicles.

text: Their instructions were to avoid collision with the Corinthian fleet except under certain circumstances.
text_raw:
Their instructions were to avoid collision
with the Corinthian fleet except under certain circumstances.

text: If it sailed to Corcyra and threatened a landing on her coast, or in any of her possessions, they were to do their utmost to prevent it.
text_raw:
If it sailed to Corcyra and
threatened a landing on her coast, or in any of her possessions, they were to do their
utmost to prevent it.

text: These instructions were prompted by an anxiety to avoid a breach of the treaty.
text_raw:
These instructions were prompted by an anxiety to avoid a breach of
the treaty.

text: Meanwhile the Corinthians completed their preparations, and sailed for Corcyra with a hundred and fifty ships.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the Corinthians completed their preparations, and sailed for Corcyra with a
hundred and fifty ships.

text: Of these Elis furnished ten, Megara twelve, Leucas ten, Ambracia twenty-seven, Anactorium one, and Corinth herself ninety.
text_raw:
Of these Elis furnished ten, Megara twelve, Leucas ten, Ambracia
twenty-seven, Anactorium one, and Corinth herself ninety.

text: Each of these contingents had its own admiral, the Corinthian being under the command of Xenoclides, son of Euthycles, with four colleagues.
text_raw:
Each of these contingents had
its own admiral, the Corinthian being under the command of Xenoclides, son of
Euthycles, with four colleagues.

text: Sailing from Leucas, they made land at the part of the continent opposite Corcyra.
text_raw:
Sailing from Leucas, they made land at the part of the
continent opposite Corcyra.

text: They anchored in the harbour of Chimerium, in the territory of Thesprotis, above which, at some distance from the sea, lies the city of Ephyre, in the
text_raw:
They anchored in the harbour of Chimerium, in the territory
of Thesprotis, above which, at some distance from the sea, lies the city of Ephyre, in the

text: Elean district.
text_raw: Elean district.

text: By this city the Acherusian lake pours its waters into the sea.
text_raw: By this city the Acherusian lake pours its waters into the sea.

text: It gets its name from the river Acheron, which flows through Thesprotis and falls into the lake.
text_raw:
It gets its
name from the river Acheron, which flows through Thesprotis and falls into the lake.

text: There also the river Thyamis flows, forming the boundary between Thesprotis and Kestrine; and between these rivers rises the point of Chimerium.
text_raw:
There also the river Thyamis flows, forming the boundary between Thesprotis and
Kestrine; and between these rivers rises the point of Chimerium.

text: In this part of the continent the Corinthians now came to anchor, and formed an encampment.
text_raw:
In this part of the
continent the Corinthians now came to anchor, and formed an encampment.

text: When the Corcyraeans saw them coming, they manned a hundred and ten ships, commanded by Meikiades, Aisimides, and Eurybatus, and stationed themselves at one of the Sybota isles; the ten Athenian ships being present.
text_raw:
When the
Corcyraeans saw them coming, they manned a hundred and ten ships, commanded by
Meikiades, Aisimides, and Eurybatus, and stationed themselves at one of the Sybota isles;
the ten Athenian ships being present.

text: On Point Leukimme they posted their land forces, and a thousand heavy infantry who had come from Zacynthus to their assistance.
text_raw:
On Point Leukimme they posted their land forces,
and a thousand heavy infantry who had come from Zacynthus to their assistance.

text: Nor were the Corinthians on the mainland without their allies.
text_raw:
Nor were
the Corinthians on the mainland without their allies.

text: The barbarians flocked in large numbers to their assistance, the inhabitants of this part of the continent being old allies of theirs.
text_raw:
The barbarians flocked in large
numbers to their assistance, the inhabitants of this part of the continent being old allies of
theirs.

text: When the Corinthian preparations were completed, they took three days’ provisions and put out from Chimerium by night, ready for action.
text_raw:
When the Corinthian preparations were completed, they took three days’ provisions and
put out from Chimerium by night, ready for action.

text: Sailing with the dawn, they sighted the Corcyraean fleet out at sea and coming towards them.
text_raw:
Sailing with the dawn, they sighted the
Corcyraean fleet out at sea and coming towards them.

text: When they perceived each other, both sides formed in order of battle.
text_raw:
When they perceived each other,
both sides formed in order of battle.

text: On the Corcyraean right wing lay the Athenian ships, the rest of the line being occupied by their own vessels formed in three squadrons, each of which was commanded by one of the three admirals.
text_raw:
On the Corcyraean right wing lay the Athenian ships,
the rest of the line being occupied by their own vessels formed in three squadrons, each of
which was commanded by one of the three admirals.

text: Such was the Corcyraean formation.
text_raw: Such was the Corcyraean formation.

text: The Corinthian was as follows: on the right wing lay the Megarian and Ambraciot ships, in the centre the rest of the allies in order.
text_raw:
The Corinthian was as follows: on the right wing lay the Megarian and Ambraciot ships,
in the centre the rest of the allies in order.

text: But the left was composed of the best sailers in the Corinthian navy, to encounter the Athenians and the right wing of the Corcyraeans.
text_raw:
But the left was composed of the best sailers in
the Corinthian navy, to encounter the Athenians and the right wing of the Corcyraeans.

text: As soon as the signals were raised on either side, they joined battle.
text_raw:
As
soon as the signals were raised on either side, they joined battle.

text: Both sides had a large number of heavy infantry on their decks, and a large number of archers and darters, the old imperfect armament still prevailing.
text_raw:
Both sides had a large
number of heavy infantry on their decks, and a large number of archers and darters, the old
imperfect armament still prevailing.

text: The sea-fight was an obstinate one, though not remarkable for its science; indeed it was more like a battle by land.
text_raw:
The sea-fight was an obstinate one, though not
remarkable for its science; indeed it was more like a battle by land.

text: Whenever they charged each other, the multitude and crush of the vessels made it by no means easy to get loose; besides, their hopes of victory lay principally in the heavy infantry on the decks, who stood and fought in order, the ships remaining stationary.
text_raw:
Whenever they
charged each other, the multitude and crush of the vessels made it by no means easy to get
loose; besides, their hopes of victory lay principally in the heavy infantry on the decks,
who stood and fought in order, the ships remaining stationary.

text: The manoeuvre of breaking the line was not tried; in short, strength and pluck had more share in the fight than science.
text_raw:
The manoeuvre of breaking
the line was not tried; in short, strength and pluck had more share in the fight than science.

text: Everywhere tumult reigned, the battle being one scene of confusion; meanwhile the Athenian ships, by coming up to the Corcyraeans whenever they were pressed, served to alarm the enemy, though their commanders could not join in the battle from fear of their instructions.
text_raw:
Everywhere tumult reigned, the battle being one scene of confusion; meanwhile the
Athenian ships, by coming up to the Corcyraeans whenever they were pressed, served to
alarm the enemy, though their commanders could not join in the battle from fear of their
instructions.

text: The right wing of the Corinthians suffered most.
text_raw: The right wing of the Corinthians suffered most.

text: The Corcyraeans routed it, and chased them in disorder to the continent with twenty ships, sailed up to their camp, and burnt the tents which they found empty, and plundered the stuff.
text_raw:
The Corcyraeans routed it,
and chased them in disorder to the continent with twenty ships, sailed up to their camp,
and burnt the tents which they found empty, and plundered the stuff.

text: So in this quarter the Corinthians and their allies were defeated, and the Corcyraeans were victorious.
text_raw:
So in this quarter the
Corinthians and their allies were defeated, and the Corcyraeans were victorious.

text: But where the Corinthians themselves were, on the left, they gained a decided success; the scanty forces of the Corcyraeans being further weakened by the want of the twenty ships absent on the pursuit.
text_raw:
But
where the Corinthians themselves were, on the left, they gained a decided success; the
scanty forces of the Corcyraeans being further weakened by the want of the twenty ships
absent on the pursuit.

text: Seeing the Corcyraeans hard pressed, the Athenians began at length to assist them more unequivocally.
text_raw:
Seeing the Corcyraeans hard pressed, the Athenians began at length
to assist them more unequivocally.

text: At first, it is true, they refrained from charging any ships; but when the rout was becoming patent, and the Corinthians were pressing on, the time at last came when every one set to, and all distinction was laid aside, and it came to this point, that the Corinthians and Athenians raised their hands against each other.
text_raw:
At first, it is true, they refrained from charging any
ships; but when the rout was becoming patent, and the Corinthians were pressing on, the
time at last came when every one set to, and all distinction was laid aside, and it came to
this point, that the Corinthians and Athenians raised their hands against each other.

text: After the rout, the Corinthians, instead of employing themselves in lashing fast and
text_raw: After the rout, the Corinthians, instead of employing themselves in lashing fast and

text: hauling after them the hulls of the vessels which they had disabled, turned their attention to the men, whom they butchered as they sailed through, not caring so much to make prisoners.
text_raw:
hauling after them the hulls of the vessels which they had disabled, turned their attention
to the men, whom they butchered as they sailed through, not caring so much to make
prisoners.

text: Some even of their own friends were slain by them, by mistake, in their ignorance of the defeat of the right wing For the number of the ships on both sides, and the distance to which they covered the sea, made it difficult, after they had once joined, to distinguish between the conquering and the conquered; this battle proving far greater than any before it, any at least between Hellenes, for the number of vessels engaged.
text_raw:
Some even of their own friends were slain by them, by mistake, in their
ignorance of the defeat of the right wing For the number of the ships on both sides, and the
distance to which they covered the sea, made it difficult, after they had once joined, to
distinguish between the conquering and the conquered; this battle proving far greater than
any before it, any at least between Hellenes, for the number of vessels engaged.

text: After the Corinthians had chased the Corcyraeans to the land, they turned to the wrecks and their dead, most of whom they succeeded in getting hold of and conveying to Sybota, the rendezvous of the land forces furnished by their barbarian allies.
text_raw:
After the
Corinthians had chased the Corcyraeans to the land, they turned to the wrecks and their
dead, most of whom they succeeded in getting hold of and conveying to Sybota, the
rendezvous of the land forces furnished by their barbarian allies.

text: Sybota, it must be known, is a desert harbour of Thesprotis.
text_raw:
Sybota, it must be
known, is a desert harbour of Thesprotis.

text: This task over, they mustered anew, and sailed against the Corcyraeans, who on their part advanced to meet them with all their ships that were fit for service and remaining to them, accompanied by the Athenian vessels, fearing that they might attempt a landing in their territory.
text_raw:
This task over, they mustered anew, and sailed
against the Corcyraeans, who on their part advanced to meet them with all their ships that
were fit for service and remaining to them, accompanied by the Athenian vessels, fearing
that they might attempt a landing in their territory.

text: It was by this time getting late, and the paean had been sung for the attack, when the Corinthians suddenly began to back water.
text_raw:
It was by this time getting late, and the
paean had been sung for the attack, when the Corinthians suddenly began to back water.

text: They had observed twenty Athenian ships sailing up, which had been sent out afterwards to reinforce the ten vessels by the Athenians, who feared, as it turned out justly, the defeat of the Corcyraeans and the inability of their handful of ships to protect them.
text_raw:
They had observed twenty Athenian ships sailing up, which had been sent out afterwards
to reinforce the ten vessels by the Athenians, who feared, as it turned out justly, the defeat
of the Corcyraeans and the inability of their handful of ships to protect them.

text: These ships were thus seen by the Corinthians first.
text_raw:
These ships
were thus seen by the Corinthians first.

text: They suspected that they were from Athens, and that those which they saw were not all, but that there were more behind; they accordingly began to retire.
text_raw:
They suspected that they were from Athens, and
that those which they saw were not all, but that there were more behind; they accordingly
began to retire.

text: The Corcyraeans meanwhile had not sighted them, as they were advancing from a point which they could not so well see, and were wondering why the Corinthians were backing water, when some caught sight of them, and cried out that there were ships in sight ahead.
text_raw:
The Corcyraeans meanwhile had not sighted them, as they were advancing
from a point which they could not so well see, and were wondering why the Corinthians
were backing water, when some caught sight of them, and cried out that there were ships
in sight ahead.

text: Upon this they also retired; for it was now getting dark, and the retreat of the Corinthians had suspended hostilities.
text_raw:
Upon this they also retired; for it was now getting dark, and the retreat of
the Corinthians had suspended hostilities.

text: Thus they parted from each other, and the battle ceased with night.
text_raw:
Thus they parted from each other, and the battle
ceased with night.

text: The Corcyraeans were in their camp at Leukimme, when these twenty ships from Athens, under the command of Glaucon, the son of Leagrus, and Andocides, son of Leogoras, bore on through the corpses and the wrecks, and sailed up to the camp, not long after they were sighted.
text_raw:
The Corcyraeans were in their camp at Leukimme, when these twenty
ships from Athens, under the command of Glaucon, the son of Leagrus, and Andocides,
son of Leogoras, bore on through the corpses and the wrecks, and sailed up to the camp,
not long after they were sighted.

text: It was now night, and the Corcyraeans feared that they might be hostile vessels; but they soon knew them, and the ships came to anchor.
text_raw:
It was now night, and the Corcyraeans feared that they
might be hostile vessels; but they soon knew them, and the ships came to anchor.

text: The next day the thirty Athenian vessels put out to sea, accompanied by all the Corcyraean ships that were seaworthy, and sailed to the harbour at Sybota, where the Corinthians lay, to see if they would engage.
text_raw:
The next day the thirty Athenian vessels put out to sea, accompanied by all the
Corcyraean ships that were seaworthy, and sailed to the harbour at Sybota, where the
Corinthians lay, to see if they would engage.

text: The Corinthians put out from the land and formed a line in the open sea, but beyond this made no further movement, having no intention of assuming the offensive.
text_raw:
The Corinthians put out from the land and
formed a line in the open sea, but beyond this made no further movement, having no
intention of assuming the offensive.

text: For they saw reinforcements arrived fresh from Athens, and themselves confronted by numerous difficulties, such as the necessity of guarding the prisoners whom they had on board and the want of all means of refitting their ships in a desert place.
text_raw:
For they saw reinforcements arrived fresh from
Athens, and themselves confronted by numerous difficulties, such as the necessity of
guarding the prisoners whom they had on board and the want of all means of refitting their
ships in a desert place.

text: What they were thinking more about was how their voyage home was to be effected; they feared that the Athenians might consider that the treaty was dissolved by the collision which had occurred, and forbid their departure.
text_raw:
What they were thinking more about was how their voyage home
was to be effected; they feared that the Athenians might consider that the treaty was
dissolved by the collision which had occurred, and forbid their departure.

text: Accordingly they resolved to put some men on board a boat, and send them without a herald’s wand to the Athenians, as an experiment.
text_raw:
Accordingly they resolved to put some men on board a boat, and send them without a
herald’s wand to the Athenians, as an experiment.

text: Having done so, they spoke as follows: “You do wrong, Athenians, to begin war and break the treaty.
text_raw:
Having done so, they spoke as follows:
“You do wrong, Athenians, to begin war and break the treaty.

text: Engaged in chastising our enemies, we find you placing yourselves in our path in arms against us.
text_raw:
Engaged in chastising our
enemies, we find you placing yourselves in our path in arms against us.

text: Now if your
text_raw: Now if your

text: intentions are to prevent us sailing to Corcyra, or anywhere else that we may wish, and if you are for breaking the treaty, first take us that are here and treat us as enemies.” Such was what they said, and all the Corcyraean armament that were within hearing immediately called out to take them and kill them.
text_raw:
intentions are to prevent us sailing to Corcyra, or anywhere else that we may wish, and if
you are for breaking the treaty, first take us that are here and treat us as enemies.” Such
was what they said, and all the Corcyraean armament that were within hearing
immediately called out to take them and kill them.

text: But the Athenians answered as follows: “Neither are we beginning war, Peloponnesians, nor are we breaking the treaty; but these Corcyraeans are our allies, and we are come to help them.
text_raw:
But the Athenians answered as follows:
“Neither are we beginning war, Peloponnesians, nor are we breaking the treaty; but these
Corcyraeans are our allies, and we are come to help them.

text: So if you want to sail anywhere else, we place no obstacle in your way; but if you are going to sail against Corcyra, or any of her possessions, we shall do our best to stop you.” Receiving this answer from the Athenians, the Corinthians commenced preparations for their voyage home, and set up a trophy in Sybota, on the continent; while the Corcyraeans took up the wrecks and dead that had been carried out to them by the current, and by a wind which rose in the night and scattered them in all directions, and set up their trophy in Sybota, on the island, as victors.
text_raw:
So if you want to sail anywhere
else, we place no obstacle in your way; but if you are going to sail against Corcyra, or any
of her possessions, we shall do our best to stop you.”
Receiving this answer from the Athenians, the Corinthians commenced preparations for
their voyage home, and set up a trophy in Sybota, on the continent; while the Corcyraeans
took up the wrecks and dead that had been carried out to them by the current, and by a
wind which rose in the night and scattered them in all directions, and set up their trophy in
Sybota, on the island, as victors.

text: The reasons each side had for claiming the victory were these.
text_raw:
The reasons each side had for claiming the victory were
these.

text: The Corinthians had been victorious in the sea-fight until night; and having thus been enabled to carry off most wrecks and dead, they were in possession of no fewer than a thousand prisoners of war, and had sunk close upon seventy vessels.
text_raw:
The Corinthians had been victorious in the sea-fight until night; and having thus
been enabled to carry off most wrecks and dead, they were in possession of no fewer than
a thousand prisoners of war, and had sunk close upon seventy vessels.

text: The Corcyraeans had destroyed about thirty ships, and after the arrival of the Athenians had taken up the wrecks and dead on their side; they had besides seen the Corinthians retire before them, backing water on sight of the Athenian vessels, and upon the arrival of the Athenians refuse to sail out against them from Sybota.
text_raw:
The Corcyraeans
had destroyed about thirty ships, and after the arrival of the Athenians had taken up the
wrecks and dead on their side; they had besides seen the Corinthians retire before them,
backing water on sight of the Athenian vessels, and upon the arrival of the Athenians
refuse to sail out against them from Sybota.

text: Thus both sides claimed the victory.
text_raw: Thus both sides claimed the victory.

text: The Corinthians on the voyage home took Anactorium, which stands at the mouth of the Ambracian gulf.
text_raw:
The Corinthians on the voyage home took Anactorium, which stands at the mouth of the
Ambracian gulf.

text: The place was taken by treachery, being common ground to the Corcyraeans and Corinthians.
text_raw:
The place was taken by treachery, being common ground to the
Corcyraeans and Corinthians.

text: After establishing Corinthian settlers there, they retired home.
text_raw:
After establishing Corinthian settlers there, they retired
home.

text: Eight hundred of the Corcyraeans were slaves; these they sold; two hundred and fifty they retained in captivity, and treated with great attention, in the hope that they might bring over their country to Corinth on their return; most of them being, as it happened, men of very high position in Corcyra.
text_raw:
Eight hundred of the Corcyraeans were slaves; these they sold; two hundred and
fifty they retained in captivity, and treated with great attention, in the hope that they might
bring over their country to Corinth on their return; most of them being, as it happened,
men of very high position in Corcyra.

text: In this way Corcyra maintained her political existence in the war with Corinth, and the Athenian vessels left the island.
text_raw:
In this way Corcyra maintained her political
existence in the war with Corinth, and the Athenian vessels left the island.

text: This was the first cause of the war that Corinth had against the Athenians, viz., that they had fought against them with the Corcyraeans in time of treaty.
text_raw:
This was the
first cause of the war that Corinth had against the Athenians, viz., that they had fought
against them with the Corcyraeans in time of treaty.

text: Almost immediately after this, fresh differences arose between the Athenians and Peloponnesians, and contributed their share to the war.
text_raw:
Almost immediately after this, fresh differences arose between the Athenians and
Peloponnesians, and contributed their share to the war.

text: Corinth was forming schemes for retaliation, and Athens suspected her hostility.
text_raw:
Corinth was forming schemes for
retaliation, and Athens suspected her hostility.

text: The Potidaeans, who inhabit the isthmus of Pallene, being a Corinthian colony, but tributary allies of Athens, were ordered to raze the wall looking towards Pallene, to give hostages, to dismiss the Corinthian magistrates, and in future not to receive the persons sent from Corinth annually to succeed them.
text_raw:
The Potidaeans, who inhabit the isthmus of
Pallene, being a Corinthian colony, but tributary allies of Athens, were ordered to raze the
wall looking towards Pallene, to give hostages, to dismiss the Corinthian magistrates, and
in future not to receive the persons sent from Corinth annually to succeed them.

text: It was feared that they might be persuaded by Perdiccas and the Corinthians to revolt, and might draw the rest of the allies in the direction of Thrace to revolt with them.
text_raw:
It was
feared that they might be persuaded by Perdiccas and the Corinthians to revolt, and might
draw the rest of the allies in the direction of Thrace to revolt with them.

text: These precautions against the Potidaeans were taken by the Athenians immediately after the battle at Corcyra.
text_raw:
These precautions
against the Potidaeans were taken by the Athenians immediately after the battle at
Corcyra.

text: Not only was Corinth at length openly hostile, but Perdiccas, son of Alexander, king of the Macedonians, had from an old friend and ally been made an enemy.
text_raw:
Not only was Corinth at length openly hostile, but Perdiccas, son of Alexander,
king of the Macedonians, had from an old friend and ally been made an enemy.

text: He had been made an enemy by the Athenians entering into alliance with his brother Philip and Derdas, who were in league against him.
text_raw:
He had
been made an enemy by the Athenians entering into alliance with his brother Philip and
Derdas, who were in league against him.

text: In his alarm he had sent to Lacedaemon to try
text_raw: In his alarm he had sent to Lacedaemon to try

text: and involve the Athenians in a war with the Peloponnesians, and was endeavouring to win over Corinth in order to bring about the revolt of Potidaea.
text_raw:
and involve the Athenians in a war with the Peloponnesians, and was endeavouring to win
over Corinth in order to bring about the revolt of Potidaea.

text: He also made overtures to the Chalcidians in the direction of Thrace, and to the Bottiaeans, to persuade them to join in the revolt; for he thought that if these places on the border could be made his allies, it would be easier to carry on the war with their co-operation.
text_raw:
He also made overtures to the
Chalcidians in the direction of Thrace, and to the Bottiaeans, to persuade them to join in
the revolt; for he thought that if these places on the border could be made his allies, it
would be easier to carry on the war with their co-operation.

text: Alive to all this, and wishing to anticipate the revolt of the cities, the Athenians acted as follows.
text_raw:
Alive to all this, and wishing
to anticipate the revolt of the cities, the Athenians acted as follows.

text: They were just then sending off thirty ships and a thousand heavy infantry for his country under the command of Archestratus, son of Lycomedes, with four colleagues.
text_raw:
They were just then
sending off thirty ships and a thousand heavy infantry for his country under the command
of Archestratus, son of Lycomedes, with four colleagues.

text: They instructed the captains to take hostages of the Potidaeans, to raze the wall, and to be on their guard against the revolt of the neighbouring cities.
text_raw:
They instructed the captains to
take hostages of the Potidaeans, to raze the wall, and to be on their guard against the revolt
of the neighbouring cities.

text: Meanwhile the Potidaeans sent envoys to Athens on the chance of persuading them to take no new steps in their matters; they also went to Lacedaemon with the Corinthians to secure support in case of need.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the Potidaeans sent envoys to Athens on the chance of persuading them to
take no new steps in their matters; they also went to Lacedaemon with the Corinthians to
secure support in case of need.

text: Failing after prolonged negotiation to obtain anything satisfactory from the Athenians; being unable, for all they could say, to prevent the vessels that were destined for Macedonia from also sailing against them; and receiving from the Lacedaemonian government a promise to invade Attica, if the Athenians should attack Potidaea, the Potidaeans, thus favoured by the moment, at last entered into league with the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans, and revolted.
text_raw:
Failing after prolonged negotiation to obtain anything
satisfactory from the Athenians; being unable, for all they could say, to prevent the vessels
that were destined for Macedonia from also sailing against them; and receiving from the
Lacedaemonian government a promise to invade Attica, if the Athenians should attack
Potidaea, the Potidaeans, thus favoured by the moment, at last entered into league with the
Chalcidians and Bottiaeans, and revolted.

text: And Perdiccas induced the Chalcidians to abandon and demolish their towns on the seaboard and, settling inland at Olynthus, to make that one city a strong place: meanwhile to those who followed his advice he gave a part of his territory in Mygdonia round Lake Bolbe as a place of abode while the war against the Athenians should last.
text_raw:
And Perdiccas induced the Chalcidians to
abandon and demolish their towns on the seaboard and, settling inland at Olynthus, to
make that one city a strong place: meanwhile to those who followed his advice he gave a
part of his territory in Mygdonia round Lake Bolbe as a place of abode while the war
against the Athenians should last.

text: They accordingly demolished their towns, removed inland and prepared for war.
text_raw:
They accordingly demolished their towns, removed
inland and prepared for war.

text: The thirty ships of the Athenians, arriving before the Thracian places, found Potidaea and the rest in revolt.
text_raw:
The thirty ships of the Athenians, arriving before the
Thracian places, found Potidaea and the rest in revolt.

text: Their commanders, considering it to be quite impossible with their present force to carry on war with Perdiccas and with the confederate towns as well turned to Macedonia, their original destination, and, having established themselves there, carried on war in co-operation with Philip, and the brothers of Derdas, who had invaded the country from the interior.
text_raw:
Their commanders, considering it to
be quite impossible with their present force to carry on war with Perdiccas and with the
confederate towns as well turned to Macedonia, their original destination, and, having
established themselves there, carried on war in co-operation with Philip, and the brothers
of Derdas, who had invaded the country from the interior.

text: Meanwhile the Corinthians, with Potidaea in revolt and the Athenian ships on the coast of Macedonia, alarmed for the safety of the place and thinking its danger theirs, sent volunteers from Corinth, and mercenaries from the rest of Peloponnese, to the number of sixteen hundred heavy infantry in all, and four hundred light troops.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the Corinthians, with Potidaea in revolt and the Athenian ships on the coast
of Macedonia, alarmed for the safety of the place and thinking its danger theirs, sent
volunteers from Corinth, and mercenaries from the rest of Peloponnese, to the number of
sixteen hundred heavy infantry in all, and four hundred light troops.

text: Aristeus, son of Adimantus, who was always a steady friend to the Potidaeans, took command of the expedition, and it was principally for love of him that most of the men from Corinth volunteered.
text_raw:
Aristeus, son of
Adimantus, who was always a steady friend to the Potidaeans, took command of the
expedition, and it was principally for love of him that most of the men from Corinth
volunteered.

text: They arrived in Thrace forty days after the revolt of Potidaea.
text_raw: They arrived in Thrace forty days after the revolt of Potidaea.

text: The Athenians also immediately received the news of the revolt of the cities.
text_raw: The Athenians also immediately received the news of the revolt of the cities.

text: On being informed that Aristeus and his reinforcements were on their way, they sent two thousand heavy infantry of their own citizens and forty ships against the places in revolt, under the command of Callias, son of Calliades, and four colleagues.
text_raw:
On being
informed that Aristeus and his reinforcements were on their way, they sent two thousand
heavy infantry of their own citizens and forty ships against the places in revolt, under the
command of Callias, son of Calliades, and four colleagues.

text: They arrived in Macedonia first, and found the force of a thousand men that had been first sent out, just become masters of Therme and besieging Pydna.
text_raw:
They arrived in Macedonia
first, and found the force of a thousand men that had been first sent out, just become
masters of Therme and besieging Pydna.

text: Accordingly they also joined in the investment, and besieged Pydna for a while.
text_raw:
Accordingly they also joined in the investment,
and besieged Pydna for a while.

text: Subsequently they came to terms and concluded a forced alliance with Perdiccas, hastened by the calls of Potidaea and by the arrival of Aristeus at
text_raw:
Subsequently they came to terms and concluded a forced
alliance with Perdiccas, hastened by the calls of Potidaea and by the arrival of Aristeus at

text: that place.
text_raw: that place.

text: They withdrew from Macedonia, going to Beroea and thence to Strepsa, and, after a futile attempt on the latter place, they pursued by land their march to Potidaea with three thousand heavy infantry of their own citizens, besides a number of their allies, and six hundred Macedonian horsemen, the followers of Philip and Pausanias.
text_raw:
They withdrew from Macedonia, going to Beroea and thence to Strepsa, and,
after a futile attempt on the latter place, they pursued by land their march to Potidaea with
three thousand heavy infantry of their own citizens, besides a number of their allies, and
six hundred Macedonian horsemen, the followers of Philip and Pausanias.

text: With these sailed seventy ships along the coast.
text_raw:
With these
sailed seventy ships along the coast.

text: Advancing by short marches, on the third day they arrived at Gigonus, where they encamped.
text_raw:
Advancing by short marches, on the third day they
arrived at Gigonus, where they encamped.

text: Meanwhile the Potidaeans and the Peloponnesians with Aristeus were encamped on the side looking towards Olynthus on the isthmus, in expectation of the Athenians, and had established their market outside the city.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the Potidaeans and the Peloponnesians with Aristeus were encamped on the
side looking towards Olynthus on the isthmus, in expectation of the Athenians, and had
established their market outside the city.

text: The allies had chosen Aristeus general of all the infantry; while the command of the cavalry was given to Perdiccas, who had at once left the alliance of the Athenians and gone back to that of the Potidaeans, having deputed Iolaus as his general:
text_raw:
The allies had chosen Aristeus general of all the
infantry; while the command of the cavalry was given to Perdiccas, who had at once left
the alliance of the Athenians and gone back to that of the Potidaeans, having deputed
Iolaus as his general:

text: The plan of Aristeus was to keep his own force on the isthmus, and await the attack of the Athenians; leaving the Chalcidians and the allies outside the isthmus, and the two hundred cavalry from Perdiccas in Olynthus to act upon the Athenian rear, on the occasion of their advancing against him; and thus to place the enemy between two fires.
text_raw:
The plan of Aristeus was to keep his own force on the isthmus, and
await the attack of the Athenians; leaving the Chalcidians and the allies outside the
isthmus, and the two hundred cavalry from Perdiccas in Olynthus to act upon the Athenian
rear, on the occasion of their advancing against him; and thus to place the enemy between
two fires.

text: While Callias the Athenian general and his colleagues dispatched the Macedonian horse and a few of the allies to Olynthus, to prevent any movement being made from that quarter, the Athenians themselves broke up their camp and marched against Potidaea.
text_raw:
While Callias the Athenian general and his colleagues dispatched the
Macedonian horse and a few of the allies to Olynthus, to prevent any movement being
made from that quarter, the Athenians themselves broke up their camp and marched
against Potidaea.

text: After they had arrived at the isthmus, and saw the enemy preparing for battle, they formed against him, and soon afterwards engaged.
text_raw:
After they had arrived at the isthmus, and saw the enemy preparing for
battle, they formed against him, and soon afterwards engaged.

text: The wing of Aristeus, with the Corinthians and other picked troops round him, routed the wing opposed to it, and followed for a considerable distance in pursuit.
text_raw:
The wing of Aristeus, with
the Corinthians and other picked troops round him, routed the wing opposed to it, and
followed for a considerable distance in pursuit.

text: But the rest of the army of the Potidaeans and of the Peloponnesians was defeated by the Athenians, and took refuge within the fortifications.
text_raw:
But the rest of the army of the Potidaeans
and of the Peloponnesians was defeated by the Athenians, and took refuge within the
fortifications.

text: Returning from the pursuit, Aristeus perceived the defeat of the rest of the army.
text_raw:
Returning from the pursuit, Aristeus perceived the defeat of the rest of the
army.

text: Being at a loss which of the two risks to choose, whether to go to Olynthus or to Potidaea, he at last determined to draw his men into as small a space as possible, and force his way with a run into Potidaea.
text_raw:
Being at a loss which of the two risks to choose, whether to go to Olynthus or to
Potidaea, he at last determined to draw his men into as small a space as possible, and force
his way with a run into Potidaea.

text: Not without difficulty, through a storm of missiles, he passed along by the breakwater through the sea, and brought off most of his men safe, though a few were lost.
text_raw:
Not without difficulty, through a storm of missiles, he
passed along by the breakwater through the sea, and brought off most of his men safe,
though a few were lost.

text: Meanwhile the auxiliaries of the Potidaeans from Olynthus, which is about seven miles off and in sight of Potidaea, when the battle began and the signals were raised, advanced a little way to render assistance; and the Macedonian horse formed against them to prevent it.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the auxiliaries of the Potidaeans from Olynthus, which
is about seven miles off and in sight of Potidaea, when the battle began and the signals
were raised, advanced a little way to render assistance; and the Macedonian horse formed
against them to prevent it.

text: But on victory speedily declaring for the Athenians and the signals being taken down, they retired back within the wall; and the Macedonians returned to the Athenians.
text_raw:
But on victory speedily declaring for the Athenians and the
signals being taken down, they retired back within the wall; and the Macedonians returned
to the Athenians.

text: Thus there were no cavalry present on either side.
text_raw: Thus there were no cavalry present on either side.

text: After the battle the Athenians set up a trophy, and gave back their dead to the Potidaeans under truce.
text_raw:
After the battle the
Athenians set up a trophy, and gave back their dead to the Potidaeans under truce.

text: The Potidaeans and their allies had close upon three hundred killed; the Athenians a hundred and fifty of their own citizens, and Callias their general.
text_raw:
The
Potidaeans and their allies had close upon three hundred killed; the Athenians a hundred
and fifty of their own citizens, and Callias their general.

text: The wall on the side of the isthmus had now works at once raised against it, and manned by the Athenians.
text_raw:

text: Congress of the Peloponnesian Confederacy at Lacedaemon The Athenians and Peloponnesians had these antecedent grounds of complaint against each other: the complaint of Corinth was that her colony of Potidaea, and Corinthian and Peloponnesian citizens within it, were being besieged; that of Athens against the Peloponnesians that they had incited a town of hers, a member of her alliance and a contributor to her revenue, to revolt, and had come and were openly fighting against her on the side of the Potidaeans.

Congress of the Peloponnesian Confederacy at Lacedaemon
The Athenians and Peloponnesians had these antecedent grounds of complaint against
each other: the complaint of Corinth was that her colony of Potidaea, and Corinthian and
Peloponnesian citizens within it, were being besieged; that of Athens against the
Peloponnesians that they had incited a town of hers, a member of her alliance and a
contributor to her revenue, to revolt, and had come and were openly fighting against her
on the side of the Potidaeans.

text: For all this, war had not yet broken out: there was still truce for a while; for this was a private enterprise on the part of Corinth.

text: But the siege of Potidaea put an end to her inaction; she had men inside it: besides, she feared for the place.

But the siege of Potidaea put an end to her inaction; she had men inside it: besides, she

text: Immediately summoning the allies to Lacedaemon, she came and loudly accused Athens of breach of the treaty and aggression on the rights of Peloponnese.
text_raw:

text: With her, the Aeginetans, formally unrepresented from fear of Athens, in secret proved not the least urgent of the advocates for war, asserting that they had not the independence guaranteed to them by the treaty.

text: Last of all the Corinthians came forward, and having let those who preceded them inflame the Lacedaemonians, now followed with a speech to this effect: “Lacedaemonians! the confidence which you feel in your constitution and social order, inclines you to receive any reflections of ours on other powers with a certain scepticism.

text: Hence springs your moderation, but hence also the rather limited knowledge which you betray in dealing with foreign politics.

Hence springs your moderation, but hence also the rather limited knowledge which you

text: Time after time was our voice raised to warn you of the blows about to be dealt us by Athens, and time after time, instead of taking the trouble to ascertain the worth of our communications, you contented yourselves with suspecting the speakers of being inspired by private interest.

text: And so, instead of calling these allies together before the blow fell, you have delayed to do so till we are smarting under it; allies among whom we have not the worst title to speak, as having the greatest complaints to make, complaints of Athenian outrage and Lacedaemonian neglect.

And so, instead of calling these allies
together before the blow fell, you have delayed to do so till we are smarting under it; allies

text: Now if these assaults on the rights of Hellas had been made in the dark, you might be unacquainted with the facts, and it would be our duty to enlighten you.

text: As it is, long speeches are not needed where you see servitude accomplished for some of us, meditated for others—in particular for our allies—and prolonged preparations in the aggressor against the hour of war.

text: For the true author of the subjugation of a people is not so much the immediate agent, as the power which permits it having the means to prevent it; particularly if that power aspires to the glory of being the liberator of Hellas.
We are at last assembled.

text: You, Lacedaemonians, of all the Hellenes are alone inactive, and defend yourselves not by doing anything but by looking as if you would do something; you alone wait till the power of an enemy is becoming twice its original size, instead of crushing it in its infancy.
text_raw:

and defend yourselves not by doing anything but by looking as if you would do

text: And yet the world used to say that you were to be depended upon; but in your case, we fear, it said more than the truth.

And yet the world used to say that you were to be

text: Well, Athens at all events is a near neighbour, and yet Athens you utterly disregard; against Athens you prefer to act on the defensive instead of on the offensive, and to make it an affair of chances by deferring the struggle till she has grown far stronger than at first.

And yet you know that on the whole the rock on which the barbarian was wrecked was himself, and that if our present enemy Athens has not again and again annihilated us, we owe it more to her blunders than to your protection;

Indeed, expectations from you have before now been the ruin of some, whose faith induced them to omit preparation. “We hope that none of you will consider these words of remonstrance to be rather words of hostility; men remonstrate with friends who are in error, accusations they reserve for enemies who have wronged them.
text_raw:
Indeed, expectations from you have
before now been the ruin of some, whose faith induced them to omit preparation.

text: Besides, we consider that we have as good a right as any one to point out a neighbour’s faults, particularly when we contemplate the great contrast between the two national characters; a contrast of which, as far as we can see, you have little perception, having never yet considered what sort of antagonists you will encounter in the Athenians, how widely, how absolutely different from yourselves.
text_raw:
Besides, we consider that we have as good a right as
any one to point out a neighbour’s faults, particularly when we contemplate the great
contrast between the two national characters; a contrast of which, as far as we can see, you
have little perception, having never yet considered what sort of antagonists you will
encounter in the Athenians, how widely, how absolutely different from yourselves.

text: The Athenians are addicted to innovation, and their designs are characterized by swiftness alike in conception and execution; you have a genius for keeping what you have got, accompanied by a total want of invention, and when forced to act you never go far enough.
text_raw:
The
Athenians are addicted to innovation, and their designs are characterized by swiftness
alike in conception and execution; you have a genius for keeping what you have got,
accompanied by a total want of invention, and when forced to act you never go far
enough.

text: Again, they are adventurous beyond their power, and daring beyond their judgment, and in danger they are sanguine; your wont is to attempt less than is justified by your power, to mistrust even what is sanctioned by your judgment, and to fancy that from danger there is no release.
text_raw:
Again, they are adventurous beyond their power, and daring beyond their
judgment, and in danger they are sanguine; your wont is to attempt less than is justified by
your power, to mistrust even what is sanctioned by your judgment, and to fancy that from
danger there is no release.

text: Further, there is promptitude on their side against procrastination on yours; they are never at home, you are never from it: for they hope by their absence to extend their acquisitions, you fear by your advance to endanger what you have left behind.
text_raw:
Further, there is promptitude on their side against
procrastination on yours; they are never at home, you are never from it: for they hope by

text: They are swift to follow up a success, and slow to recoil from a reverse.
text_raw: They are swift to follow up a success, and slow to recoil from a reverse.

text: Their bodies they spend ungrudgingly in their country’s cause; their intellect they

text: The deficiency created by the miscarriage of an undertaking is soon filled up by fresh hopes; for they alone are enabled to call a thing hoped for a thing got, by the speed with which they act upon their resolutions.

text: Thus they toil on in trouble and danger all the days of their life, with little opportunity for enjoying, being ever engaged in getting: their only idea of a holiday is to do what the occasion demands, and to them laborious occupation is less of a misfortune than the peace of a quiet life.

Thus they toil on in trouble and danger all the days of their life, with little
opportunity for enjoying, being ever engaged in getting: their only idea of a holiday is to
do what the occasion demands, and to them laborious occupation is less of a misfortune
than the peace of a quiet life.

text: To describe their character in a word, one might truly say that they were born into the world to take no rest themselves and to give none to others. “Such is Athens, your antagonist.

To describe their character in a word, one might truly say

text: And yet, Lacedaemonians, you still delay, and fail to see that peace stays longest with those, who are not more careful to use their power justly than to show their determination not to submit to injustice.

see that peace stays longest with those, who are not more careful to use their power justly

text: On the contrary, your ideal of fair dealing is based on the principle that, if you do not injure others, you need not risk your own fortunes in preventing others from injuring you.

text: Now you could scarcely have succeeded in such a policy even with a neighbour like yourselves; but in the present instance, as we have just shown, your habits are old-fashioned as compared with theirs.

succeeded in such a policy even with a neighbour like yourselves; but in the present

text: It is the law as in art, so in politics, that improvements ever prevail; and though fixed usages may be best for undisturbed communities, constant necessities of action must be accompanied by the constant improvement of methods.

It

text: Thus it happens that the vast experience of Athens has carried her further than you on the path of innovation. “Here, at least, let your procrastination end.

text: For the present, assist your allies and Potidaea in particular, as you promised, by a speedy invasion of Attica, and do not sacrifice friends and kindred to their bitterest enemies, and drive the rest of us in despair to some other alliance.
