text: We assert, therefore, that we conferred on you quite as much as we received.
text_raw: We assert, therefore, that we conferred on you quite as much as we received.

text: For you had a stake to fight for; the cities which you had left were still filled with your homes, and you had the prospect of enjoying them again; and your coming was prompted quite as much by fear for yourselves as for us; at all events, you never appeared till we had nothing left to lose.
text_raw:
For you had a stake to fight for; the cities which you had left were still filled with your
homes, and you had the prospect of enjoying them again; and your coming was prompted
quite as much by fear for yourselves as for us; at all events, you never appeared till we had
nothing left to lose.

text: But we left behind us a city that was a city no longer, and staked our lives for a city that had an existence only in desperate hope, and so bore our full share in your deliverance and in ours.
text_raw:
But we left behind us a city that was a city no longer, and staked our
lives for a city that had an existence only in desperate hope, and so bore our full share in
your deliverance and in ours.

text: But if we had copied others, and allowed fears for our territory to make us give in our adhesion to the Mede before you came, or if we had suffered our ruin to break our spirit and prevent us embarking in our ships, your naval inferiority would have made a sea-fight unnecessary, and his objects would have been peaceably attained. “Surely, Lacedaemonians, neither by the patriotism that we displayed at that crisis, nor
text_raw:
But if we had copied others, and allowed fears for our
territory to make us give in our adhesion to the Mede before you came, or if we had
suffered our ruin to break our spirit and prevent us embarking in our ships, your naval
inferiority would have made a sea-fight unnecessary, and his objects would have been
peaceably attained.
“Surely, Lacedaemonians, neither by the patriotism that we displayed at that crisis, nor

text: by the wisdom of our counsels, do we merit our extreme unpopularity with the Hellenes, not at least unpopularity for our empire.
text_raw:
by the wisdom of our counsels, do we merit our extreme unpopularity with the Hellenes,
not at least unpopularity for our empire.

text: That empire we acquired by no violent means, but because you were unwilling to prosecute to its conclusion the war against the barbarian, and because the allies attached themselves to us and spontaneously asked us to assume the command.
text_raw:
That empire we acquired by no violent means, but
because you were unwilling to prosecute to its conclusion the war against the barbarian,
and because the allies attached themselves to us and spontaneously asked us to assume the
command.

text: And the nature of the case first compelled us to advance our empire to its present height; fear being our principal motive, though honour and interest afterwards came in.
text_raw:
And the nature of the case first compelled us to advance our empire to its
present height; fear being our principal motive, though honour and interest afterwards
came in.

text: And at last, when almost all hated us, when some had already revolted and had been subdued, when you had ceased to be the friends that you once were, and had become objects of suspicion and dislike, it appeared no longer safe to give up our empire; especially as all who left us would fall to you.
text_raw:
And at last, when almost all hated us, when some had already revolted and had
been subdued, when you had ceased to be the friends that you once were, and had become
objects of suspicion and dislike, it appeared no longer safe to give up our empire;
especially as all who left us would fall to you.

text: And no one can quarrel with a people for making, in matters of tremendous risk, the best provision that it can for its interest. “You, at all events, Lacedaemonians, have used your supremacy to settle the states in Peloponnese as is agreeable to you.
text_raw:
And no one can quarrel with a people for
making, in matters of tremendous risk, the best provision that it can for its interest.
“You, at all events, Lacedaemonians, have used your supremacy to settle the states in
Peloponnese as is agreeable to you.

text: And if at the period of which we were speaking you had persevered to the end of the matter, and had incurred hatred in your command, we are sure that you would have made yourselves just as galling to the allies, and would have been forced to choose between a strong government and danger to yourselves.
text_raw:
And if at the period of which we were speaking you
had persevered to the end of the matter, and had incurred hatred in your command, we are
sure that you would have made yourselves just as galling to the allies, and would have
been forced to choose between a strong government and danger to yourselves.

text: It follows that it was not a very wonderful action, or contrary to the common practice of mankind, if we did accept an empire that was offered to us, and refused to give it up under the pressure of three of the strongest motives, fear, honour, and interest.
text_raw:
It follows
that it was not a very wonderful action, or contrary to the common practice of mankind, if
we did accept an empire that was offered to us, and refused to give it up under the pressure
of three of the strongest motives, fear, honour, and interest.

text: And it was not we who set the example, for it has always been law that the weaker should be subject to the stronger.
text_raw:
And it was not we who set the
example, for it has always been law that the weaker should be subject to the stronger.

text: Besides, we believed ourselves to be worthy of our position, and so you thought us till now, when calculations of interest have made you take up the cry of justice—a consideration which no one ever yet brought forward to hinder his ambition when he had a chance of gaining anything by might.
text_raw:
Besides, we believed ourselves to be worthy of our position, and so you thought us till
now, when calculations of interest have made you take up the cry of justice—a
consideration which no one ever yet brought forward to hinder his ambition when he had a
chance of gaining anything by might.

text: And praise is due to all who, if not so superior to human nature as to refuse dominion, yet respect justice more than their position compels them to do. “We imagine that our moderation would be best demonstrated by the conduct of others who should be placed in our position; but even our equity has very unreasonably subjected us to condemnation instead of approval.
text_raw:
And praise is due to all who, if not so superior to
human nature as to refuse dominion, yet respect justice more than their position compels
them to do.
“We imagine that our moderation would be best demonstrated by the conduct of others
who should be placed in our position; but even our equity has very unreasonably subjected
us to condemnation instead of approval.

text: Our abatement of our rights in the contract trials with our allies, and our causing them to be decided by impartial laws at Athens, have gained us the character of being litigious.
text_raw:
Our abatement of our rights in the contract trials
with our allies, and our causing them to be decided by impartial laws at Athens, have
gained us the character of being litigious.

text: And none care to inquire why this reproach is not brought against other imperial powers, who treat their subjects with less moderation than we do; the secret being that where force can be used, law is not needed.
text_raw:
And none care to inquire why this reproach is
not brought against other imperial powers, who treat their subjects with less moderation
than we do; the secret being that where force can be used, law is not needed.

text: But our subjects are so habituated to associate with us as equals that any defeat whatever that clashes with their notions of justice, whether it proceeds from a legal judgment or from the power which our empire gives us, makes them forget to be grateful for being allowed to retain most of their possessions, and more vexed at a part being taken, than if we had from the first cast law aside and openly gratified our covetousness.
text_raw:
But our
subjects are so habituated to associate with us as equals that any defeat whatever that
clashes with their notions of justice, whether it proceeds from a legal judgment or from the
power which our empire gives us, makes them forget to be grateful for being allowed to
retain most of their possessions, and more vexed at a part being taken, than if we had from
the first cast law aside and openly gratified our covetousness.

text: If we had done so, not even would they have disputed that the weaker must give way to the stronger.
text_raw:
If we had done so, not even
would they have disputed that the weaker must give way to the stronger.

text: Men’s indignation, it seems, is more excited by legal wrong than by violent wrong; the first looks like being cheated by an equal, the second like being compelled by a superior.
text_raw:
Men’s
indignation, it seems, is more excited by legal wrong than by violent wrong; the first looks
like being cheated by an equal, the second like being compelled by a superior.

text: At all events they contrived to put up with much worse treatment than this from the Mede, yet they think our rule severe, and this is to be expected, for the present always weighs heavy on the conquered.
text_raw:
At all
events they contrived to put up with much worse treatment than this from the Mede, yet
they think our rule severe, and this is to be expected, for the present always weighs heavy
on the conquered.

text: This at least is certain.
text_raw: This at least is certain.

text: If you were to succeed in overthrowing us and in
text_raw: If you were to succeed in overthrowing us and in

text: taking our place, you would speedily lose the popularity with which fear of us has invested you, if your policy of to-day is at all to tally with the sample that you gave of it during the brief period of your command against the Mede.
text_raw:
taking our place, you would speedily lose the popularity with which fear of us has
invested you, if your policy of to-day is at all to tally with the sample that you gave of it
during the brief period of your command against the Mede.

text: Not only is your life at home regulated by rules and institutions incompatible with those of others, but your citizens abroad act neither on these rules nor on those which are recognized by the rest of Hellas. “Take time then in forming your resolution, as the matter is of great importance; and do not be persuaded by the opinions and complaints of others to bring trouble on yourselves, but consider the vast influence of accident in war, before you are engaged in it.
text_raw:
Not only is your life at home
regulated by rules and institutions incompatible with those of others, but your citizens
abroad act neither on these rules nor on those which are recognized by the rest of Hellas.
“Take time then in forming your resolution, as the matter is of great importance; and do
not be persuaded by the opinions and complaints of others to bring trouble on yourselves,
but consider the vast influence of accident in war, before you are engaged in it.

text: As it continues, it generally becomes an affair of chances, chances from which neither of us is exempt, and whose event we must risk in the dark.
text_raw:
As it
continues, it generally becomes an affair of chances, chances from which neither of us is
exempt, and whose event we must risk in the dark.

text: It is a common mistake in going to war to begin at the wrong end, to act first, and wait for disaster to discuss the matter.
text_raw:
It is a common mistake in going to war
to begin at the wrong end, to act first, and wait for disaster to discuss the matter.

text: But we are not yet by any means so misguided, nor, so far as we can see, are you; accordingly, while it is still open to us both to choose aright, we bid you not to dissolve the treaty, or to break your oaths, but to have our differences settled by arbitration according to our agreement.
text_raw:
But we
are not yet by any means so misguided, nor, so far as we can see, are you; accordingly,
while it is still open to us both to choose aright, we bid you not to dissolve the treaty, or to
break your oaths, but to have our differences settled by arbitration according to our
agreement.

text: Or else we take the gods who heard the oaths to witness, and if you begin hostilities, whatever line of action you choose, we will try not to be behindhand in repelling you.” Such were the words of the Athenians.
text_raw:
Or else we take the gods who heard the oaths to witness, and if you begin
hostilities, whatever line of action you choose, we will try not to be behindhand in
repelling you.”
Such were the words of the Athenians.

text: After the Lacedaemonians had heard the complaints of the allies against the Athenians, and the observations of the latter, they made all withdraw, and consulted by themselves on the question before them.
text_raw:
After the Lacedaemonians had heard the
complaints of the allies against the Athenians, and the observations of the latter, they made
all withdraw, and consulted by themselves on the question before them.

text: The opinions of the majority all led to the same conclusion; the Athenians were open aggressors, and war must be declared at once.
text_raw:
The opinions of
the majority all led to the same conclusion; the Athenians were open aggressors, and war
must be declared at once.

text: But Archidamus, the Lacedaemonian king, came forward, who had the reputation of being at once a wise and a moderate man, and made the following speech: “I have not lived so long, Lacedaemonians, without having had the experience of many wars, and I see those among you of the same age as myself, who will not fall into the common misfortune of longing for war from inexperience or from a belief in its advantage and its safety.
text_raw:
But Archidamus, the Lacedaemonian king, came forward, who
had the reputation of being at once a wise and a moderate man, and made the following
speech:
“I have not lived so long, Lacedaemonians, without having had the experience of many
wars, and I see those among you of the same age as myself, who will not fall into the
common misfortune of longing for war from inexperience or from a belief in its advantage
and its safety.

text: This, the war on which you are now debating, would be one of the greatest magnitude, on a sober consideration of the matter.
text_raw:
This, the war on which you are now debating, would be one of the greatest
magnitude, on a sober consideration of the matter.

text: In a struggle with Peloponnesians and neighbours our strength is of the same character, and it is possible to move swiftly on the different points.
text_raw:
In a struggle with Peloponnesians and
neighbours our strength is of the same character, and it is possible to move swiftly on the
different points.

text: But a struggle with a people who live in a distant land, who have also an extraordinary familiarity with the sea, and who are in the highest state of preparation in every other department; with wealth private and public, with ships, and horses, and heavy infantry, and a population such as no one other Hellenic place can equal, and lastly a number of tributary allies—what can justify us in rashly beginning such a struggle? wherein is our trust that we should rush on it unprepared?
text_raw:
But a struggle with a people who live in a distant land, who have also an
extraordinary familiarity with the sea, and who are in the highest state of preparation in
every other department; with wealth private and public, with ships, and horses, and heavy
infantry, and a population such as no one other Hellenic place can equal, and lastly a
number of tributary allies—what can justify us in rashly beginning such a struggle?
wherein is our trust that we should rush on it unprepared?

text: Is it in our ships?
text_raw: Is it in our ships?

text: There we are inferior; while if we are to practise and become a match for them, time must intervene.
text_raw:
There we are
inferior; while if we are to practise and become a match for them, time must intervene.

text: Is it in our money?
text_raw:
Is
it in our money?

text: There we have a far greater deficiency.
text_raw: There we have a far greater deficiency.

text: We neither have it in our treasury, nor are we ready to contribute it from our private funds.
text_raw:
We neither have it in our treasury,
nor are we ready to contribute it from our private funds.

text: Confidence might possibly be felt in our superiority in heavy infantry and population, which will enable us to invade and devastate their lands.
text_raw:
Confidence might possibly be felt
in our superiority in heavy infantry and population, which will enable us to invade and
devastate their lands.

text: But the Athenians have plenty of other land in their empire, and can import what they want by sea.
text_raw:
But the Athenians have plenty of other land in their empire, and can
import what they want by sea.

text: Again, if we are to attempt an insurrection of their allies, these will have to be supported with a fleet, most of them being islanders.
text_raw:
Again, if we are to attempt an insurrection of their allies,
these will have to be supported with a fleet, most of them being islanders.

text: What then is to
text_raw: What then is to

text: be our war?
text_raw: be our war?

text: For unless we can either beat them at sea, or deprive them of the revenues which feed their navy, we shall meet with little but disaster.
text_raw:
For unless we can either beat them at sea, or deprive them of the revenues
which feed their navy, we shall meet with little but disaster.

text: Meanwhile our honour will be pledged to keeping on, particularly if it be the opinion that we began the quarrel.
text_raw:
Meanwhile our honour will be
pledged to keeping on, particularly if it be the opinion that we began the quarrel.

text: For let us never be elated by the fatal hope of the war being quickly ended by the devastation of their lands.
text_raw:
For let us
never be elated by the fatal hope of the war being quickly ended by the devastation of their
lands.

text: I fear rather that we may leave it as a legacy to our children; so improbable is it that the Athenian spirit will be the slave of their land, or Athenian experience be cowed by war. “Not that I would bid you be so unfeeling as to suffer them to injure your allies, and to refrain from unmasking their intrigues; but I do bid you not to take up arms at once, but to send and remonstrate with them in a tone not too suggestive of war, nor again too suggestive of submission, and to employ the interval in perfecting our own preparations.
text_raw:
I fear rather that we may leave it as a legacy to our children; so improbable is it that
the Athenian spirit will be the slave of their land, or Athenian experience be cowed by
war.
“Not that I would bid you be so unfeeling as to suffer them to injure your allies, and to
refrain from unmasking their intrigues; but I do bid you not to take up arms at once, but to
send and remonstrate with them in a tone not too suggestive of war, nor again too
suggestive of submission, and to employ the interval in perfecting our own preparations.

text: The means will be, first, the acquisition of allies, Hellenic or barbarian it matters not, so long as they are an accession to our strength naval or pecuniary—I say Hellenic or barbarian, because the odium of such an accession to all who like us are the objects of the designs of the Athenians is taken away by the law of self-preservation—and secondly the development of our home resources.
text_raw:
The means will be, first, the acquisition of allies, Hellenic or barbarian it matters not, so
long as they are an accession to our strength naval or pecuniary—I say Hellenic or
barbarian, because the odium of such an accession to all who like us are the objects of the
designs of the Athenians is taken away by the law of self-preservation—and secondly the
development of our home resources.

text: If they listen to our embassy, so much the better; but if not, after the lapse of two or three years our position will have become materially strengthened, and we can then attack them if we think proper.
text_raw:
If they listen to our embassy, so much the better; but
if not, after the lapse of two or three years our position will have become materially
strengthened, and we can then attack them if we think proper.

text: Perhaps by that time the sight of our preparations, backed by language equally significant, will have disposed them to submission, while their land is still untouched, and while their counsels may be directed to the retention of advantages as yet undestroyed.
text_raw:
Perhaps by that time the
sight of our preparations, backed by language equally significant, will have disposed them
to submission, while their land is still untouched, and while their counsels may be directed
to the retention of advantages as yet undestroyed.

text: For the only light in which you can view their land is that of a hostage in your hands, a hostage the more valuable the better it is cultivated.
text_raw:
For the only light in which you can view
their land is that of a hostage in your hands, a hostage the more valuable the better it is
cultivated.

text: This you ought to spare as long as possible, and not make them desperate, and so increase the difficulty of dealing with them.
text_raw:
This you ought to spare as long as possible, and not make them desperate, and
so increase the difficulty of dealing with them.

text: For if while still unprepared, hurried away by the complaints of our allies, we are induced to lay it waste, have a care that we do not bring deep disgrace and deep perplexity upon Peloponnese.
text_raw:
For if while still unprepared, hurried away
by the complaints of our allies, we are induced to lay it waste, have a care that we do not
bring deep disgrace and deep perplexity upon Peloponnese.

text: Complaints, whether of communities or individuals, it is possible to adjust; but war undertaken by a coalition for sectional interests, whose progress there is no means of foreseeing, does not easily admit of creditable settlement. “And none need think it cowardice for a number of confederates to pause before they attack a single city.
text_raw:
Complaints, whether of
communities or individuals, it is possible to adjust; but war undertaken by a coalition for
sectional interests, whose progress there is no means of foreseeing, does not easily admit
of creditable settlement.
“And none need think it cowardice for a number of confederates to pause before they
attack a single city.

text: The Athenians have allies as numerous as our own, and allies that pay tribute, and war is a matter not so much of arms as of money, which makes arms of use.
text_raw:
The Athenians have allies as numerous as our own, and allies that pay
tribute, and war is a matter not so much of arms as of money, which makes arms of use.

text: And this is more than ever true in a struggle between a continental and a maritime power.
text_raw: And this is more than ever true in a struggle between a continental and a maritime power.

text: First, then, let us provide money, and not allow ourselves to be carried away by the talk of our allies before we have done so: as we shall have the largest share of responsibility for the consequences be they good or bad, we have also a right to a tranquil inquiry respecting them. “And the slowness and procrastination, the parts of our character that are most assailed by their criticism, need not make you blush.
text_raw:
First, then, let us provide money, and not allow ourselves to be carried away by the talk of
our allies before we have done so: as we shall have the largest share of responsibility for
the consequences be they good or bad, we have also a right to a tranquil inquiry respecting
them.
“And the slowness and procrastination, the parts of our character that are most assailed
by their criticism, need not make you blush.

text: If we undertake the war without preparation, we should by hastening its commencement only delay its conclusion: further, a free and a famous city has through all time been ours.
text_raw:
If we undertake the war without preparation,
we should by hastening its commencement only delay its conclusion: further, a free and a
famous city has through all time been ours.

text: The quality which they condemn is really nothing but a wise moderation; thanks to its possession, we alone do not become insolent in success and give way less than others in misfortune; we are not carried away by the
text_raw:
The quality which they condemn is really
nothing but a wise moderation; thanks to its possession, we alone do not become insolent
in success and give way less than others in misfortune; we are not carried away by the

text: pleasure of hearing ourselves cheered on to risks which our judgment condemns; nor, if annoyed, are we any the more convinced by attempts to exasperate us by accusation.
text_raw:
pleasure of hearing ourselves cheered on to risks which our judgment condemns; nor, if
annoyed, are we any the more convinced by attempts to exasperate us by accusation.

text: We are both warlike and wise, and it is our sense of order that makes us so.
text_raw:
We
are both warlike and wise, and it is our sense of order that makes us so.

text: We are warlike, because self-control contains honour as a chief constituent, and honour bravery.
text_raw:
We are warlike,
because self-control contains honour as a chief constituent, and honour bravery.

text: And we are wise, because we are educated with too little learning to despise the laws, and with too severe a self-control to disobey them, and are brought up not to be too knowing in useless matters—such as the knowledge which can give a specious criticism of an enemy’s plans in theory, but fails to assail them with equal success in practice—but are taught to consider that the schemes of our enemies are not dissimilar to our own, and that the freaks of chance are not determinable by calculation.
text_raw:
And we
are wise, because we are educated with too little learning to despise the laws, and with too
severe a self-control to disobey them, and are brought up not to be too knowing in useless
matters—such as the knowledge which can give a specious criticism of an enemy’s plans
in theory, but fails to assail them with equal success in practice—but are taught to consider
that the schemes of our enemies are not dissimilar to our own, and that the freaks of
chance are not determinable by calculation.

text: In practice we always base our preparations against an enemy on the assumption that his plans are good; indeed, it is right to rest our hopes not on a belief in his blunders, but on the soundness of our provisions.
text_raw:
In practice we always base our preparations
against an enemy on the assumption that his plans are good; indeed, it is right to rest our
hopes not on a belief in his blunders, but on the soundness of our provisions.

text: Nor ought we to believe that there is much difference between man and man, but to think that the superiority lies with him who is reared in the severest school.
text_raw:
Nor ought
we to believe that there is much difference between man and man, but to think that the
superiority lies with him who is reared in the severest school.

text: These practices, then, which our ancestors have delivered to us, and by whose maintenance we have always profited, must not be given up.
text_raw:
These practices, then, which
our ancestors have delivered to us, and by whose maintenance we have always profited,
must not be given up.

text: And we must not be hurried into deciding in a day’s brief space a question which concerns many lives and fortunes and many cities, and in which honour is deeply involved—but we must decide calmly.
text_raw:
And we must not be hurried into deciding in a day’s brief space a
question which concerns many lives and fortunes and many cities, and in which honour is
deeply involved—but we must decide calmly.

text: This our strength peculiarly enables us to do.
text_raw:
This our strength peculiarly enables us to
do.

text: As for the Athenians, send to them on the matter of Potidaea, send on the matter of the alleged wrongs of the allies, particularly as they are prepared with legal satisfaction; and to proceed against one who offers arbitration as against a wrongdoer, law forbids.
text_raw:
As for the Athenians, send to them on the matter of Potidaea, send on the matter of the
alleged wrongs of the allies, particularly as they are prepared with legal satisfaction; and
to proceed against one who offers arbitration as against a wrongdoer, law forbids.

text: Meanwhile do not omit preparation for war.
text_raw: Meanwhile do not omit preparation for war.

text: This decision will be the best for yourselves, the most terrible to your opponents.” Such were the words of Archidamus.
text_raw:
This decision will be the best for yourselves,
the most terrible to your opponents.”
Such were the words of Archidamus.

text: Last came forward Sthenelaidas, one of the ephors for that year, and spoke to the Lacedaemonians as follows: “The long speech of the Athenians I do not pretend to understand.
They said a good deal in praise of themselves, but nowhere denied that they are injuring our allies and Peloponnese.
text_raw:
They said a good deal
in praise of themselves, but nowhere denied that they are injuring our allies and
Peloponnese.

text: And yet if they behaved well against the Mede then, but ill towards us now, they deserve double punishment for having ceased to be good and for having become bad.
text_raw:
And yet if they behaved well against the Mede then, but ill towards us now,
they deserve double punishment for having ceased to be good and for having become bad.

text: We meanwhile are the same then and now, and shall not, if we are wise, disregard the wrongs of our allies, or put off till to-morrow the duty of assisting those who must suffer to-day.
text_raw:
We meanwhile are the same then and now, and shall not, if we are wise, disregard the
wrongs of our allies, or put off till to-morrow the duty of assisting those who must suffer
to-day.

text: Others have much money and ships and horses, but we have good allies whom we must not give up to the Athenians, nor by lawsuits and words decide the matter, as it is anything but in word that we are harmed, but render instant and powerful help.
text_raw:
Others have much money and ships and horses, but we have good allies whom we
must not give up to the Athenians, nor by lawsuits and words decide the matter, as it is
anything but in word that we are harmed, but render instant and powerful help.

text: And let us not be told that it is fitting for us to deliberate under injustice; long deliberation is rather fitting for those who have injustice in contemplation.
text_raw:
And let us
not be told that it is fitting for us to deliberate under injustice; long deliberation is rather
fitting for those who have injustice in contemplation.

text: Vote therefore, Lacedaemonians, for war, as the honour of Sparta demands, and neither allow the further aggrandizement of Athens, nor betray our allies to ruin, but with the gods let us advance against the aggressors.” With these words he, as ephor, himself put the question to the assembly of the Lacedaemonians.
text_raw:
Vote therefore, Lacedaemonians, for
war, as the honour of Sparta demands, and neither allow the further aggrandizement of
Athens, nor betray our allies to ruin, but with the gods let us advance against the
aggressors.”
With these words he, as ephor, himself put the question to the assembly of the
Lacedaemonians.

text: He said that he could not determine which was the loudest acclamation (their mode of decision is by acclamation not by voting); the fact being that he wished to make them declare their opinion openly and thus to increase their ardour for war.
text_raw:
He said that he could not determine which was the loudest acclamation
(their mode of decision is by acclamation not by voting); the fact being that he wished to
make them declare their opinion openly and thus to increase their ardour for war.

text: Accordingly he said: “All Lacedaemonians who are of opinion that the treaty has been broken, and that Athens is guilty, leave your seats and go there,” pointing out a certain place; “all who are of the opposite opinion, there.” They accordingly stood up and divided; and those who held that the treaty had been broken were in a decided majority.
text_raw:
Accordingly he said: “All Lacedaemonians who are of opinion that the treaty has been
broken, and that Athens is guilty, leave your seats and go there,” pointing out a certain
place; “all who are of the opposite opinion, there.” They accordingly stood up and
divided; and those who held that the treaty had been broken were in a decided majority.

text: Summoning the allies, they told them that their opinion was that Athens had been guilty of injustice, but that they wished to convoke all the allies and put it to the vote; in order that they might make war, if they decided to do so, on a common resolution.
text_raw:
Summoning the allies, they told them that their opinion was that Athens had been guilty of
injustice, but that they wished to convoke all the allies and put it to the vote; in order that
they might make war, if they decided to do so, on a common resolution.

text: Having thus gained their point, the delegates returned home at once; the Athenian envoys a little later, when they had dispatched the objects of their mission.
text_raw:
Having thus
gained their point, the delegates returned home at once; the Athenian envoys a little later,
when they had dispatched the objects of their mission.

text: This decision of the assembly, judging that the treaty had been broken, was made in the fourteenth year of the thirty years’ truce, which was entered into after the affair of Euboea.
text_raw:
This decision of the assembly,
judging that the treaty had been broken, was made in the fourteenth year of the thirty
years’ truce, which was entered into after the affair of Euboea.

text: The Lacedaemonians voted that the treaty had been broken, and that the war must be declared, not so much because they were persuaded by the arguments of the allies, as because they feared the growth of the power of the Athenians, seeing most of Hellas already subject to them.
text_raw:
The Lacedaemonians voted that the treaty had been broken, and that the war must be
declared, not so much because they were persuaded by the arguments of the allies, as
because they feared the growth of the power of the Athenians, seeing most of Hellas
already subject to them.

text: From the end of the Persian to the beginning of the Peloponnesian War—The Progress from Supremacy to Empire The way in which Athens came to be placed in the circumstances under which her power grew was this.
text_raw:
From the end of the Persian to the beginning of the Peloponnesian War—The Progress
from Supremacy to Empire
The way in which Athens came to be placed in the circumstances under which her power
grew was this.

text: After the Medes had returned from Europe, defeated by sea and land by the Hellenes, and after those of them who had fled with their ships to Mycale had been destroyed, Leotychides, king of the Lacedaemonians, the commander of the Hellenes at Mycale, departed home with the allies from Peloponnese.
text_raw:
After the Medes had returned from Europe, defeated by sea and land by the
Hellenes, and after those of them who had fled with their ships to Mycale had been
destroyed, Leotychides, king of the Lacedaemonians, the commander of the Hellenes at
Mycale, departed home with the allies from Peloponnese.

text: But the Athenians and the allies from Ionia and Hellespont, who had now revolted from the King, remained and laid siege to Sestos, which was still held by the Medes.
text_raw:
But the Athenians and the allies
from Ionia and Hellespont, who had now revolted from the King, remained and laid siege
to Sestos, which was still held by the Medes.

text: After wintering before it, they became masters of the place on its evacuation by the barbarians; and after this they sailed away from Hellespont to their respective cities.
text_raw:
After wintering before it, they became
masters of the place on its evacuation by the barbarians; and after this they sailed away
from Hellespont to their respective cities.

text: Meanwhile the Athenian people, after the departure of the barbarian from their country, at once proceeded to carry over their children and wives, and such property as they had left, from the places where they had deposited them, and prepared to rebuild their city and their walls.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the Athenian people, after the
departure of the barbarian from their country, at once proceeded to carry over their
children and wives, and such property as they had left, from the places where they had
deposited them, and prepared to rebuild their city and their walls.

text: For only isolated portions of the circumference had been left standing, and most of the houses were in ruins; though a few remained, in which the Persian grandees had taken up their quarters.
Perceiving what they were going to do, the Lacedaemonians sent an embassy to Athens.
text_raw: Perceiving what they were going to do, the Lacedaemonians sent an embassy to Athens.

text: They would have themselves preferred to see neither her nor any other city in possession of a wall; though here they acted principally at the instigation of their allies, who were alarmed at the strength of her newly acquired navy and the valour which she had displayed in the war with the Medes.
text_raw:
They would have themselves preferred to see neither her nor any other city in possession
of a wall; though here they acted principally at the instigation of their allies, who were
alarmed at the strength of her newly acquired navy and the valour which she had displayed
in the war with the Medes.

text: They begged her not only to abstain from building walls for herself, but also to join them in throwing down the walls that still held together of the ultra-Peloponnesian cities.
text_raw:
They begged her not only to abstain from building walls for
herself, but also to join them in throwing down the walls that still held together of the
ultra-Peloponnesian cities.

text: The real meaning of their advice, the suspicion that it contained against the Athenians, was not proclaimed; it was urged that so the barbarian, in the event of a third invasion, would not have any strong place, such as he now had in Thebes, for his base of operations; and that Peloponnese would suffice for all as a base both for retreat and offence.
text_raw:
The real meaning of their advice, the suspicion that it contained
against the Athenians, was not proclaimed; it was urged that so the barbarian, in the event
of a third invasion, would not have any strong place, such as he now had in Thebes, for his
base of operations; and that Peloponnese would suffice for all as a base both for retreat
and offence.

text: After the Lacedaemonians had thus spoken, they were, on the advice of Themistocles, immediately dismissed by the Athenians, with the answer that ambassadors should be sent to Sparta to discuss the question.
text_raw:
After the Lacedaemonians had thus spoken, they were, on the advice of
Themistocles, immediately dismissed by the Athenians, with the answer that ambassadors
should be sent to Sparta to discuss the question.

text: Themistocles told the Athenians to send him off with all speed to Lacedaemon, but not to dispatch his colleagues as soon as they had selected them, but to wait until they had raised their wall to the height from which defence was possible.
text_raw:
Themistocles told the Athenians to send
him off with all speed to Lacedaemon, but not to dispatch his colleagues as soon as they
had selected them, but to wait until they had raised their wall to the height from which
defence was possible.

text: Meanwhile the whole population in the city was to labour at the wall, the Athenians, their wives, and their children, sparing no edifice, private or public, which might be of any use to the work, but throwing all down.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the whole population in the city was to labour at the
wall, the Athenians, their wives, and their children, sparing no edifice, private or public,
which might be of any use to the work, but throwing all down.

text: After giving these instructions, and adding that he would be responsible for all other matters there, he departed.
text_raw:
After giving these
instructions, and adding that he would be responsible for all other matters there, he
departed.

text: Arrived at Lacedaemon he did not seek an audience with the authorities, but tried to gain time and made excuses.
text_raw:
Arrived at Lacedaemon he did not seek an audience with the authorities, but
tried to gain time and made excuses.

text: When any of the government asked him why he did not appear in the assembly, he would say that he was waiting for his colleagues, who had been detained in Athens by some engagement; however, that he expected their speedy arrival, and wondered that they were not yet there.
text_raw:
When any of the government asked him why he did
not appear in the assembly, he would say that he was waiting for his colleagues, who had
been detained in Athens by some engagement; however, that he expected their speedy
arrival, and wondered that they were not yet there.

text: At first the Lacedaemonians trusted the words of Themistocles, through their friendship for him; but when others arrived, all
text_raw:
At first the Lacedaemonians trusted the
words of Themistocles, through their friendship for him; but when others arrived, all

text: distinctly declaring that the work was going on and already attaining some elevation, they did not know how to disbelieve it.
text_raw:
distinctly declaring that the work was going on and already attaining some elevation, they
did not know how to disbelieve it.

text: Aware of this, he told them that rumours are deceptive, and should not be trusted; they should send some reputable persons from Sparta to inspect, whose report might be trusted.
text_raw:
Aware of this, he told them that rumours are deceptive,
and should not be trusted; they should send some reputable persons from Sparta to inspect,
whose report might be trusted.

text: They dispatched them accordingly.
text_raw: They dispatched them accordingly.

text: Concerning these Themistocles secretly sent word to the Athenians to detain them as far as possible without putting them under open constraint, and not to let them go until they had themselves returned.
text_raw:
Concerning these
Themistocles secretly sent word to the Athenians to detain them as far as possible without
putting them under open constraint, and not to let them go until they had themselves
returned.

text: For his colleagues had now joined him, Abronichus, son of Lysicles, and Aristides, son of Lysimachus, with the news that the wall was sufficiently advanced; and he feared that when the Lacedaemonians heard the facts, they might refuse to let them go.
text_raw:
For his colleagues had now joined him, Abronichus, son of Lysicles, and
Aristides, son of Lysimachus, with the news that the wall was sufficiently advanced; and
he feared that when the Lacedaemonians heard the facts, they might refuse to let them go.

text: So the Athenians detained the envoys according to his message, and Themistocles had an audience with the Lacedaemonians, and at last openly told them that Athens was now fortified sufficiently to protect its inhabitants; that any embassy which the Lacedaemonians or their allies might wish to send to them should in future proceed on the assumption that the people to whom they were going was able to distinguish both its own and the general interests.
text_raw:
So the Athenians detained the envoys according to his message, and Themistocles had an
audience with the Lacedaemonians, and at last openly told them that Athens was now
fortified sufficiently to protect its inhabitants; that any embassy which the
Lacedaemonians or their allies might wish to send to them should in future proceed on the
assumption that the people to whom they were going was able to distinguish both its own
and the general interests.

text: That when the Athenians thought fit to abandon their city and to embark in their ships, they ventured on that perilous step without consulting them; and that on the other hand, wherever they had deliberated with the Lacedaemonians, they had proved themselves to be in judgment second to none.
text_raw:
That when the Athenians thought fit to abandon their city and to
embark in their ships, they ventured on that perilous step without consulting them; and
that on the other hand, wherever they had deliberated with the Lacedaemonians, they had
proved themselves to be in judgment second to none.

text: That they now thought it fit that their city should have a wall, and that this would be more for the advantage of both the citizens of Athens and the Hellenic confederacy; for without equal military strength it was impossible to contribute equal or fair counsel to the common interest.
text_raw:
That they now thought it fit that their
city should have a wall, and that this would be more for the advantage of both the citizens
of Athens and the Hellenic confederacy; for without equal military strength it was
impossible to contribute equal or fair counsel to the common interest.

text: It followed, he observed, either that all the members of the confederacy should be without walls, or that the present step should be considered a right one.
text_raw:
It followed, he
observed, either that all the members of the confederacy should be without walls, or that
the present step should be considered a right one.

text: The Lacedaemonians did not betray any open signs of anger against the Athenians at what they heard.
text_raw:
The Lacedaemonians did not betray any open signs of anger against the Athenians at
what they heard.

text: The embassy, it seems, was prompted not by a desire to obstruct, but to guide the counsels of their government: besides, Spartan feeling was at that time very friendly towards Athens on account of the patriotism which she had displayed in the struggle with the Mede.
text_raw:
The embassy, it seems, was prompted not by a desire to obstruct, but to
guide the counsels of their government: besides, Spartan feeling was at that time very
friendly towards Athens on account of the patriotism which she had displayed in the
struggle with the Mede.

text: Still the defeat of their wishes could not but cause them secret annoyance.
text_raw:
Still the defeat of their wishes could not but cause them secret
annoyance.

text: The envoys of each state departed home without complaint.
text_raw: The envoys of each state departed home without complaint.

text: In this way the Athenians walled their city in a little while.
text_raw: In this way the Athenians walled their city in a little while.

text: To this day the building shows signs of the haste of its execution; the foundations are laid of stones of all kinds, and in some places not wrought or fitted, but placed just in the order in which they were brought by the different hands; and many columns, too, from tombs, and sculptured stones were put in with the rest.
text_raw:
To this day the building
shows signs of the haste of its execution; the foundations are laid of stones of all kinds,
and in some places not wrought or fitted, but placed just in the order in which they were
brought by the different hands; and many columns, too, from tombs, and sculptured stones
were put in with the rest.

text: For the bounds of the city were extended at every point of the circumference; and so they laid hands on everything without exception in their haste.
text_raw:
For the bounds of the city were extended at every point of the
circumference; and so they laid hands on everything without exception in their haste.

text: Themistocles also persuaded them to finish the walls of Piraeus, which had been begun before, in his year of office as archon; being influenced alike by the fineness of a locality that has three natural harbours, and by the great start which the Athenians would gain in the acquisition of power by becoming a naval people.
text_raw:
Themistocles also persuaded them to finish the walls of Piraeus, which had been begun
before, in his year of office as archon; being influenced alike by the fineness of a locality
that has three natural harbours, and by the great start which the Athenians would gain in
the acquisition of power by becoming a naval people.

text: For he first ventured to tell them to stick to the sea and forthwith began to lay the foundations of the empire.
text_raw:
For he first ventured to tell them to
stick to the sea and forthwith began to lay the foundations of the empire.

text: It was by his advice, too, that they built the walls of that thickness which can still be discerned round Piraeus, the stones being brought up by two wagons meeting each other.
text_raw:
It was by his
advice, too, that they built the walls of that thickness which can still be discerned round
Piraeus, the stones being brought up by two wagons meeting each other.

text: Between the walls thus formed there was neither rubble nor mortar, but great stones hewn square and fitted together, cramped to each other on the outside with iron and lead.
text_raw:
Between the
walls thus formed there was neither rubble nor mortar, but great stones hewn square and
fitted together, cramped to each other on the outside with iron and lead.

text: About half the
text_raw: About half the

text: height that he intended was finished.
text_raw: height that he intended was finished.

text: His idea was by their size and thickness to keep off the attacks of an enemy; he thought that they might be adequately defended by a small garrison of invalids, and the rest be freed for service in the fleet.
text_raw:
His idea was by their size and thickness to keep off
the attacks of an enemy; he thought that they might be adequately defended by a small
garrison of invalids, and the rest be freed for service in the fleet.

text: For the fleet claimed most of his attention.
text_raw:
For the fleet claimed
most of his attention.

text: He saw, as I think, that the approach by sea was easier for the king’s army than that by land: he also thought Piraeus more valuable than the upper city; indeed, he was always advising the Athenians, if a day should come when they were hard pressed by land, to go down into Piraeus, and defy the world with their fleet.
text_raw:
He saw, as I think, that the approach by sea was easier for the king’s
army than that by land: he also thought Piraeus more valuable than the upper city; indeed,
he was always advising the Athenians, if a day should come when they were hard pressed
by land, to go down into Piraeus, and defy the world with their fleet.

text: Thus, therefore, the Athenians completed their wall, and commenced their other buildings immediately after the retreat of the Mede.
text_raw:
Thus, therefore, the
Athenians completed their wall, and commenced their other buildings immediately after
the retreat of the Mede.

text: Meanwhile Pausanias, son of Cleombrotus, was sent out from Lacedaemon as commander-in-chief of the Hellenes, with twenty ships from Peloponnese.
text_raw:
Meanwhile Pausanias, son of Cleombrotus, was sent out from Lacedaemon as
commander-in-chief of the Hellenes, with twenty ships from Peloponnese.

text: With him sailed the Athenians with thirty ships, and a number of the other allies.
text_raw:
With him sailed
the Athenians with thirty ships, and a number of the other allies.

text: They made an expedition against Cyprus and subdued most of the island, and afterwards against Byzantium, which was in the hands of the Medes, and compelled it to surrender.
text_raw:
They made an expedition
against Cyprus and subdued most of the island, and afterwards against Byzantium, which
was in the hands of the Medes, and compelled it to surrender.

text: This event took place while the Spartans were still supreme.
text_raw:
This event took place while
the Spartans were still supreme.

text: But the violence of Pausanias had already begun to be disagreeable to the Hellenes, particularly to the Ionians and the newly liberated populations.
text_raw:
But the violence of Pausanias had already begun to be
disagreeable to the Hellenes, particularly to the Ionians and the newly liberated
populations.

text: These resorted to the Athenians and requested them as their kinsmen to become their leaders, and to stop any attempt at violence on the part of Pausanias.
text_raw:
These resorted to the Athenians and requested them as their kinsmen to
become their leaders, and to stop any attempt at violence on the part of Pausanias.

text: The Athenians accepted their overtures, and determined to put down any attempt of the kind and to settle everything else as their interests might seem to demand.
text_raw:
The
Athenians accepted their overtures, and determined to put down any attempt of the kind
and to settle everything else as their interests might seem to demand.

text: In the meantime the Lacedaemonians recalled Pausanias for an investigation of the reports which had reached them.
text_raw:
In the meantime the
Lacedaemonians recalled Pausanias for an investigation of the reports which had reached
them.

text: Manifold and grave accusations had been brought against him by Hellenes arriving in Sparta; and, to all appearance, there had been in him more of the mimicry of a despot than of the attitude of a general.
text_raw:
Manifold and grave accusations had been brought against him by Hellenes arriving
in Sparta; and, to all appearance, there had been in him more of the mimicry of a despot
than of the attitude of a general.

text: As it happened, his recall came just at the time when the hatred which he had inspired had induced the allies to desert him, the soldiers from Peloponnese excepted, and to range themselves by the side of the Athenians.
text_raw:
As it happened, his recall came just at the time when the
hatred which he had inspired had induced the allies to desert him, the soldiers from
Peloponnese excepted, and to range themselves by the side of the Athenians.

text: On his arrival at Lacedaemon, he was censured for his private acts of oppression, but was acquitted on the heaviest counts and pronounced not guilty; it must be known that the charge of Medism formed one of the principal, and to all appearance one of the best founded, articles against him.
text_raw:
On his
arrival at Lacedaemon, he was censured for his private acts of oppression, but was
acquitted on the heaviest counts and pronounced not guilty; it must be known that the
charge of Medism formed one of the principal, and to all appearance one of the best
founded, articles against him.

text: The Lacedaemonians did not, however, restore him to his command, but sent out Dorkis and certain others with a small force; who found the allies no longer inclined to concede to them the supremacy.
text_raw:
The Lacedaemonians did not, however, restore him to his
command, but sent out Dorkis and certain others with a small force; who found the allies
no longer inclined to concede to them the supremacy.

text: Perceiving this they departed, and the Lacedaemonians did not send out any to succeed them.
text_raw:
Perceiving this they departed, and
the Lacedaemonians did not send out any to succeed them.

text: They feared for those who went out a deterioration similar to that observable in Pausanias; besides, they desired to be rid of the Median War, and were satisfied of the competency of the Athenians for the position, and of their friendship at the time towards themselves.
text_raw:
They feared for those who
went out a deterioration similar to that observable in Pausanias; besides, they desired to be
rid of the Median War, and were satisfied of the competency of the Athenians for the
position, and of their friendship at the time towards themselves.

text: The Athenians, having thus succeeded to the supremacy by the voluntary act of the allies through their hatred of Pausanias, fixed which cities were to contribute money against the barbarian, which ships; their professed object being to retaliate for their sufferings by ravaging the King’s country.
text_raw:
The Athenians, having thus succeeded to the supremacy by the voluntary act of the allies
through their hatred of Pausanias, fixed which cities were to contribute money against the
barbarian, which ships; their professed object being to retaliate for their sufferings by
ravaging the King’s country.

text: Now was the time that the office of “Treasurers for Hellas” was first instituted by the Athenians.
text_raw:
Now was the time that the office of “Treasurers for Hellas”
was first instituted by the Athenians.

text: These officers received the tribute, as the money contributed was called.
text_raw:
These officers received the tribute, as the money
contributed was called.

text: The tribute was first fixed at four hundred and sixty talents.
text_raw: The tribute was first fixed at four hundred and sixty talents.

text: The common treasury was at Delos, and the congresses were held in the temple.
text_raw:
The
common treasury was at Delos, and the congresses were held in the temple.

text: Their supremacy commenced with independent allies who acted on the resolutions of a common
text_raw:
Their
supremacy commenced with independent allies who acted on the resolutions of a common

text: congress.
text_raw: congress.

text: It was marked by the following undertakings in war and in administration during the interval between the Median and the present war, against the barbarian, against their own rebel allies, and against the Peloponnesian powers which would come in contact with them on various occasions.
text_raw:
It was marked by the following undertakings in war and in administration during
the interval between the Median and the present war, against the barbarian, against their
own rebel allies, and against the Peloponnesian powers which would come in contact with

text: My excuse for relating these events, and for venturing on this digression, is that this passage of history has been omitted by all my predecessors, who have confined themselves either to Hellenic history before the Median War, or the Median War itself.
text_raw:
My excuse for relating these events, and for venturing on this
digression, is that this passage of history has been omitted by all my predecessors, who

text: Hellanicus, it is true, did touch on these events in his Athenian history; but he is somewhat concise and not accurate in his dates.
text_raw:
Hellanicus, it is true, did touch on these events in his Athenian history; but he is

text: Besides, the history of these events contains an explanation of the growth of the Athenian empire.
text_raw:
Besides, the history of these events
contains an explanation of the growth of the Athenian empire.

text: First the Athenians besieged and captured Eion on the Strymon from the Medes, and made slaves of the inhabitants, being under the command of Cimon, son of Miltiades.
text_raw:
First the Athenians besieged and captured Eion on the Strymon from the Medes, and
made slaves of the inhabitants, being under the command of Cimon, son of Miltiades.

text: Next they enslaved Scyros, the island in the Aegean, containing a Dolopian population, and colonized it themselves.
text_raw:
Next they enslaved Scyros, the island in the Aegean, containing a Dolopian population,
and colonized it themselves.

text: This was followed by a war against Carystus, in which the rest of Euboea remained neutral, and which was ended by surrender on conditions.
text_raw:
This was followed by a war against Carystus, in which the
rest of Euboea remained neutral, and which was ended by surrender on conditions.

text: After this Naxos left the confederacy, and a war ensued, and she had to return after a siege; this was the first instance of the engagement being broken by the subjugation of an allied city, a precedent which was followed by that of the rest in the order which circumstances prescribed.
text_raw:
After
this Naxos left the confederacy, and a war ensued, and she had to return after a siege; this

text: Of all the causes of defection, that connected with arrears of tribute and vessels, and with failure of service, was the chief; for the Athenians were very severe and exacting, and made themselves offensive by applying the screw of necessity to men who were not used to and in fact not disposed for any continuous labour.
text_raw:
Of all the causes of defection, that connected with arrears of tribute and
vessels, and with failure of service, was the chief; for the Athenians were very severe and
exacting, and made themselves offensive by applying the screw of necessity to men who
were not used to and in fact not disposed for any continuous labour.

text: In some other respects the Athenians were not the old popular rulers they had been at first; and if they had more than their fair share of service, it was correspondingly easy for them to reduce any that tried to leave the confederacy.
text_raw:
In some other respects
the Athenians were not the old popular rulers they had been at first; and if they had more
than their fair share of service, it was correspondingly easy for them to reduce any that
tried to leave the confederacy.

text: For this the allies had themselves to blame; the wish to get off service making most of them arrange to pay their share of the expense in money instead of in ships, and so to avoid having to leave their homes.
text_raw:
For this the allies had themselves to blame; the wish to get
off service making most of them arrange to pay their share of the expense in money
instead of in ships, and so to avoid having to leave their homes.

text: Thus while Athens was increasing her navy with the funds which they contributed, a revolt always found them without resources or experience for war.
text_raw:
Thus while Athens was
increasing her navy with the funds which they contributed, a revolt always found them

text: Next we come to the actions by land and by sea at the river Eurymedon, between the Athenians with their allies, and the Medes, when the Athenians won both battles on the same day under the conduct of Cimon, son of Miltiades, and captured and destroyed the whole Phoenician fleet, consisting of two hundred vessels.
text_raw:
Next we come to the actions by land and by sea at the river Eurymedon, between the
Athenians with their allies, and the Medes, when the Athenians won both battles on the

text: Some time afterwards occurred the defection of the Thasians, caused by disagreements about the marts on the opposite coast of Thrace, and about the mine in their possession.
text_raw:
Some time afterwards occurred
the defection of the Thasians, caused by disagreements about the marts on the opposite

text: Sailing with a fleet to Thasos, the Athenians defeated them at sea and effected a landing on the island.
text_raw:
Sailing with a fleet to Thasos, the

text: About the same time they sent ten thousand settlers of their own citizens and the allies to settle the place then called Ennea Hodoi or Nine Ways, now Amphipolis.
text_raw:
About the same time
they sent ten thousand settlers of their own citizens and the allies to settle the place then

text: They succeeded in gaining possession of Ennea Hodoi from the Edonians, but on advancing into the interior of Thrace were cut off in Drabescus, a town of the Edonians, by the assembled Thracians, who regarded the settlement of the place Ennea Hodoi as an act of hostility.
text_raw:
They succeeded in gaining
possession of Ennea Hodoi from the Edonians, but on advancing into the interior of
Thrace were cut off in Drabescus, a town of the Edonians, by the assembled Thracians,
