text: Meanwhile the Thasians being defeated in the field and suffering siege, appealed to Lacedaemon, and desired her to assist them by an invasion of Attica.
text_raw:
Meanwhile
the Thasians being defeated in the field and suffering siege, appealed to Lacedaemon, and
desired her to assist them by an invasion of Attica.

text: Without informing Athens, she promised and intended to do so, but was prevented by the occurrence of the earthquake, accompanied by the secession of the Helots and the Thuriats and Aethaeans of the
text_raw:
Without informing Athens, she
promised and intended to do so, but was prevented by the occurrence of the earthquake,
accompanied by the secession of the Helots and the Thuriats and Aethaeans of the

text: Perioeci to Ithome.
text_raw: Perioeci to Ithome.

text: Most of the Helots were the descendants of the old Messenians that were enslaved in the famous war; and so all of them came to be called Messenians.
text_raw:
Most of the Helots were the descendants of the old Messenians that
were enslaved in the famous war; and so all of them came to be called Messenians.

text: So the Lacedaemonians being engaged in a war with the rebels in Ithome, the Thasians in the third year of the siege obtained terms from the Athenians by razing their walls, delivering up their ships, and arranging to pay the moneys demanded at once, and tribute in future; giving up their possessions on the continent together with the mine.
text_raw:
So the
Lacedaemonians being engaged in a war with the rebels in Ithome, the Thasians in the
third year of the siege obtained terms from the Athenians by razing their walls, delivering
up their ships, and arranging to pay the moneys demanded at once, and tribute in future;
giving up their possessions on the continent together with the mine.

text: The Lacedaemonians, meanwhile, finding the war against the rebels in Ithome likely to last, invoked the aid of their allies, and especially of the Athenians, who came in some force under the command of Cimon.
text_raw:
The Lacedaemonians, meanwhile, finding the war against the rebels in Ithome likely to
last, invoked the aid of their allies, and especially of the Athenians, who came in some
force under the command of Cimon.

text: The reason for this pressing summons lay in their reputed skill in siege operations; a long siege had taught the Lacedaemonians their own deficiency in this art, else they would have taken the place by assault.
text_raw:
The reason for this pressing summons lay in their
reputed skill in siege operations; a long siege had taught the Lacedaemonians their own
deficiency in this art, else they would have taken the place by assault.

text: The first open quarrel between the Lacedaemonians and Athenians arose out of this expedition.
text_raw:
The first open
quarrel between the Lacedaemonians and Athenians arose out of this expedition.

text: The Lacedaemonians, when assault failed to take the place, apprehensive of the enterprising and revolutionary character of the Athenians, and further looking upon them as of alien extraction, began to fear that, if they remained, they might be tempted by the besieged in Ithome to attempt some political changes.
text_raw:
The
Lacedaemonians, when assault failed to take the place, apprehensive of the enterprising
and revolutionary character of the Athenians, and further looking upon them as of alien
extraction, began to fear that, if they remained, they might be tempted by the besieged in
Ithome to attempt some political changes.

text: They accordingly dismissed them alone of the allies, without declaring their suspicions, but merely saying that they had now no need of them.
text_raw:
They accordingly dismissed them alone of the
allies, without declaring their suspicions, but merely saying that they had now no need of
them.

text: But the Athenians, aware that their dismissal did not proceed from the more honourable reason of the two, but from suspicions which had been conceived, went away deeply offended, and conscious of having done nothing to merit such treatment from the Lacedaemonians; and the instant that they returned home they broke off the alliance which had been made against the Mede, and allied themselves with Sparta’s enemy Argos; each of the contracting parties taking the same oaths and making the same alliance with the Thessalians.
text_raw:
But the Athenians, aware that their dismissal did not proceed from the more
honourable reason of the two, but from suspicions which had been conceived, went away
deeply offended, and conscious of having done nothing to merit such treatment from the
Lacedaemonians; and the instant that they returned home they broke off the alliance which
had been made against the Mede, and allied themselves with Sparta’s enemy Argos; each
of the contracting parties taking the same oaths and making the same alliance with the
Thessalians.

text: Meanwhile the rebels in Ithome, unable to prolong further a ten years’ resistance, surrendered to Lacedaemon; the conditions being that they should depart from Peloponnese under safe conduct, and should never set foot in it again: any one who might hereafter be found there was to be the slave of his captor.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the rebels in Ithome, unable to prolong further a ten years’ resistance,
surrendered to Lacedaemon; the conditions being that they should depart from
Peloponnese under safe conduct, and should never set foot in it again: any one who might
hereafter be found there was to be the slave of his captor.

text: It must be known that the Lacedaemonians had an old oracle from Delphi, to the effect that they should let go the suppliant of Zeus at Ithome.
text_raw:
It must be known that the
Lacedaemonians had an old oracle from Delphi, to the effect that they should let go the
suppliant of Zeus at Ithome.

text: So they went forth with their children and their wives, and being received by Athens from the hatred that she now felt for the Lacedaemonians, were located at Naupactus, which she had lately taken from the Ozolian Locrians.
text_raw:
So they went forth with their children and their wives, and
being received by Athens from the hatred that she now felt for the Lacedaemonians, were
located at Naupactus, which she had lately taken from the Ozolian Locrians.

text: The Athenians received another addition to their confederacy in the Megarians; who left the Lacedaemonian alliance, annoyed by a war about boundaries forced on them by Corinth.
text_raw:
The
Athenians received another addition to their confederacy in the Megarians; who left the
Lacedaemonian alliance, annoyed by a war about boundaries forced on them by Corinth.

text: The Athenians occupied Megara and Pegae, and built the Megarians their long walls from the city to Nisaea, in which they placed an Athenian garrison.
text_raw:
The Athenians occupied Megara and Pegae, and built the Megarians their long walls from
the city to Nisaea, in which they placed an Athenian garrison.

text: This was the principal cause of the Corinthians conceiving such a deadly hatred against Athens.
text_raw:
This was the principal cause
of the Corinthians conceiving such a deadly hatred against Athens.

text: Meanwhile Inaros, son of Psammetichus, a Libyan king of the Libyans on the Egyptian border, having his headquarters at Marea, the town above Pharos, caused a revolt of almost the whole of Egypt from King Artaxerxes and, placing himself at its head, invited the Athenians to his assistance.
text_raw:
Meanwhile Inaros, son of Psammetichus, a Libyan king of the Libyans on the Egyptian
border, having his headquarters at Marea, the town above Pharos, caused a revolt of
almost the whole of Egypt from King Artaxerxes and, placing himself at its head, invited
the Athenians to his assistance.

text: Abandoning a Cyprian expedition upon which they happened to be engaged with two hundred ships of their own and their allies, they arrived in Egypt and sailed from the sea into the Nile, and making themselves masters of the river
text_raw:
Abandoning a Cyprian expedition upon which they
happened to be engaged with two hundred ships of their own and their allies, they arrived
in Egypt and sailed from the sea into the Nile, and making themselves masters of the river

text: and two-thirds of Memphis, addressed themselves to the attack of the remaining third, which is called White Castle.
text_raw:
and two-thirds of Memphis, addressed themselves to the attack of the remaining third,
which is called White Castle.

text: Within it were Persians and Medes who had taken refuge there, and Egyptians who had not joined the rebellion.
text_raw:
Within it were Persians and Medes who had taken refuge
there, and Egyptians who had not joined the rebellion.

text: Meanwhile the Athenians, making a descent from their fleet upon Haliae, were engaged by a force of Corinthians and Epidaurians; and the Corinthians were victorious.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the Athenians, making a descent from their fleet upon Haliae, were engaged
by a force of Corinthians and Epidaurians; and the Corinthians were victorious.

text: Afterwards the Athenians engaged the Peloponnesian fleet off Cecruphalia; and the Athenians were victorious.
text_raw:
Afterwards the Athenians engaged the Peloponnesian fleet off Cecruphalia; and the
Athenians were victorious.

text: Subsequently war broke out between Aegina and Athens, and there was a great battle at sea off Aegina between the Athenians and Aeginetans, each being aided by their allies; in which victory remained with the Athenians, who took seventy of the enemy’s ships, and landed in the country and commenced a siege under the command of Leocrates, son of Stroebus.
text_raw:
Subsequently war broke out between Aegina and Athens, and
there was a great battle at sea off Aegina between the Athenians and Aeginetans, each
being aided by their allies; in which victory remained with the Athenians, who took
seventy of the enemy’s ships, and landed in the country and commenced a siege under the
command of Leocrates, son of Stroebus.

text: Upon this the Peloponnesians, desirous of aiding the Aeginetans, threw into Aegina a force of three hundred heavy infantry, who had before been serving with the Corinthians and Epidaurians.
text_raw:
Upon this the Peloponnesians, desirous of aiding
the Aeginetans, threw into Aegina a force of three hundred heavy infantry, who had before
been serving with the Corinthians and Epidaurians.

text: Meanwhile the Corinthians and their allies occupied the heights of Geraneia, and marched down into the Megarid, in the belief that, with a large force absent in Aegina and Egypt, Athens would be unable to help the Megarians without raising the siege of Aegina.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the Corinthians and their
allies occupied the heights of Geraneia, and marched down into the Megarid, in the belief
that, with a large force absent in Aegina and Egypt, Athens would be unable to help the
Megarians without raising the siege of Aegina.

text: But the Athenians, instead of moving the army of Aegina, raised a force of the old and young men that had been left in the city, and marched into the Megarid under the command of Myronides.
text_raw:
But the Athenians, instead of moving the
army of Aegina, raised a force of the old and young men that had been left in the city, and
marched into the Megarid under the command of Myronides.

text: After a drawn battle with the Corinthians, the rival hosts parted, each with the impression that they had gained the victory.
text_raw:
After a drawn battle with the
Corinthians, the rival hosts parted, each with the impression that they had gained the
victory.

text: The Athenians, however, if anything, had rather the advantage, and on the departure of the Corinthians set up a trophy.
text_raw:
The Athenians, however, if anything, had rather the advantage, and on the
departure of the Corinthians set up a trophy.

text: Urged by the taunts of the elders in their city, the Corinthians made their preparations, and about twelve days afterwards came and set up their trophy as victors.
text_raw:
Urged by the taunts of the elders in their city,
the Corinthians made their preparations, and about twelve days afterwards came and set
up their trophy as victors.

text: Sallying out from Megara, the Athenians cut off the party that was employed in erecting the trophy, and engaged and defeated the rest.
text_raw:
Sallying out from Megara, the Athenians cut off the party that
was employed in erecting the trophy, and engaged and defeated the rest.

text: In the retreat of the vanquished army, a considerable division, pressed by the pursuers and mistaking the road, dashed into a field on some private property, with a deep trench all round it, and no way out.
text_raw:
In the retreat of
the vanquished army, a considerable division, pressed by the pursuers and mistaking the
road, dashed into a field on some private property, with a deep trench all round it, and no
way out.

text: Being acquainted with the place, the Athenians hemmed their front with heavy infantry and, placing the light troops round in a circle, stoned all who had gone in.
text_raw:
Being acquainted with the place, the Athenians hemmed their front with heavy
infantry and, placing the light troops round in a circle, stoned all who had gone in.

text: Corinth here suffered a severe blow.
text_raw:
Corinth
here suffered a severe blow.

text: The bulk of her army continued its retreat home.
text_raw: The bulk of her army continued its retreat home.

text: About this time the Athenians began to build the long walls to the sea, that towards Phalerum and that towards Piraeus.
text_raw:
About this time the Athenians began to build the long walls to the sea, that towards
Phalerum and that towards Piraeus.

text: Meanwhile the Phocians made an expedition against Doris, the old home of the Lacedaemonians, containing the towns of Boeum, Kitinium, and Erineum.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the Phocians made an expedition against
Doris, the old home of the Lacedaemonians, containing the towns of Boeum, Kitinium,
and Erineum.

text: They had taken one of these towns, when the Lacedaemonians under Nicomedes, son of Cleombrotus, commanding for King Pleistoanax, son of Pausanias, who was still a minor, came to the aid of the Dorians with fifteen hundred heavy infantry of their own, and ten thousand of their allies.
text_raw:
They had taken one of these towns, when the Lacedaemonians under
Nicomedes, son of Cleombrotus, commanding for King Pleistoanax, son of Pausanias,
who was still a minor, came to the aid of the Dorians with fifteen hundred heavy infantry
of their own, and ten thousand of their allies.

text: After compelling the Phocians to restore the town on conditions, they began their retreat.
text_raw:
After compelling the Phocians to restore the
town on conditions, they began their retreat.

text: The route by sea, across the Crissaean Gulf, exposed them to the risk of being stopped by the Athenian fleet; that across Geraneia seemed scarcely safe, the Athenians holding Megara and Pegae.
text_raw:
The route by sea, across the Crissaean Gulf,
exposed them to the risk of being stopped by the Athenian fleet; that across Geraneia
seemed scarcely safe, the Athenians holding Megara and Pegae.

text: For the pass was a difficult one, and was always guarded by the Athenians; and, in the present instance, the Lacedaemonians had information that they meant to dispute their passage.
text_raw:
For the pass was a
difficult one, and was always guarded by the Athenians; and, in the present instance, the
Lacedaemonians had information that they meant to dispute their passage.

text: So they resolved to remain in Boeotia, and to consider which would be the safest line of march.
text_raw:
So they
resolved to remain in Boeotia, and to consider which would be the safest line of march.

text: They had also another reason for this resolve.
text_raw: They had also another reason for this resolve.

text: Secret encouragement had been given them by a party in Athens, who hoped to put an end to the reign of democracy and the building
text_raw:
Secret encouragement had been given them
by a party in Athens, who hoped to put an end to the reign of democracy and the building

text: of the Long Walls.
text_raw: of the Long Walls.

text: Meanwhile the Athenians marched against them with their whole levy and a thousand Argives and the respective contingents of the rest of their allies.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the Athenians marched against them with their whole levy
and a thousand Argives and the respective contingents of the rest of their allies.

text: Altogether they were fourteen thousand strong.
text_raw:
Altogether
they were fourteen thousand strong.

text: The march was prompted by the notion that the Lacedaemonians were at a loss how to effect their passage, and also by suspicions of an attempt to overthrow the democracy.
text_raw:
The march was prompted by the notion that the
Lacedaemonians were at a loss how to effect their passage, and also by suspicions of an
attempt to overthrow the democracy.

text: Some cavalry also joined the Athenians from their Thessalian allies; but these went over to the Lacedaemonians during the battle.
text_raw:
Some cavalry also joined the Athenians from their
Thessalian allies; but these went over to the Lacedaemonians during the battle.

text: The battle was fought at Tanagra in Boeotia.
text_raw: The battle was fought at Tanagra in Boeotia.

text: After heavy loss on both sides, victory declared for the Lacedaemonians and their allies.
text_raw:
After heavy loss on both sides, victory
declared for the Lacedaemonians and their allies.

text: After entering the Megarid and cutting down the fruit trees, the Lacedaemonians returned home across Geraneia and the isthmus.
text_raw:
After entering the Megarid and cutting
down the fruit trees, the Lacedaemonians returned home across Geraneia and the isthmus.

text: Sixty-two days after the battle the Athenians marched into Boeotia under the command of Myronides, defeated the Boeotians in battle at Oenophyta, and became masters of Boeotia and Phocis.
text_raw:
Sixty-two days after the battle the Athenians marched into Boeotia under the command of
Myronides, defeated the Boeotians in battle at Oenophyta, and became masters of Boeotia
and Phocis.

text: They dismantled the walls of the Tanagraeans, took a hundred of the richest men of the Opuntian Locrians as hostages, and finished their own long walls.
text_raw:
They dismantled the walls of the Tanagraeans, took a hundred of the richest
men of the Opuntian Locrians as hostages, and finished their own long walls.

text: This was followed by the surrender of the Aeginetans to Athens on conditions; they pulled down their walls, gave up their ships, and agreed to pay tribute in future.
text_raw:
This was
followed by the surrender of the Aeginetans to Athens on conditions; they pulled down
their walls, gave up their ships, and agreed to pay tribute in future.

text: The Athenians sailed round Peloponnese under Tolmides, son of Tolmaeus, burnt the arsenal of Lacedaemon, took Chalcis, a town of the Corinthians, and in a descent upon Sicyon defeated the Sicyonians in battle.
text_raw:
The Athenians sailed
round Peloponnese under Tolmides, son of Tolmaeus, burnt the arsenal of Lacedaemon,
took Chalcis, a town of the Corinthians, and in a descent upon Sicyon defeated the
Sicyonians in battle.

text: Meanwhile the Athenians in Egypt and their allies were still there, and encountered all the vicissitudes of war.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the Athenians in Egypt and their allies were still there, and encountered all
the vicissitudes of war.

text: First the Athenians were masters of Egypt, and the King sent Megabazus a Persian to Lacedaemon with money to bribe the Peloponnesians to invade Attica and so draw off the Athenians from Egypt.
text_raw:
First the Athenians were masters of Egypt, and the King sent
Megabazus a Persian to Lacedaemon with money to bribe the Peloponnesians to invade
Attica and so draw off the Athenians from Egypt.

text: Finding that the matter made no progress, and that the money was only being wasted, he recalled Megabazus with the remainder of the money, and sent Megabuzus, son of Zopyrus, a Persian, with a large army to Egypt.
text_raw:
Finding that the matter made no
progress, and that the money was only being wasted, he recalled Megabazus with the
remainder of the money, and sent Megabuzus, son of Zopyrus, a Persian, with a large
army to Egypt.

text: Arriving by land he defeated the Egyptians and their allies in a battle, and drove the Hellenes out of Memphis, and at length shut them up in the island of Prosopitis, where he besieged them for a year and six months.
text_raw:
Arriving by land he defeated the Egyptians and their allies in a battle, and
drove the Hellenes out of Memphis, and at length shut them up in the island of Prosopitis,
where he besieged them for a year and six months.

text: At last, draining the canal of its waters, which he diverted into another channel, he left their ships high and dry and joined most of the island to the mainland, and then marched over on foot and captured it.
text_raw:
At last, draining the canal of its waters,
which he diverted into another channel, he left their ships high and dry and joined most of
the island to the mainland, and then marched over on foot and captured it.

text: Thus the enterprise of the Hellenes came to ruin after six years of war.
text_raw:
Thus the
enterprise of the Hellenes came to ruin after six years of war.

text: Of all that large host a few travelling through Libya reached Cyrene in safety, but most of them perished.
text_raw:
Of all that large host a few
travelling through Libya reached Cyrene in safety, but most of them perished.

text: And thus Egypt returned to its subjection to the King, except Amyrtaeus, the king in the marshes, whom they were unable to capture from the extent of the marsh; the marshmen being also the most warlike of the Egyptians.
text_raw:
And thus
Egypt returned to its subjection to the King, except Amyrtaeus, the king in the marshes,
whom they were unable to capture from the extent of the marsh; the marshmen being also
the most warlike of the Egyptians.

text: Inaros, the Libyan king, the sole author of the Egyptian revolt, was betrayed, taken, and crucified.
text_raw:
Inaros, the Libyan king, the sole author of the Egyptian
revolt, was betrayed, taken, and crucified.

text: Meanwhile a relieving squadron of fifty vessels had sailed from Athens and the rest of the confederacy for Egypt.
text_raw:
Meanwhile a relieving squadron of fifty vessels
had sailed from Athens and the rest of the confederacy for Egypt.

text: They put in to shore at the Mendesian mouth of the Nile, in total ignorance of what had occurred.
text_raw:
They put in to shore at
the Mendesian mouth of the Nile, in total ignorance of what had occurred.

text: Attacked on the land side by the troops, and from the sea by the Phoenician navy, most of the ships were destroyed; the few remaining being saved by retreat.
text_raw:
Attacked on the
land side by the troops, and from the sea by the Phoenician navy, most of the ships were
destroyed; the few remaining being saved by retreat.

text: Such was the end of the great expedition of the Athenians and their allies to Egypt.
text_raw:
Such was the end of the great
expedition of the Athenians and their allies to Egypt.

text: Meanwhile Orestes, son of Echecratidas, the Thessalian king, being an exile from Thessaly, persuaded the Athenians to restore him.
text_raw:
Meanwhile Orestes, son of Echecratidas, the Thessalian king, being an exile from
Thessaly, persuaded the Athenians to restore him.

text: Taking with them the Boeotians and Phocians their allies, the Athenians marched to Pharsalus in Thessaly.
text_raw:
Taking with them the Boeotians and
Phocians their allies, the Athenians marched to Pharsalus in Thessaly.

text: They became
text_raw: They became

text: masters of the country, though only in the immediate vicinity of the camp; beyond which they could not go for fear of the Thessalian cavalry.
text_raw:
masters of the country, though only in the immediate vicinity of the camp; beyond which
they could not go for fear of the Thessalian cavalry.

text: But they failed to take the city or to attain any of the other objects of their expedition, and returned home with Orestes without having effected anything.
text_raw:
But they failed to take the city or to
attain any of the other objects of their expedition, and returned home with Orestes without
having effected anything.

text: Not long after this a thousand of the Athenians embarked in the vessels that were at Pegae (Pegae, it must be remembered, was now theirs), and sailed along the coast to Sicyon under the command of Pericles, son of Xanthippus.
text_raw:
Not long after this a thousand of the Athenians embarked in the
vessels that were at Pegae (Pegae, it must be remembered, was now theirs), and sailed
along the coast to Sicyon under the command of Pericles, son of Xanthippus.

text: Landing in Sicyon and defeating the Sicyonians who engaged them, they immediately took with them the Achaeans and, sailing across, marched against and laid siege to Oeniadae in Acarnania.
text_raw:
Landing in
Sicyon and defeating the Sicyonians who engaged them, they immediately took with them
the Achaeans and, sailing across, marched against and laid siege to Oeniadae in

text: Failing however to take it, they returned home.
text_raw: Failing however to take it, they returned home.

text: Three years afterwards a truce was made between the Peloponnesians and Athenians for five years.
text_raw:
Three years afterwards a truce was made between the Peloponnesians and Athenians for
five years.

text: Released from Hellenic war, the Athenians made an expedition to Cyprus with two hundred vessels of their own and their allies, under the command of Cimon.
text_raw:
Released from Hellenic war, the Athenians made an expedition to Cyprus with
two hundred vessels of their own and their allies, under the command of Cimon.

text: Sixty of these were detached to Egypt at the instance of Amyrtaeus, the king in the marshes; the rest laid siege to Kitium, from which, however, they were compelled to retire by the death of Cimon and by scarcity of provisions.
text_raw:
Sixty of
these were detached to Egypt at the instance of Amyrtaeus, the king in the marshes; the

text: Sailing off Salamis in Cyprus, they fought with the Phoenicians, Cyprians, and Cilicians by land and sea, and, being victorious on both elements departed home, and with them the returned squadron from Egypt.
text_raw:
Sailing off Salamis in Cyprus, they fought with
the Phoenicians, Cyprians, and Cilicians by land and sea, and, being victorious on both
elements departed home, and with them the returned squadron from Egypt.

text: After this the Lacedaemonians marched out on a sacred war, and, becoming masters of the temple at Delphi, it in the hands of the Delphians.
text_raw:
After this the
Lacedaemonians marched out on a sacred war, and, becoming masters of the temple at
Delphi, it in the hands of the Delphians.

text: Immediately after their retreat, the Athenians marched out, became masters of the temple, and placed it in the hands of the Phocians.
text_raw:
Immediately after their retreat, the Athenians
marched out, became masters of the temple, and placed it in the hands of the Phocians.

text: Some time after this, Orchomenus, Chaeronea, and some other places in Boeotia being in the hands of the Boeotian exiles, the Athenians marched against the above-mentioned hostile places with a thousand Athenian heavy infantry and the allied contingents, under the command of Tolmides, son of Tolmaeus.
text_raw:
Some time after this, Orchomenus, Chaeronea, and some other places in Boeotia being in
the hands of the Boeotian exiles, the Athenians marched against the above-mentioned
hostile places with a thousand Athenian heavy infantry and the allied contingents, under

text: They took Chaeronea, and made slaves of the inhabitants, and, leaving a garrison, commenced their return.
text_raw:
They took Chaeronea, and made slaves of the
inhabitants, and, leaving a garrison, commenced their return.

text: On their road they were attacked at Coronea by the Boeotian exiles from Orchomenus, with some Locrians and Euboean exiles, and others who were of the same way of thinking, were defeated in battle, and some killed, others taken captive.
text_raw:

attacked at Coronea by the Boeotian exiles from Orchomenus, with some Locrians and

text: The Athenians evacuated all Boeotia by a treaty providing for the recovery of the men; and the exiled Boeotians returned, and with all the rest regained their independence.
text_raw:
The Athenians evacuated all Boeotia by a treaty
providing for the recovery of the men; and the exiled Boeotians returned, and with all the

text: This was soon afterwards followed by the revolt of Euboea from Athens.
text_raw: This was soon afterwards followed by the revolt of Euboea from Athens.

text: Pericles had already crossed over with an army of Athenians to the island, when news was brought to him that Megara had revolted, that the Peloponnesians were on the point of invading Attica, and that the Athenian garrison had been cut off by the Megarians, with the exception of a few who had taken refuge in Nisaea.
text_raw:
Pericles had
already crossed over with an army of Athenians to the island, when news was brought to
him that Megara had revolted, that the Peloponnesians were on the point of invading
Attica, and that the Athenian garrison had been cut off by the Megarians, with the

text: The Megarians had introduced the Corinthians, Sicyonians, and Epidaurians into the town before they revolted.
text_raw:
The Megarians had introduced the
Corinthians, Sicyonians, and Epidaurians into the town before they revolted.

text: Meanwhile Pericles brought his army back in all haste from Euboea.
text_raw:
Meanwhile

During this interval the Athenians succeeded in placing their empire on a

text: The Lacedaemonians, though fully aware of it, opposed it only for a little while, but remained inactive during most of the period, being of old slow to go to war except under the pressure of necessity, and in the present instance being hampered by wars at home; until the growth of the Athenian power could be no longer ignored, and their own confederacy became the object of its encroachments.

text: They then felt that they could endure it no longer, but that the time had come for them to throw themselves heart and soul upon the hostile power, and break it, if they could, by commencing the present war.

text: If wise men remain quiet, while they are not injured, brave
text_raw: If wise men remain quiet, while they are not injured, brave

men abandon peace for war when they are injured, returning to an understanding on a

text: A single defeat at sea is in all likelihood their ruin: should they hold out, in that case there will be the more time for us to exercise ourselves in naval matters; and as soon as we have arrived at an equality in science, we need scarcely ask whether we shall be their superiors in courage.

text: For the future we must provide by maintaining what the present gives us and redoubling our efforts; it is hereditary to us to win virtue as the fruit of labour, and you must not change the habit, even though you should have a slight advantage in wealth and resources; for it is not right that what was won in want should be lost in plenty; no, we must boldly advance to the war for many reasons; the god has commanded it and promised to be with us, and the rest of Hellas will all join in the struggle, part from fear, part from interest.

text: It is celebrated outside the city, and the whole people sacrifice not real victims but a number of bloodless offerings peculiar to the country.

It is celebrated outside the city, and the whole
people sacrifice not real victims but a number of bloodless offerings peculiar to the
country.

text: However, fancying he had chosen the right time, he made the attempt.
text_raw: However, fancying he had chosen the right time, he made the attempt.

text: As soon as the Athenians perceived it, they flocked in, one and all, from the country, and sat down, and laid siege to the citadel.
text_raw:
As soon as
the Athenians perceived it, they flocked in, one and all, from the country, and sat down,
and laid siege to the citadel.

text: But as time went on, weary of the labour of blockade, most of them departed; the responsibility of keeping guard being left to the nine archons, with plenary powers to arrange everything according to their good judgment.
text_raw:
But as time went on, weary of the labour of blockade, most of
them departed; the responsibility of keeping guard being left to the nine archons, with
plenary powers to arrange everything according to their good judgment.

text: It must be known that at that time most political functions were discharged by the nine archons.
text_raw:
It must be known
that at that time most political functions were discharged by the nine archons.

text: Meanwhile Cylon and his besieged companions were distressed for want of food and water.
text_raw:
Meanwhile
Cylon and his besieged companions were distressed for want of food and water.

text: Accordingly Cylon and his brother made their escape; but the rest being hard pressed, and some even dying of famine, seated themselves as suppliants at the altar in the Acropolis.
text_raw:
Accordingly Cylon and his brother made their escape; but the rest being hard pressed, and
some even dying of famine, seated themselves as suppliants at the altar in the Acropolis.

text: The Athenians who were charged with the duty of keeping guard, when they saw them at the point of death in the temple, raised them up on the understanding that no harm should be done to them, led them out, and slew them.
text_raw:
The Athenians who were charged with the duty of keeping guard, when they saw them at
the point of death in the temple, raised them up on the understanding that no harm should
be done to them, led them out, and slew them.

text: Some who as they passed by took refuge at the altars of the awful goddesses were dispatched on the spot.
text_raw:
Some who as they passed by took refuge at
the altars of the awful goddesses were dispatched on the spot.

text: From this deed the men who killed them were called accursed and guilty against the goddess, they and their descendants.
text_raw:
From this deed the men who
killed them were called accursed and guilty against the goddess, they and their
descendants.

text: Accordingly these cursed ones were driven out by the Athenians, driven out again by Cleomenes of Lacedaemon and an Athenian faction; the living were driven out, and the bones of the dead were taken up; thus they were cast out.
text_raw:
Accordingly these cursed ones were driven out by the Athenians, driven out
again by Cleomenes of Lacedaemon and an Athenian faction; the living were driven out,
and the bones of the dead were taken up; thus they were cast out.

text: For all that, they came back afterwards, and their descendants are still in the city.
text_raw:
For all that, they came
back afterwards, and their descendants are still in the city.

text: This, then was the curse that the Lacedaemonians ordered them to drive out.
text_raw: This, then was the curse that the Lacedaemonians ordered them to drive out.

text: They were actuated primarily, as they pretended, by a care for the honour of the gods; but they also know that Pericles, son of Xanthippus, was connected with the curse on his mother’s side, and they thought that his banishment would materially advance their designs on Athens.
text_raw:
They were
actuated primarily, as they pretended, by a care for the honour of the gods; but they also
know that Pericles, son of Xanthippus, was connected with the curse on his mother’s side,
and they thought that his banishment would materially advance their designs on Athens.

text: Not that they really hoped to succeed in procuring this; they rather thought to create a prejudice against him in the eyes of his countrymen from the feeling that the war would be partly caused by his misfortune.
text_raw:
Not that they really hoped to succeed in procuring this; they rather thought to create a
prejudice against him in the eyes of his countrymen from the feeling that the war would be
partly caused by his misfortune.

text: For being the most powerful man of his time, and the leading Athenian statesman, he opposed the Lacedaemonians in everything, and would have no concessions, but ever urged the Athenians on to war.
text_raw:
For being the most powerful man of his time, and the
leading Athenian statesman, he opposed the Lacedaemonians in everything, and would
have no concessions, but ever urged the Athenians on to war.

text: The Athenians retorted by ordering the Lacedaemonians to drive out the curse of Taenarus.
text_raw:
The Athenians retorted by ordering the Lacedaemonians to drive out the curse of
Taenarus.

text: The Lacedaemonians had once raised up some Helot suppliants from the temple of Poseidon at Taenarus, led them away and slain them; for which they believe the great earthquake at Sparta to have been a retribution.
text_raw:
The Lacedaemonians had once raised up some Helot suppliants from the temple
of Poseidon at Taenarus, led them away and slain them; for which they believe the great
earthquake at Sparta to have been a retribution.

text: The Athenians also ordered them to drive
text_raw: The Athenians also ordered them to drive

text: out the curse of the goddess of the Brazen House; the history of which is as follows.
text_raw: out the curse of the goddess of the Brazen House; the history of which is as follows.

text: After Pausanias the Lacedaemonian had been recalled by the Spartans from his command in the Hellespont (this is his first recall), and had been tried by them and acquitted, not being again sent out in a public capacity, he took a galley of Hermione on his own responsibility, without the authority of the Lacedaemonians, and arrived as a private person in the Hellespont.
text_raw:
After
Pausanias the Lacedaemonian had been recalled by the Spartans from his command in the
Hellespont (this is his first recall), and had been tried by them and acquitted, not being
again sent out in a public capacity, he took a galley of Hermione on his own responsibility,
without the authority of the Lacedaemonians, and arrived as a private person in the
Hellespont.

text: He came ostensibly for the Hellenic war, really to carry on his intrigues with the King, which he had begun before his recall, being ambitious of reigning over Hellas.
text_raw:
He came ostensibly for the Hellenic war, really to carry on his intrigues with
the King, which he had begun before his recall, being ambitious of reigning over Hellas.

text: The circumstance which first enabled him to lay the King under an obligation, and to make a beginning of the whole design, was this.
text_raw:
The circumstance which first enabled him to lay the King under an obligation, and to
make a beginning of the whole design, was this.

text: Some connections and kinsmen of the King had been taken in Byzantium, on its capture from the Medes, when he was first there, after the return from Cyprus.
text_raw:
Some connections and kinsmen of the
King had been taken in Byzantium, on its capture from the Medes, when he was first
there, after the return from Cyprus.

text: These captives he sent off to the King without the knowledge of the rest of the allies, the account being that they had escaped from him.
text_raw:
These captives he sent off to the King without the
knowledge of the rest of the allies, the account being that they had escaped from him.

text: He managed this with the help of Gongylus, an Eretrian, whom he had placed in charge of Byzantium and the prisoners.
text_raw:
He
managed this with the help of Gongylus, an Eretrian, whom he had placed in charge of
Byzantium and the prisoners.

text: He also gave Gongylus a letter for the King, the contents of which were as follows, as was afterwards discovered: “Pausanias, the general of Sparta, anxious to do you a favour, sends you these his prisoners of war.
text_raw:
He also gave Gongylus a letter for the King, the contents of
which were as follows, as was afterwards discovered: “Pausanias, the general of Sparta,
anxious to do you a favour, sends you these his prisoners of war.

text: I propose also, with your approval, to marry your daughter, and to make Sparta and the rest of Hellas subject to you.
text_raw:
I propose also, with your
approval, to marry your daughter, and to make Sparta and the rest of Hellas subject to you.

text: I may say that I think I am able to do this, with your co-operation.
text_raw: I may say that I think I am able to do this, with your co-operation.

text: Accordingly if any of this please you, send a safe man to the sea through whom we may in future conduct our correspondence.” This was all that was revealed in the writing, and Xerxes was pleased with the letter.
text_raw:
Accordingly if any of
this please you, send a safe man to the sea through whom we may in future conduct our
correspondence.”
This was all that was revealed in the writing, and Xerxes was pleased with the letter.

text: He sent off Artabazus, son of Pharnaces, to the sea with orders to supersede Megabates, the previous governor in the satrapy of Daskylion, and to send over as quickly as possible to Pausanias at Byzantium a letter which he entrusted to him; to show him the royal signet, and to execute any commission which he might receive from Pausanias on the King’s matters with all care and fidelity.
text_raw:
He
sent off Artabazus, son of Pharnaces, to the sea with orders to supersede Megabates, the
previous governor in the satrapy of Daskylion, and to send over as quickly as possible to
Pausanias at Byzantium a letter which he entrusted to him; to show him the royal signet,
and to execute any commission which he might receive from Pausanias on the King’s
matters with all care and fidelity.

text: Artabazus on his arrival carried the King’s orders into effect, and sent over the letter, which contained the following answer: “Thus saith King Xerxes to Pausanias.
text_raw:
Artabazus on his arrival carried the King’s orders into
effect, and sent over the letter, which contained the following answer: “Thus saith King
Xerxes to Pausanias.

text: For the men whom you have saved for me across sea from Byzantium, an obligation is laid up for you in our house, recorded for ever; and with your proposals I am well pleased.
text_raw:
For the men whom you have saved for me across sea from
Byzantium, an obligation is laid up for you in our house, recorded for ever; and with your
proposals I am well pleased.

text: Let neither night nor day stop you from diligently performing any of your promises to me; neither for cost of gold nor of silver let them be hindered, nor yet for number of troops, wherever it may be that their presence is needed; but with Artabazus, an honourable man whom I send you, boldly advance my objects and yours, as may be most for the honour and interest of us both.” Before held in high honour by the Hellenes as the hero of Plataea, Pausanias, after the receipt of this letter, became prouder than ever, and could no longer live in the usual style, but went out of Byzantium in a Median dress, was attended on his march through Thrace by a bodyguard of Medes and Egyptians, kept a Persian table, and was quite unable to contain his intentions, but betrayed by his conduct in trifles what his ambition looked one day to enact on a grander scale.
text_raw:
Let neither night nor day stop you from diligently performing
any of your promises to me; neither for cost of gold nor of silver let them be hindered, nor
yet for number of troops, wherever it may be that their presence is needed; but with
Artabazus, an honourable man whom I send you, boldly advance my objects and yours, as
may be most for the honour and interest of us both.”
Before held in high honour by the Hellenes as the hero of Plataea, Pausanias, after the
receipt of this letter, became prouder than ever, and could no longer live in the usual style,
but went out of Byzantium in a Median dress, was attended on his march through Thrace
by a bodyguard of Medes and Egyptians, kept a Persian table, and was quite unable to
contain his intentions, but betrayed by his conduct in trifles what his ambition looked one
day to enact on a grander scale.

text: He also made himself difficult of access, and displayed so violent a temper to every one without exception that no one could come near him.
text_raw:
He also made himself difficult of access, and displayed so
violent a temper to every one without exception that no one could come near him.

text: Indeed, this was the principal reason why the confederacy went over to the Athenians.
text_raw:
Indeed,
this was the principal reason why the confederacy went over to the Athenians.

text: The above-mentioned conduct, coming to the ears of the Lacedaemonians, occasioned
text_raw: The above-mentioned conduct, coming to the ears of the Lacedaemonians, occasioned

text: his first recall.
text_raw: his first recall.

text: And after his second voyage out in the ship of Hermione, without their orders, he gave proofs of similar behaviour.
text_raw:
And after his second voyage out in the ship of Hermione, without their
orders, he gave proofs of similar behaviour.

text: Besieged and expelled from Byzantium by the Athenians, he did not return to Sparta; but news came that he had settled at Colonae in the Troad, and was intriguing with the barbarians, and that his stay there was for no good purpose; and the ephors, now no longer hesitating, sent him a herald and a scytale with orders to accompany the herald or be declared a public enemy.
text_raw:
Besieged and expelled from Byzantium by the
Athenians, he did not return to Sparta; but news came that he had settled at Colonae in the
Troad, and was intriguing with the barbarians, and that his stay there was for no good
purpose; and the ephors, now no longer hesitating, sent him a herald and a scytale with
orders to accompany the herald or be declared a public enemy.

text: Anxious above everything to avoid suspicion, and confident that he could quash the charge by means of money, he returned a second time to Sparta.
text_raw:
Anxious above everything
to avoid suspicion, and confident that he could quash the charge by means of money, he
returned a second time to Sparta.

text: At first thrown into prison by the ephors (whose powers enable them to do this to the King), soon compromised the matter and came out again, and offered himself for trial to any who wished to institute an inquiry concerning him.
text_raw:
At first thrown into prison by the ephors (whose powers
enable them to do this to the King), soon compromised the matter and came out again, and
offered himself for trial to any who wished to institute an inquiry concerning him.

text: Now the Spartans had no tangible proof against him—neither his enemies nor the nation —of that indubitable kind required for the punishment of a member of the royal family, and at that moment in high office; he being regent for his first cousin King Pleistarchus, Leonidas’s son, who was still a minor.
text_raw:
Now the Spartans had no tangible proof against him—neither his enemies nor the nation
—of that indubitable kind required for the punishment of a member of the royal family,
and at that moment in high office; he being regent for his first cousin King Pleistarchus,
Leonidas’s son, who was still a minor.

text: But by his contempt of the laws and imitation of the barbarians, he gave grounds for much suspicion of his being discontented with things established; all the occasions on which he had in any way departed from the regular customs were passed in review, and it was remembered that he had taken upon himself to have inscribed on the tripod at Delphi, which was dedicated by the Hellenes as the first- fruits of the spoil of the Medes, the following couplet:
text_raw:
But by his contempt of the laws and imitation of the
barbarians, he gave grounds for much suspicion of his being discontented with things
established; all the occasions on which he had in any way departed from the regular
customs were passed in review, and it was remembered that he had taken upon himself to
have inscribed on the tripod at Delphi, which was dedicated by the Hellenes as the first-
fruits of the spoil of the Medes, the following couplet:

text: The Mede defeated, great Pausanias raised This monument, that Phoebus might be praised.
text_raw:
The Mede defeated, great Pausanias raised
This monument, that Phoebus might be praised.

text: At the time the Lacedaemonians had at once erased the couplet, and inscribed the names of the cities that had aided in the overthrow of the barbarian and dedicated the offering.
text_raw:
At the time the Lacedaemonians had at once erased the couplet, and inscribed the names
of the cities that had aided in the overthrow of the barbarian and dedicated the offering.

text: Yet it was considered that Pausanias had here been guilty of a grave offence, which, interpreted by the light of the attitude which he had since assumed, gained a new significance, and seemed to be quite in keeping with his present schemes.
text_raw:
Yet it was considered that Pausanias had here been guilty of a grave offence, which,
interpreted by the light of the attitude which he had since assumed, gained a new
significance, and seemed to be quite in keeping with his present schemes.

text: Besides, they were informed that he was even intriguing with the Helots; and such indeed was the fact, for he promised them freedom and citizenship if they would join him in insurrection and would help him to carry out his plans to the end.
text_raw:
Besides, they
were informed that he was even intriguing with the Helots; and such indeed was the fact,
for he promised them freedom and citizenship if they would join him in insurrection and
would help him to carry out his plans to the end.

text: Even now, mistrusting the evidence even of the Helots themselves, the ephors would not consent to take any decided step against him; in accordance with their regular custom towards themselves, namely, to be slow in taking any irrevocable resolve in the matter of a Spartan citizen without indisputable proof.
text_raw:
Even now, mistrusting the evidence even
of the Helots themselves, the ephors would not consent to take any decided step against
him; in accordance with their regular custom towards themselves, namely, to be slow in
taking any irrevocable resolve in the matter of a Spartan citizen without indisputable
proof.

text: At last, it is said, the person who was going to carry to Artabazus the last letter for the King, a man of Argilus, once the favourite and most trusty servant of Pausanias, turned informer.
text_raw:
At last, it is said, the person who was going to carry to Artabazus the last letter for
the King, a man of Argilus, once the favourite and most trusty servant of Pausanias, turned
informer.

text: Alarmed by the reflection that none of the previous messengers had ever returned, having counterfeited the seal, in order that, if he found himself mistaken in his surmises, or if Pausanias should ask to make some correction, he might not be discovered, he undid the letter, and found the postscript that he had suspected, viz. an order to put him to death.
text_raw:
Alarmed by the reflection that none of the previous messengers had ever
returned, having counterfeited the seal, in order that, if he found himself mistaken in his
surmises, or if Pausanias should ask to make some correction, he might not be discovered,
he undid the letter, and found the postscript that he had suspected, viz. an order to put him
to death.

text: On being shown the letter, the ephors now felt more certain.
text_raw: On being shown the letter, the ephors now felt more certain.

text: Still, they wished to hear Pausanias commit himself with their own ears.
text_raw:
Still, they wished to hear
Pausanias commit himself with their own ears.

text: Accordingly the man went by appointment to Taenarus as a suppliant, and there built himself a hut divided into two by a partition; within which he concealed some of the ephors and let them hear the whole matter plainly.

For Pausanias came to him and asked him the reason of his suppliant position; and the man reproached him with the order that he had written concerning him, and one by one declared all the rest of the circumstances, how he who had never yet brought him into any danger, while employed as agent between him and the King, was yet just like the mass of his servants to be rewarded with death.
text_raw:
For Pausanias came to him and asked him the reason of his suppliant position; and the
man reproached him with the order that he had written concerning him, and one by one
declared all the rest of the circumstances, how he who had never yet brought him into any
danger, while employed as agent between him and the King, was yet just like the mass of
his servants to be rewarded with death.

text: Admitting all this, and telling him not to be angry about the matter, Pausanias gave him the pledge of raising him up from the temple, and begged him to set off as quickly as possible, and not to hinder the business in hand.
text_raw:
Admitting all this, and telling him not to be angry
about the matter, Pausanias gave him the pledge of raising him up from the temple, and
begged him to set off as quickly as possible, and not to hinder the business in hand.

text: The ephors listened carefully, and then departed, taking no action for the moment, but, having at last attained to certainty, were preparing to arrest him in the city.
text_raw:
The ephors listened carefully, and then departed, taking no action for the moment, but,
having at last attained to certainty, were preparing to arrest him in the city.

text: It is reported that, as he was about to be arrested in the street, he saw from the face of one of the ephors what he was coming for; another, too, made him a secret signal, and betrayed it to him from kindness.
text_raw:
It is reported
that, as he was about to be arrested in the street, he saw from the face of one of the ephors
what he was coming for; another, too, made him a secret signal, and betrayed it to him
from kindness.

text: Setting off with a run for the temple of the goddess of the Brazen House, the enclosure of which was near at hand, he succeeded in taking sanctuary before they took him, and entering into a small chamber, which formed part of the temple, to avoid being exposed to the weather, lay still there.
text_raw:
Setting off with a run for the temple of the goddess of the Brazen House,
the enclosure of which was near at hand, he succeeded in taking sanctuary before they
took him, and entering into a small chamber, which formed part of the temple, to avoid
being exposed to the weather, lay still there.

text: The ephors, for the moment distanced in the pursuit, afterwards took off the roof of the chamber, and having made sure that he was inside, shut him in, barricaded the doors, and staying before the place, reduced him by starvation.
text_raw:
The ephors, for the moment distanced in the
pursuit, afterwards took off the roof of the chamber, and having made sure that he was
inside, shut him in, barricaded the doors, and staying before the place, reduced him by
starvation.

text: When they found that he was on the point of expiring, just as he was, in the chamber, they brought him out of the temple, while the breath was still in him, and as soon as he was brought out he died.
text_raw:
When they found that he was on the point of expiring, just as he was, in the
chamber, they brought him out of the temple, while the breath was still in him, and as soon
as he was brought out he died.

text: They were going to throw him into the Kaiadas, where they cast criminals, but finally decided to inter him somewhere near.
text_raw:
They were going to throw him into the Kaiadas, where they
cast criminals, but finally decided to inter him somewhere near.

text: But the god at Delphi afterwards ordered the Lacedaemonians to remove the tomb to the place of his death— where he now lies in the consecrated ground, as an inscription on a monument declares— and, as what had been done was a curse to them, to give back two bodies instead of one to the goddess of the Brazen House.
text_raw:
But the god at Delphi
afterwards ordered the Lacedaemonians to remove the tomb to the place of his death—
where he now lies in the consecrated ground, as an inscription on a monument declares—
and, as what had been done was a curse to them, to give back two bodies instead of one to
the goddess of the Brazen House.

text: So they had two brazen statues made, and dedicated them as a substitute for Pausanias.
text_raw:
So they had two brazen statues made, and dedicated
them as a substitute for Pausanias.

text: The Athenians retorted by telling the Lacedaemonians to drive out what the god himself had pronounced to be a curse.
text_raw:
The Athenians retorted by telling the Lacedaemonians
to drive out what the god himself had pronounced to be a curse.

text: To return to the Medism of Pausanias.
text_raw: To return to the Medism of Pausanias.

text: Matter was found in the course of the inquiry to implicate Themistocles; and the Lacedaemonians accordingly sent envoys to the Athenians and required them to punish him as they had punished Pausanias.
text_raw:
Matter was found in the course of the inquiry to
implicate Themistocles; and the Lacedaemonians accordingly sent envoys to the
Athenians and required them to punish him as they had punished Pausanias.

text: The Athenians consented to do so.
text_raw:
The
Athenians consented to do so.

text: But he had, as it happened, been ostracized, and, with a residence at Argos, was in the habit of visiting other parts of Peloponnese.
text_raw:
But he had, as it happened, been ostracized, and, with a
residence at Argos, was in the habit of visiting other parts of Peloponnese.

text: So they sent with the Lacedaemonians, who were ready to join in the pursuit, persons with instructions to take him wherever they found him.
text_raw:
So they sent
with the Lacedaemonians, who were ready to join in the pursuit, persons with instructions
to take him wherever they found him.

text: But Themistocles got scent of their intentions, and fled from Peloponnese to Corcyra, which was under obligations towards him.
text_raw:
But Themistocles got scent of their intentions, and
fled from Peloponnese to Corcyra, which was under obligations towards him.

text: But the Corcyraeans alleged that they could not venture to shelter him at the cost of offending Athens and Lacedaemon, and they conveyed him over to the continent opposite.
text_raw:
But the
Corcyraeans alleged that they could not venture to shelter him at the cost of offending
Athens and Lacedaemon, and they conveyed him over to the continent opposite.

text: Pursued by the officers who hung on the report of his movements, at a loss where to turn, he was compelled to stop at the house of Admetus, the Molossian king, though they were not on friendly terms.
text_raw:
Pursued
by the officers who hung on the report of his movements, at a loss where to turn, he was
compelled to stop at the house of Admetus, the Molossian king, though they were not on
friendly terms.

text: Admetus happened not to be indoors, but his wife, to whom he made himself a suppliant, instructed him to take their child in his arms and sit down by the hearth.
text_raw:
Admetus happened not to be indoors, but his wife, to whom he made
himself a suppliant, instructed him to take their child in his arms and sit down by the
hearth.

text: Soon afterwards Admetus came in, and Themistocles told him who he was, and begged him not to revenge on Themistocles in exile any opposition which his requests might have experienced from Themistocles at Athens.
text_raw:
Soon afterwards Admetus came in, and Themistocles told him who he was, and
begged him not to revenge on Themistocles in exile any opposition which his requests
might have experienced from Themistocles at Athens.

text: Indeed, he was now far too low for
text_raw: Indeed, he was now far too low for

text: his revenge; retaliation was only honourable between equals.
text_raw: his revenge; retaliation was only honourable between equals.

text: Besides, his opposition to the king had only affected the success of a request, not the safety of his person; if the king were to give him up to the pursuers that he mentioned, and the fate which they intended for him, he would just be consigning him to certain death.
text_raw:
Besides, his opposition to
the king had only affected the success of a request, not the safety of his person; if the king
were to give him up to the pursuers that he mentioned, and the fate which they intended
for him, he would just be consigning him to certain death.

text: The King listened to him and raised him up with his son, as he was sitting with him in his arms after the most effectual method of supplication, and on the arrival of the Lacedaemonians not long afterwards, refused to give him up for anything they could say, but sent him off by land to the other sea to Pydna in Alexander’s dominions, as he wished to go to the Persian king.
text_raw:
The King listened to him and raised him up with his son, as he was sitting with him in
his arms after the most effectual method of supplication, and on the arrival of the
Lacedaemonians not long afterwards, refused to give him up for anything they could say,
but sent him off by land to the other sea to Pydna in Alexander’s dominions, as he wished
to go to the Persian king.

text: There he met with a merchantman on the point of starting for Ionia.
text_raw:
There he met with a merchantman on the point of starting for
Ionia.

text: Going on board, he was carried by a storm to the Athenian squadron which was blockading Naxos.
text_raw:
Going on board, he was carried by a storm to the Athenian squadron which was
blockading Naxos.

text: In his alarm—he was luckily unknown to the people in the vessel—he told the master who he was and what he was flying for, and said that, if he refused to save him, he would declare that he was taking him for a bribe.
text_raw:
In his alarm—he was luckily unknown to the people in the vessel—he
told the master who he was and what he was flying for, and said that, if he refused to save
him, he would declare that he was taking him for a bribe.

text: Meanwhile their safety consisted in letting no one leave the ship until a favourable time for sailing should arise.
text_raw:
Meanwhile their safety consisted
in letting no one leave the ship until a favourable time for sailing should arise.

text: If he complied with his wishes, he promised him a proper recompense.
text_raw:
If he
complied with his wishes, he promised him a proper recompense.

text: The master acted as he desired, and, after lying to for a day and a night out of reach of the squadron, at length arrived at Ephesus.
text_raw:
The master acted as he
desired, and, after lying to for a day and a night out of reach of the squadron, at length

text: After having rewarded him with a present of money, as soon as he received some from his friends at Athens and from his secret hoards at Argos, Themistocles started inland with one of the coast Persians, and sent a letter to King Artaxerxes, Xerxes’s son, who had just come to the throne.
text_raw:
After having rewarded him with a present of money, as soon as he received some from
his friends at Athens and from his secret hoards at Argos, Themistocles started inland with
one of the coast Persians, and sent a letter to King Artaxerxes, Xerxes’s son, who had just
come to the throne.

text: Its contents were as follows: “I, Themistocles, am come to you, who did your house more harm than any of the Hellenes, when I was compelled to defend myself against your father’s invasion—harm, however, far surpassed by the good that I did him during his retreat, which brought no danger for me but much for him.
text_raw:
Its contents were as follows: “I, Themistocles, am come to you, who
did your house more harm than any of the Hellenes, when I was compelled to defend
myself against your father’s invasion—harm, however, far surpassed by the good that I did
him during his retreat, which brought no danger for me but much for him.

text: For the past, you are a good turn in my debt”—here he mentioned the warning sent to Xerxes from Salamis to retreat, as well as his finding the bridges unbroken, which, as he falsely pretended, was due to him—“for the present, able to do you great service, I am here, pursued by the Hellenes for my friendship for you.
text_raw:
For the past,
you are a good turn in my debt”—here he mentioned the warning sent to Xerxes from
Salamis to retreat, as well as his finding the bridges unbroken, which, as he falsely
pretended, was due to him—“for the present, able to do you great service, I am here,
pursued by the Hellenes for my friendship for you.

text: However, I desire a year’s grace, when I shall be able to declare in person the objects of my coming.” It is said that the King approved his intention, and told him to do as he said.
text_raw:
However, I desire a year’s grace, when
I shall be able to declare in person the objects of my coming.”
It is said that the King approved his intention, and told him to do as he said.

text: He employed the interval in making what progress he could in the study of the Persian tongue, and of the customs of the country.
text_raw:
He
employed the interval in making what progress he could in the study of the Persian
tongue, and of the customs of the country.

text: Arrived at court at the end of the year, he attained to very high consideration there, such as no Hellene has ever possessed before or since; partly from his splendid antecedents, partly from the hopes which he held out of effecting for him the subjugation of Hellas, but principally by the proof which experience daily gave of his capacity.
text_raw:
Arrived at court at the end of the year, he
attained to very high consideration there, such as no Hellene has ever possessed before or
since; partly from his splendid antecedents, partly from the hopes which he held out of
effecting for him the subjugation of Hellas, but principally by the proof which experience
daily gave of his capacity.

text: For Themistocles was a man who exhibited the most indubitable signs of genius; indeed, in this particular he has a claim on our admiration quite extraordinary and unparalleled.
text_raw:
For Themistocles was a man who exhibited the most
indubitable signs of genius; indeed, in this particular he has a claim on our admiration
quite extraordinary and unparalleled.

text: By his own native capacity, alike unformed and unsupplemented by study, he was at once the best judge in those sudden crises which admit of little or of no deliberation, and the best prophet of the future, even to its most distant possibilities.
text_raw:
By his own native capacity, alike unformed and
unsupplemented by study, he was at once the best judge in those sudden crises which
admit of little or of no deliberation, and the best prophet of the future, even to its most
distant possibilities.

text: An able theoretical expositor of all that came within the sphere of his practice, he was not without the power of passing an adequate judgment in matters in which he had no experience.
text_raw:
An able theoretical expositor of all that came within the sphere of his
practice, he was not without the power of passing an adequate judgment in matters in
which he had no experience.

text: He could also excellently divine the good and evil which lay
text_raw: He could also excellently divine the good and evil which lay

text: hid in the unseen future.
text_raw: hid in the unseen future.

text: In fine, whether we consider the extent of his natural powers, or the slightness of his application, this extraordinary man must be allowed to have surpassed all others in the faculty of intuitively meeting an emergency.
text_raw:
In fine, whether we consider the extent of his natural powers, or
the slightness of his application, this extraordinary man must be allowed to have surpassed

text: Disease was the real cause of his death; though there is a story of his having ended his life by poison, on finding himself unable to fulfil his promises to the king.
text_raw:
Disease was the real cause of

text: However this may be, there is a monument to him in the marketplace of Asiatic Magnesia.
text_raw:
However this may be, there is a monument to him
in the marketplace of Asiatic Magnesia.

text: He was governor of the district, the King having given him Magnesia, which brought in fifty talents a year, for bread, Lampsacus, which was considered to be the richest wine country, for wine, and Myos for other provisions.
text_raw:
He was governor of the district, the King having
given him Magnesia, which brought in fifty talents a year, for bread, Lampsacus, which

text: His bones, it is said, were conveyed home by his relatives in accordance with his wishes, and interred in Attic ground.
text_raw:
His bones, it is said, were conveyed home by his relatives in accordance with his wishes,

text: This was done without the knowledge of the Athenians; as it is against the law to bury in Attica an outlaw for treason.
text_raw:
This was done without the knowledge of the Athenians; as it

text: So ends the history of Pausanias and Themistocles, the Lacedaemonian and the Athenian, the most famous men of their time in Hellas.
text_raw:
So ends the history of Pausanias
and Themistocles, the Lacedaemonian and the Athenian, the most famous men of their
