text: To return to the Lacedaemonians.
text_raw: To return to the Lacedaemonians.

text: The history of their first embassy, the injunctions which it conveyed, and the rejoinder which it provoked, concerning the expulsion of the accursed persons, have been related already.
text_raw:
The history of their first embassy, the injunctions
which it conveyed, and the rejoinder which it provoked, concerning the expulsion of the
accursed persons, have been related already.

text: It was followed by a second, which ordered Athens to raise the siege of Potidaea, and to respect the independence of Aegina.
text_raw:
It was followed by a second, which ordered
Athens to raise the siege of Potidaea, and to respect the independence of Aegina.

text: Above all, it gave her most distinctly to understand that war might be prevented by the revocation of the Megara decree, excluding the Megarians from the use of Athenian harbours and of the market of Athens.
text_raw:
Above
all, it gave her most distinctly to understand that war might be prevented by the revocation
of the Megara decree, excluding the Megarians from the use of Athenian harbours and of
the market of Athens.

text: But Athens was not inclined either to revoke the decree, or to entertain their other proposals; she accused the Megarians of pushing their cultivation into the consecrated ground and the unenclosed land on the border, and of harbouring her runaway slaves.
text_raw:
But Athens was not inclined either to revoke the decree, or to
entertain their other proposals; she accused the Megarians of pushing their cultivation into
the consecrated ground and the unenclosed land on the border, and of harbouring her
runaway slaves.

text: At last an embassy arrived with the Lacedaemonian ultimatum.
text_raw: At last an embassy arrived with the Lacedaemonian ultimatum.

text: The ambassadors were Ramphias, Melesippus, and Agesander.
text_raw:
The
ambassadors were Ramphias, Melesippus, and Agesander.

text: Not a word was said on any of the old subjects; there was simply this: “Lacedaemon wishes the peace to continue, and there is no reason why it should not, if you would leave the Hellenes independent.” Upon this the Athenians held an assembly, and laid the matter before their consideration.
text_raw:
Not a word was said on any of
the old subjects; there was simply this: “Lacedaemon wishes the peace to continue, and
there is no reason why it should not, if you would leave the Hellenes independent.” Upon
this the Athenians held an assembly, and laid the matter before their consideration.

text: It was resolved to deliberate once for all on all their demands, and to give them an answer.
text_raw:
It was
resolved to deliberate once for all on all their demands, and to give them an answer.

text: There were many speakers who came forward and gave their support to one side or the other, urging the necessity of war, or the revocation of the decree and the folly of allowing it to stand in the way of peace.
text_raw:
There
were many speakers who came forward and gave their support to one side or the other,
urging the necessity of war, or the revocation of the decree and the folly of allowing it to
stand in the way of peace.

text: Among them came forward Pericles, son of Xanthippus, the first man of his time at Athens, ablest alike in counsel and in action, and gave the following advice: “There is one principle, Athenians, which I hold to through everything, and that is the principle of no concession to the Peloponnesians.
text_raw:
Among them came forward Pericles, son of Xanthippus, the
first man of his time at Athens, ablest alike in counsel and in action, and gave the
following advice:
“There is one principle, Athenians, which I hold to through everything, and that is the
principle of no concession to the Peloponnesians.

text: I know that the spirit which inspires men while they are being persuaded to make war is not always retained in action; that as circumstances change, resolutions change.
text_raw:
I know that the spirit which inspires men
while they are being persuaded to make war is not always retained in action; that as
circumstances change, resolutions change.

text: Yet I see that now as before the same, almost literally the same, counsel is demanded of me; and I put it to those of you who are allowing yourselves to be persuaded, to support the national resolves even in the case of reverses, or to forfeit all credit for their wisdom in the event of success.
text_raw:
Yet I see that now as before the same, almost
literally the same, counsel is demanded of me; and I put it to those of you who are
allowing yourselves to be persuaded, to support the national resolves even in the case of
reverses, or to forfeit all credit for their wisdom in the event of success.

text: For sometimes the course of things is as arbitrary as the plans of man; indeed this is why we usually blame chance for whatever does not happen as we expected.
text_raw:
For sometimes the
course of things is as arbitrary as the plans of man; indeed this is why we usually blame
chance for whatever does not happen as we expected.

text: Now it was clear before that Lacedaemon entertained designs against us; it is still more clear now.
text_raw:
Now it was clear before that
Lacedaemon entertained designs against us; it is still more clear now.

text: The treaty provides that we shall mutually submit our differences to legal settlement, and that we shall
text_raw:
The treaty provides
that we shall mutually submit our differences to legal settlement, and that we shall

text: meanwhile each keep what we have.
text_raw: meanwhile each keep what we have.

text: Yet the Lacedaemonians never yet made us any such offer, never yet would accept from us any such offer; on the contrary, they wish complaints to be settled by war instead of by negotiation; and in the end we find them here dropping the tone of expostulation and adopting that of command.
text_raw:
Yet the Lacedaemonians never yet made us any such
offer, never yet would accept from us any such offer; on the contrary, they wish
complaints to be settled by war instead of by negotiation; and in the end we find them here
dropping the tone of expostulation and adopting that of command.

text: They order us to raise the siege of Potidaea, to let Aegina be independent, to revoke the Megara decree; and they conclude with an ultimatum warning us to leave the Hellenes independent.
text_raw:
They order us to raise
the siege of Potidaea, to let Aegina be independent, to revoke the Megara decree; and they
conclude with an ultimatum warning us to leave the Hellenes independent.

text: I hope that you will none of you think that we shall be going to war for a trifle if we refuse to revoke the Megara decree, which appears in front of their complaints, and the revocation of which is to save us from war, or let any feeling of self-reproach linger in your minds, as if you went to war for slight cause.
text_raw:
I hope that you
will none of you think that we shall be going to war for a trifle if we refuse to revoke the
Megara decree, which appears in front of their complaints, and the revocation of which is
to save us from war, or let any feeling of self-reproach linger in your minds, as if you went
to war for slight cause.

text: Why, this trifle contains the whole seal and trial of your resolution.
text_raw: Why, this trifle contains the whole seal and trial of your resolution.

text: If you give way, you will instantly have to meet some greater demand, as having been frightened into obedience in the first instance; while a firm refusal will make them clearly understand that they must treat you more as equals.
text_raw:
If you give way, you will instantly have to meet some greater demand, as having been
frightened into obedience in the first instance; while a firm refusal will make them clearly
understand that they must treat you more as equals.

text: Make your decision therefore at once, either to submit before you are harmed, or if we are to go to war, as I for one think we ought, to do so without caring whether the ostensible cause be great or small, resolved against making concessions or consenting to a precarious tenure of our possessions.
text_raw:
Make your decision therefore at once,
either to submit before you are harmed, or if we are to go to war, as I for one think we
ought, to do so without caring whether the ostensible cause be great or small, resolved
against making concessions or consenting to a precarious tenure of our possessions.

text: For all claims from an equal, urged upon a neighbour as commands before any attempt at legal settlement, be they great or be they small, have only one meaning, and that is slavery. “As to the war and the resources of either party, a detailed comparison will not show you the inferiority of Athens.
text_raw:
For
all claims from an equal, urged upon a neighbour as commands before any attempt at legal
settlement, be they great or be they small, have only one meaning, and that is slavery.
“As to the war and the resources of either party, a detailed comparison will not show you
the inferiority of Athens.

text: Personally engaged in the cultivation of their land, without funds either private or public, the Peloponnesians are also without experience in long wars across sea, from the strict limit which poverty imposes on their attacks upon each other.
text_raw:
Personally engaged in the cultivation of their land, without funds
either private or public, the Peloponnesians are also without experience in long wars
across sea, from the strict limit which poverty imposes on their attacks upon each other.

text: Powers of this description are quite incapable of often manning a fleet or often sending out an army: they cannot afford the absence from their homes, the expenditure from their own funds; and besides, they have not command of the sea.
text_raw:
Powers of this description are quite incapable of often manning a fleet or often sending out
an army: they cannot afford the absence from their homes, the expenditure from their own
funds; and besides, they have not command of the sea.

text: Capital, it must be remembered, maintains a war more than forced contributions.
text_raw:
Capital, it must be remembered,
maintains a war more than forced contributions.

text: Farmers are a class of men that are always more ready to serve in person than in purse.
text_raw:
Farmers are a class of men that are
always more ready to serve in person than in purse.

text: Confident that the former will survive the dangers, they are by no means so sure that the latter will not be prematurely exhausted, especially if the war last longer than they expect, which it very likely will.
text_raw:
Confident that the former will survive
the dangers, they are by no means so sure that the latter will not be prematurely exhausted,
especially if the war last longer than they expect, which it very likely will.

text: In a single battle the Peloponnesians and their allies may be able to defy all Hellas, but they are incapacitated from carrying on a war against a power different in character from their own, by the want of the single council-chamber requisite to prompt and vigorous action, and the substitution of a diet composed of various races, in which every state possesses an equal vote, and each presses its own ends, a condition of things which generally results in no action at all.
text_raw:
In a single
battle the Peloponnesians and their allies may be able to defy all Hellas, but they are
incapacitated from carrying on a war against a power different in character from their
own, by the want of the single council-chamber requisite to prompt and vigorous action,
and the substitution of a diet composed of various races, in which every state possesses an
equal vote, and each presses its own ends, a condition of things which generally results in
no action at all.

text: The great wish of some is to avenge themselves on some particular enemy, the great wish of others to save their own pocket.
text_raw:
The great wish of some is to avenge themselves on some particular enemy,
the great wish of others to save their own pocket.

text: Slow in assembling, they devote a very small fraction of the time to the consideration of any public object, most of it to the prosecution of their own objects.
text_raw:
Slow in assembling, they devote a very
small fraction of the time to the consideration of any public object, most of it to the
prosecution of their own objects.

text: Meanwhile each fancies that no harm will come of his neglect, that it is the business of somebody else to look after this or that for him; and so, by the same notion being entertained by all separately, the common cause imperceptibly decays. “But the principal point is the hindrance that they will experience from want of money.
text_raw:
Meanwhile each fancies that no harm will come of his
neglect, that it is the business of somebody else to look after this or that for him; and so,
by the same notion being entertained by all separately, the common cause imperceptibly
decays.
“But the principal point is the hindrance that they will experience from want of money.

text: The slowness with which it comes in will cause delay; but the opportunities of war wait for no man.
text_raw:
The slowness with which it comes in will cause delay; but the opportunities of war wait
for no man.

text: Again, we need not be alarmed either at the possibility of their raising
text_raw: Again, we need not be alarmed either at the possibility of their raising

text: fortifications in Attica, or at their navy.
text_raw: fortifications in Attica, or at their navy.

text: It would be difficult for any system of fortifications to establish a rival city, even in time of peace, much more, surely, in an enemy’s country, with Athens just as much fortified against it as it against Athens; while a mere post might be able to do some harm to the country by incursions and by the facilities which it would afford for desertion, but can never prevent our sailing into their country and raising fortifications there, and making reprisals with our powerful fleet.
text_raw:
It would be difficult for any system of
fortifications to establish a rival city, even in time of peace, much more, surely, in an
enemy’s country, with Athens just as much fortified against it as it against Athens; while a
mere post might be able to do some harm to the country by incursions and by the facilities
which it would afford for desertion, but can never prevent our sailing into their country
and raising fortifications there, and making reprisals with our powerful fleet.

text: For our naval skill is of more use to us for service on land, than their military skill for service at sea.
text_raw:
For our naval
skill is of more use to us for service on land, than their military skill for service at sea.

text: Familiarity with the sea they will not find an easy acquisition.
text_raw: Familiarity with the sea they will not find an easy acquisition.

text: If you who have been practising at it ever since the Median invasion have not yet brought it to perfection, is there any chance of anything considerable being effected by an agricultural, unseafaring population, who will besides be prevented from practising by the constant presence of strong squadrons of observation from Athens?
text_raw:
If you who have been
practising at it ever since the Median invasion have not yet brought it to perfection, is
there any chance of anything considerable being effected by an agricultural, unseafaring
population, who will besides be prevented from practising by the constant presence of
strong squadrons of observation from Athens?

text: With a small squadron they might hazard an engagement, encouraging their ignorance by numbers; but the restraint of a strong force will prevent their moving, and through want of practice they will grow more clumsy, and consequently more timid.
text_raw:
With a small squadron they might hazard
an engagement, encouraging their ignorance by numbers; but the restraint of a strong force
will prevent their moving, and through want of practice they will grow more clumsy, and
consequently more timid.

text: It must be kept in mind that seamanship, just like anything else, is a matter of art, and will not admit of being taken up occasionally as an occupation for times of leisure; on the contrary, it is so exacting as to leave leisure for nothing else. “Even if they were to touch the moneys at Olympia or Delphi, and try to seduce our foreign sailors by the temptation of higher pay, that would only be a serious danger if we could not still be a match for them by embarking our own citizens and the aliens resident among us.
text_raw:
It must be kept in mind that seamanship, just like anything else,
is a matter of art, and will not admit of being taken up occasionally as an occupation for
times of leisure; on the contrary, it is so exacting as to leave leisure for nothing else.
“Even if they were to touch the moneys at Olympia or Delphi, and try to seduce our
foreign sailors by the temptation of higher pay, that would only be a serious danger if we
could not still be a match for them by embarking our own citizens and the aliens resident
among us.

text: But in fact by this means we are always a match for them; and, best of all, we have a larger and higher class of native coxswains and sailors among our own citizens than all the rest of Hellas.
text_raw:
But in fact by this means we are always a match for them; and, best of all, we
have a larger and higher class of native coxswains and sailors among our own citizens
than all the rest of Hellas.

text: And to say nothing of the danger of such a step, none of our foreign sailors would consent to become an outlaw from his country, and to take service with them and their hopes, for the sake of a few days’ high pay. “This, I think, is a tolerably fair account of the position of the Peloponnesians; that of Athens is free from the defects that I have criticized in them, and has other advantages of its own, which they can show nothing to equal.
text_raw:
And to say nothing of the danger of such a step, none of our
foreign sailors would consent to become an outlaw from his country, and to take service
with them and their hopes, for the sake of a few days’ high pay.
“This, I think, is a tolerably fair account of the position of the Peloponnesians; that of
Athens is free from the defects that I have criticized in them, and has other advantages of
its own, which they can show nothing to equal.

text: If they march against our country we will sail against theirs, and it will then be found that the desolation of the whole of Attica is not the same as that of even a fraction of Peloponnese; for they will not be able to supply the deficiency except by a battle, while we have plenty of land both on the islands and the continent.
text_raw:
If they march against our country we will
sail against theirs, and it will then be found that the desolation of the whole of Attica is not
the same as that of even a fraction of Peloponnese; for they will not be able to supply the
deficiency except by a battle, while we have plenty of land both on the islands and the
continent.

text: The rule of the sea is indeed a great matter.
text_raw: The rule of the sea is indeed a great matter.

text: Consider for a moment.
text_raw: Consider for a moment.

text: Suppose that we were islanders; can you conceive a more impregnable position?
text_raw:
Suppose
that we were islanders; can you conceive a more impregnable position?

text: Well, this in future should, as far as possible, be our conception of our position.
text_raw:
Well, this in future
should, as far as possible, be our conception of our position.

text: Dismissing all thought of our land and houses, we must vigilantly guard the sea and the city.
text_raw:
Dismissing all thought of our
land and houses, we must vigilantly guard the sea and the city.

text: No irritation that we may feel for the former must provoke us to a battle with the numerical superiority of the Peloponnesians.
text_raw:
No irritation that we may
feel for the former must provoke us to a battle with the numerical superiority of the
Peloponnesians.

text: A victory would only be succeeded by another battle against the same superiority: a reverse involves the loss of our allies, the source of our strength, who will not remain quiet a day after we become unable to march against them.
text_raw:
A victory would only be succeeded by another battle against the same
superiority: a reverse involves the loss of our allies, the source of our strength, who will
not remain quiet a day after we become unable to march against them.

text: We must cry not over the loss of houses and land but of men’s lives; since houses and land do not gain men, but men them.
text_raw:
We must cry not
over the loss of houses and land but of men’s lives; since houses and land do not gain men,
but men them.

text: And if I had thought that I could persuade you, I would have bid you go out and lay them waste with your own hands, and show the Peloponnesians that this at any rate will not make you submit.
text_raw:
And if I had thought that I could persuade you, I would have bid you go out
and lay them waste with your own hands, and show the Peloponnesians that this at any
rate will not make you submit.

text: “I have many other reasons to hope for a favourable issue, if you can consent not to combine schemes of fresh conquest with the conduct of the war, and will abstain from wilfully involving yourselves in other dangers; indeed, I am more afraid of our own blunders than of the enemy’s devices.
text_raw:
“I have many other reasons to hope for a favourable issue, if you can consent not to
combine schemes of fresh conquest with the conduct of the war, and will abstain from
wilfully involving yourselves in other dangers; indeed, I am more afraid of our own
blunders than of the enemy’s devices.

text: But these matters shall be explained in another speech, as events require; for the present dismiss these men with the answer that we will allow Megara the use of our market and harbours, when the Lacedaemonians suspend their alien acts in favour of us and our allies, there being nothing in the treaty to prevent either one or the other: that we will leave the cities independent, if independent we found them when we made the treaty, and when the Lacedaemonians grant to their cities an independence not involving subservience to Lacedaemonian interests, but such as each severally may desire: that we are willing to give the legal satisfaction which our agreements specify, and that we shall not commence hostilities, but shall resist those who do commence them.
text_raw:
But these matters shall be explained in another
speech, as events require; for the present dismiss these men with the answer that we will
allow Megara the use of our market and harbours, when the Lacedaemonians suspend
their alien acts in favour of us and our allies, there being nothing in the treaty to prevent
either one or the other: that we will leave the cities independent, if independent we found
them when we made the treaty, and when the Lacedaemonians grant to their cities an
independence not involving subservience to Lacedaemonian interests, but such as each
severally may desire: that we are willing to give the legal satisfaction which our
agreements specify, and that we shall not commence hostilities, but shall resist those who
do commence them.

text: This is an answer agreeable at once to the rights and the dignity of Athens.
text_raw:
This is an answer agreeable at once to the rights and the dignity of
Athens.

text: It must be thoroughly understood that war is a necessity; but that the more readily we accept it, the less will be the ardour of our opponents, and that out of the greatest dangers communities and individuals acquire the greatest glory.
text_raw:
It must be thoroughly understood that war is a necessity; but that the more readily
we accept it, the less will be the ardour of our opponents, and that out of the greatest
dangers communities and individuals acquire the greatest glory.

text: Did not our fathers resist the Medes not only with resources far different from ours, but even when those resources had been abandoned; and more by wisdom than by fortune, more by daring than by strength, did not they beat off the barbarian and advance their affairs to their present height?
text_raw:
Did not our fathers resist
the Medes not only with resources far different from ours, but even when those resources
had been abandoned; and more by wisdom than by fortune, more by daring than by
strength, did not they beat off the barbarian and advance their affairs to their present
height?

text: We must not fall behind them, but must resist our enemies in any way and in every way, and attempt to hand down our power to our posterity unimpaired.” Such were the words of Pericles.
text_raw:
We must not fall behind them, but must resist our enemies in any way and in every

text: The Athenians are the very people of all others to do this, as they aspire to rule the rest of the world, and are more in the habit of invading and ravaging their neighbours’ territory, than of seeing their own treated in the like fashion.

text: Considering, therefore, the power of the state against which we are marching, and the greatness of the reputation which, according to the event, we shall win or lose for our ancestors and ourselves, remember as you follow where you may be led to regard discipline and vigilance as of the first importance, and to obey with alacrity the orders transmitted to you; as nothing contributes so much to the credit and safety of an army as the union of large bodies by a single discipline.” With this brief speech dismissing the assembly, Archidamus first sent off Melesippus, son of Diacritus, a Spartan, to Athens, in case she should be more inclined to submit on seeing the Peloponnesians actually on the march.
text_raw:
Considering, therefore, the power of the state against
which we are marching, and the greatness of the reputation which, according to the event,
we shall win or lose for our ancestors and ourselves, remember as you follow where you
may be led to regard discipline and vigilance as of the first importance, and to obey with
alacrity the orders transmitted to you; as nothing contributes so much to the credit and

With this brief speech dismissing the assembly, Archidamus first sent off Melesippus,
son of Diacritus, a Spartan, to Athens, in case she should be more inclined to submit on
seeing the Peloponnesians actually on the march.

text: But the Athenians did not admit into the city or to their assembly, Pericles having already carried a motion against admitting either herald or embassy from the Lacedaemonians after they had once marched out.

But the Athenians did not admit into the
city or to their assembly, Pericles having already carried a motion against admitting either

text: The herald was accordingly sent away without an audience, and ordered to be beyond the frontier that same day; in future, if those who sent him had a proposition to make, they must retire to their own territory before they dispatched embassies to Athens.
text_raw:
The herald was accordingly sent away without an audience, and ordered to be beyond the
frontier that same day; in future, if those who sent him had a proposition to make, they
must retire to their own territory before they dispatched embassies to Athens.

text: An escort was sent with Melesippus to prevent his holding communication with any one.
text_raw:
An escort
was sent with Melesippus to prevent his holding communication with any one.

text: When he reached the frontier and was just going to be dismissed, he departed with these words: “This day will be the beginning of great misfortunes to the Hellenes.” As soon as he arrived at the camp, and Archidamus learnt that the Athenians had still no thoughts of submitting, he at length began his march, and advanced with his army into their territory.
text_raw:
When he
reached the frontier and was just going to be dismissed, he departed with these words:
“This day will be the beginning of great misfortunes to the Hellenes.” As soon as he
arrived at the camp, and Archidamus learnt that the Athenians had still no thoughts of
submitting, he at length began his march, and advanced with his army into their territory.

text: Meanwhile the Boeotians, sending their contingent and cavalry to join the Peloponnesian expedition, went to Plataea with the remainder and laid waste the country.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the Boeotians, sending their contingent and cavalry to join the Peloponnesian

text: While the Peloponnesians were still mustering at the Isthmus, or on the march before they invaded Attica, Pericles, son of Xanthippus, one of the ten generals of the Athenians, finding that the invasion was to take place, conceived the idea that Archidamus, who happened to be his friend, might possibly pass by his estate without ravaging it.
text_raw:
While the Peloponnesians were still mustering at the Isthmus, or on the march before
they invaded Attica, Pericles, son of Xanthippus, one of the ten generals of the Athenians,
finding that the invasion was to take place, conceived the idea that Archidamus, who
happened to be his friend, might possibly pass by his estate without ravaging it.

text: This he might do, either from a personal wish to oblige him, or acting under instructions from Lacedaemon for the purpose of creating a prejudice against him, as had been before attempted in the demand for the expulsion of the accursed family.
text_raw:
This he
might do, either from a personal wish to oblige him, or acting under instructions from
Lacedaemon for the purpose of creating a prejudice against him, as had been before
attempted in the demand for the expulsion of the accursed family.

text: He accordingly took the precaution of announcing to the Athenians in the assembly that, although Archidamus was his friend, yet this friendship should not extend to the detriment of the state, and that in case the enemy should make his houses and lands an exception to the rest and not pillage them, he at once gave them up to be public property, so that they should not bring him into suspicion.
text_raw:
He accordingly took the
precaution of announcing to the Athenians in the assembly that, although Archidamus was
his friend, yet this friendship should not extend to the detriment of the state, and that in
case the enemy should make his houses and lands an exception to the rest and not pillage
them, he at once gave them up to be public property, so that they should not bring him into
suspicion.

text: He also gave the citizens some advice on their present affairs in the same strain as before.
text_raw:
He also gave the citizens some advice on their present affairs in the same strain
as before.

text: They were to prepare for the war, and to carry in their property from the country.
text_raw:
They were to prepare for the war, and to carry in their property from the
country.

text: They were not to go out to battle, but to come into the city and guard it, and get ready their fleet, in which their real strength lay.
text_raw:
They were not to go out to battle, but to come into the city and guard it, and get
ready their fleet, in which their real strength lay.

text: They were also to keep a tight rein on
text_raw: They were also to keep a tight rein on

their allies—the strength of Athens being derived from the money brought in by their

text: Apart from other sources of income, an average revenue of six hundred talents of silver was drawn from the tribute of the allies; and there were still six thousand talents of coined silver in the Acropolis, out of nine thousand seven hundred that had once been there, from which the money had been taken for the porch of the Acropolis, the other public buildings, and for Potidaea.

text: This did not include the uncoined gold and silver in public and private offerings, the sacred vessels for the processions and games, the Median spoils, and similar resources to the amount of five hundred talents.

This did not include the uncoined gold and silver in

text: To this he added the treasures of the other temples.
text_raw:
To this he added the
treasures of the other temples.

text: These were by no means inconsiderable, and might fairly be used.
text_raw:
These were by no means inconsiderable, and might fairly

text: Nay, if they were ever absolutely driven to it, they might take even the gold ornaments of Athene herself; for the statue contained forty talents of pure gold and it was all removable.
text_raw:
Nay, if they were ever absolutely driven to it, they might take even the gold

text: This might be used for self-preservation, and must every penny of it be restored.

This might be used for self-preservation, and must every penny of it be

text: Such was their financial position—surely a satisfactory one.
text_raw: Such was their financial position—surely a satisfactory one.

text: Then they had an army of thirteen thousand heavy infantry, besides sixteen thousand more in the garrisons and on home duty at Athens.
text_raw:
Then they had an
army of thirteen thousand heavy infantry, besides sixteen thousand more in the garrisons

text: This was at first the number of men on guard in the event of an invasion: it was composed of the oldest and youngest levies and the resident aliens who had heavy armour.
text_raw:
This was at first the number of men on guard in the event of
an invasion: it was composed of the oldest and youngest levies and the resident aliens who

text: The Phaleric wall ran for four miles, before it joined that round the city; and of this last nearly five had a guard, although part of it was left without one, viz., that between the Long Wall and the Phaleric.
text_raw:
The Phaleric wall ran for four miles, before it joined that round the

Then there were the Long Walls to Piraeus, a

text: Lastly, the circumference of Piraeus with Munychia was nearly seven miles and a half; only half of this, however, was guarded.

Lastly, the

text: Pericles also showed them that they had twelve hundred horse including mounted archers, with sixteen hundred archers unmounted, and three hundred galleys fit for service.
text_raw:
Pericles also showed them that they had twelve hundred horse

text: Such were the resources of Athens in the different departments when the Peloponnesian invasion was impending and hostilities were being commenced.
text_raw:
Such were the resources of Athens in the different departments
when the Peloponnesian invasion was impending and hostilities were being commenced.

text: Pericles also urged his usual arguments for expecting a favourable issue to the war.
text_raw: Pericles also urged his usual arguments for expecting a favourable issue to the war.

text: The Athenians listened to his advice, and began to carry in their wives and children from the country, and all their household furniture, even to the woodwork of their houses which they took down.
text_raw:
The Athenians listened to his advice, and began to carry in their wives and children from

text: Their sheep and cattle they sent over to Euboea and the adjacent islands.
text_raw: Their sheep and cattle they sent over to Euboea and the adjacent islands.

text: But they found it hard to move, as most of them had been always used to live in the country.

But they found it hard to move, as most of them had been always used to live in the

text: From very early times this had been more the case with the Athenians than with others.
text_raw: From very early times this had been more the case with the Athenians than with others.

text: Under Cecrops and the first kings, down to the reign of Theseus, Attica had always consisted of a number of independent townships, each with its own town hall and magistrates.
text_raw:
Under Cecrops and the first kings, down to the reign of Theseus, Attica had always
consisted of a number of independent townships, each with its own town hall and
magistrates.

text: Except in times of danger the king at Athens was not consulted; in ordinary seasons they carried on their government and settled their affairs without his interference; sometimes even they waged war against him, as in the case of the Eleusinians with Eumolpus against Erechtheus.
text_raw:
Except in times of danger the king at Athens was not consulted; in ordinary
seasons they carried on their government and settled their affairs without his interference;
sometimes even they waged war against him, as in the case of the Eleusinians with
Eumolpus against Erechtheus.

text: In Theseus, however, they had a king of equal intelligence and power; and one of the chief features in his organization of the country was to abolish the council-chambers and magistrates of the petty cities, and to merge them in the single council-chamber and town hall of the present capital.
text_raw:
In Theseus, however, they had a king of equal intelligence
and power; and one of the chief features in his organization of the country was to abolish
the council-chambers and magistrates of the petty cities, and to merge them in the single
council-chamber and town hall of the present capital.

text: Individuals might still enjoy their private property just as before, but they were henceforth compelled to have only one political centre, viz., Athens; which thus counted all the inhabitants of Attica among her
text_raw:
Individuals might still enjoy their
private property just as before, but they were henceforth compelled to have only one
political centre, viz., Athens; which thus counted all the inhabitants of Attica among her

text: Indeed, from him dates the Synoecia, or Feast of Union; which is paid for by the state, and which the Athenians still keep in honour of the goddess.
text_raw:

text: Before this the city consisted of the present citadel and the district beneath it looking rather towards the south.
text_raw:

text: This is shown by the fact that the temples of the other deities, besides that of Athene, are in the citadel; and even those that are outside it are mostly situated in this quarter of the city, as that of the Olympian Zeus, of the Pythian Apollo, of Earth, and of Dionysus in the Marshes, the same in whose honour the older Dionysia are to this day celebrated in the month of Anthesterion not only by the Athenians but also by their Ionian descendants.

This is shown by the

text: There are also other ancient temples in this quarter.
text_raw:
There are also other

text: The fountain too, which, since the alteration made by the tyrants, has been called Enneacrounos, or Nine Pipes, but which, when the spring was open, went by the name of Callirhoe, or Fairwater, was in those days, from being so near, used for the most important offices.
text_raw:
The fountain too, which, since the alteration made by the

text: Indeed, the old fashion of using the water before marriage and for other sacred purposes is still kept up.

text: Again, from their old residence in that quarter, the citadel is still known among Athenians as the city.

Again, from their old residence in

text: The Athenians thus long lived scattered over Attica in independent townships.
text_raw: The Athenians thus long lived scattered over Attica in independent townships.

text: Even after the centralization of Theseus, old habit still prevailed; and from the early times down to the present war most Athenians still lived in the country with their families and households, and were consequently not at all inclined to move now, especially as they had only just restored their establishments after the Median invasion.
text_raw:
Even after
the centralization of Theseus, old habit still prevailed; and from the early times down to
the present war most Athenians still lived in the country with their families and
households, and were consequently not at all inclined to move now, especially as they had

text: Deep was their trouble and discontent at abandoning their houses and the hereditary temples of the ancient constitution, and at having to change their habits of life and to bid farewell to what each regarded as his native city.
text_raw:
Deep was their trouble
and discontent at abandoning their houses and the hereditary temples of the ancient

text: When they arrived at Athens, though a few had houses of their own to go to, or could find an asylum with friends or relatives, by far the greater number had to take up their dwelling in the parts of the city that were not built over and in the temples and chapels of the heroes, except the Acropolis and the temple of the Eleusinian Demeter and such other Places as were always kept closed.
text_raw:
When they arrived at Athens, though a few had houses of their own to go to, or could

text: The occupation of the plot of ground lying below the citadel called the Pelasgian had been forbidden by a curse; and there was also an ominous fragment of a Pythian oracle which said:

The occupation of the plot of ground lying below the

text: Leave the Pelasgian parcel desolate, Woe worth the day that men inhabit it!
text_raw: Leave the Pelasgian parcel desolate, Woe worth the day that men inhabit it!

text: Yet this too was now built over in the necessity of the moment.

text: For the misfortunes of the state did not arise from the unlawful occupation, but the necessity of the occupation from the war; and though the god did not mention this, he foresaw that it would be an evil day for Athens in which the plot came to be inhabited.
text_raw:
For the misfortunes

text: Many also took up their quarters in the towers of the walls or wherever else they could.

text: All this while great attention was being given to the war; the allies were being mustered, and an armament of a hundred ships equipped for Peloponnese.

text: Such was the state of preparation at Athens.

text_raw: Meanwhile the army of the Peloponnesians was advancing.

The first town they came to

text: Sitting down before it, they prepared

Oenoe, standing upon the Athenian and

text_raw: This delay brought the gravest censure upon Archidamus.

text: During this interval the Athenians were carrying in their property; and it was the belief of the Peloponnesians that a quick advance would have found everything still out, had it not been for his procrastination.

text: But after he had assaulted Oenoe, and every possible attempt to take it had failed, as no herald came from Athens, he at last broke up his camp and invaded Attica.
text_raw:
But after he had assaulted Oenoe, and every possible attempt to take it had failed, as no

text: This was about eighty days after the Theban attempt upon Plataea, just in the middle of summer, when the corn was ripe, and Archidamus, son of Zeuxis, king of Lacedaemon, was in command.
text_raw:

text: Encamping in Eleusis and the Thriasian plain, they began their ravages, and putting to flight some Athenian horse at a place called Rheiti, or the Brooks, they then advanced, keeping Mount Aegaleus on their right, through Cropia, until they reached Acharnae, the largest of the Athenian demes or townships.

text: Sitting down before it, they formed a camp there, and continued their ravages for a long while.
text_raw:
Sitting down before it, they formed a camp

text: The reason why Archidamus remained in order of battle at Acharnae during this incursion, instead of descending into the plain, is said to have been this.
text_raw:
The reason why Archidamus remained in order of battle at Acharnae during this
incursion, instead of descending into the plain, is said to have been this.

text: He hoped that the Athenians might possibly be tempted by the multitude of their youth and the unprecedented efficiency of their service to come out to battle and attempt to stop the devastation of their lands.
text_raw:
He hoped that the
Athenians might possibly be tempted by the multitude of their youth and the
unprecedented efficiency of their service to come out to battle and attempt to stop the

text: Accordingly, as they had met him at Eleusis or the Thriasian plain, he tried if they could be provoked to a sally by the spectacle of a camp at Acharnae.

text: He thought the place itself a good position for encamping; and it seemed likely that such an important part of the state as the three thousand heavy infantry of the Acharnians would refuse to submit to the ruin of their property, and would force a battle on the rest of the citizens.
text_raw:
He thought the place itself a good position for encamping; and it seemed likely that such

text: On the other hand, should the Athenians not take the field during this incursion, he could then fearlessly ravage the plain in future invasions, and extend his advance up to the very walls of Athens.
text_raw:
On the other hand, should the Athenians not take the field during this incursion,
he could then fearlessly ravage the plain in future invasions, and extend his advance up to

text: After the Acharnians had lost their own property they would be less willing to risk themselves for that of their neighbours; and so there would be division in the Athenian counsels.
text_raw:

text: The territory of Athens was being ravaged before the very eyes of the Athenians, a sight which the young men had never seen before and the old only in the Median wars; and it was naturally thought a grievous insult, and the determination was universal, especially among the young men, to sally forth and stop it.

determination was universal, especially among the young men, to sally forth and stop it.

text: Knots were formed in the streets and engaged in hot discussion; for if the proposed sally was warmly recommended, it was also in some cases opposed.

text: And if our more remote ancestors deserve praise, much more do our own fathers, who added to their inheritance the empire which we now possess, and spared no pains to be able to leave their acquisitions to us of the present generation.
text_raw:

more do our own fathers, who added to their inheritance the empire which we now
possess, and spared no pains to be able to leave their acquisitions to us of the present
generation.

text: Lastly, there are few parts of our dominions that have not been augmented by those of us here, who are still more or less in the vigour of life; while the mother country has been furnished by us with everything that can enable her to depend on her own resources whether for war or for peace.

text: That part of our history which tells of the military achievements which gave us our several possessions, or of the ready valour with which either we or our fathers stemmed the tide of Hellenic or foreign aggression, is a theme too familiar to my hearers for me to dilate on, and I shall therefore pass it by.

text: But what was the road by which we reached our position, what the form of government under which our greatness grew, what the national habits out of which it sprang; these are questions which I may try to solve before I proceed to my panegyric upon these men; since I think this to be a subject upon which on the present occasion a speaker may properly dwell, and to which the whole assemblage, whether citizens or foreigners, may listen with advantage. “Our constitution does not copy the laws of neighbouring states; we are rather a pattern to others than imitators ourselves.

text: Its administration favours the many instead of the few; this is why it is called a democracy.
text_raw:

text: If we look to the laws, they afford equal justice to all in their private differences; if no social standing, advancement in public life falls to reputation for capacity, class considerations not being allowed to interfere with merit; nor again does poverty bar the way, if a man is able to serve the state, he is not hindered by the obscurity of his condition.

text: The freedom which we enjoy in our government extends also to our ordinary life.
text_raw:
The freedom which we enjoy in our government extends also to

text: There, far from exercising a jealous surveillance over each other, we do not feel called upon to be angry with our neighbour for doing what he likes, or even to indulge in those injurious looks which cannot fail to be offensive, although they inflict no positive penalty.

text: But all this ease in our private relations does not make us lawless as citizens.

text: Against this fear is our chief safeguard, teaching us to obey the magistrates and the laws, particularly such as regard the protection of the injured, whether they are actually on the statute book, or belong to that code which, although unwritten, yet cannot be broken without acknowledged disgrace. “Further, we provide plenty of means for the mind to refresh itself from business.

text: We celebrate games and sacrifices all the year round, and the elegance of our private establishments forms a daily source of pleasure and helps to banish the spleen; while the magnitude of our city draws the produce of the world into our harbour, so that to the Athenian the fruits of other countries are as familiar a luxury as those of his own. “If we turn to our military policy, there also we differ from our antagonists.

text: In proof of this it may be noticed that the Lacedaemonians do not invade our country alone, but bring with them all their confederates; while we Athenians advance unsupported into the territory of a neighbour, and fighting upon a foreign soil usually vanquish with ease men who are defending their homes.

text: Our united force was never yet encountered by any enemy, because we have at once to attend to our marine and to dispatch our citizens by land upon a hundred different services; so that, wherever they engage with some such fraction of our strength, a success against a detachment is magnified into a victory over the nation, and a defeat into a reverse suffered at the hands of our entire people.

text: And yet if with habits not of labour but of ease, and courage not of art but of nature, we are still willing to encounter danger, we have the double advantage of escaping the experience of hardships in anticipation and of facing them in the hour of need as fearlessly as those who are never free from them. “Nor are these the only points in which our city is worthy of admiration.

text: We cultivate refinement without extravagance and knowledge without effeminacy; wealth we employ more for use than for show, and place the real disgrace of poverty not in owning to the fact but in declining the struggle against it.

text: Our public men have, besides politics, their private affairs to attend to, and our ordinary citizens, though occupied with the pursuits of industry, are still fair judges of public matters; for, unlike any other nation, regarding him who takes no part in these duties not as unambitious but as useless, we Athenians are able to judge at all events if we cannot originate, and, instead of looking on discussion as a stumbling-block in the way of action, we think it an indispensable preliminary to any wise action at all.

text: Again, in our enterprises we present the singular spectacle of daring and deliberation, each carried to its highest point, and both united in the same persons; although usually decision is the fruit of ignorance, hesitation of reflection.
But the palm of courage will surely be adjudged most justly to those, who best know the difference between hardship and pleasure and yet are never tempted to shrink from danger.
text_raw:
But the palm of

text: In generosity we are equally singular, acquiring our friends by conferring, not by receiving, favours.
text_raw:
In

text: Yet, of course, the doer of the favour is the firmer friend of the two, in order by continued kindness to keep the recipient in his debt; while the debtor feels less keenly from the very consciousness that the return he makes will be a payment, not a free gift.

text: And it is only the Athenians, who, fearless of consequences, confer their benefits not from calculations of expediency, but in the confidence of liberality. “In short, I say that as a city we are the school of Hellas, while I doubt if the world can produce a man who, where he has only himself to depend upon, is equal to so many emergencies, and graced by so happy a versatility, as the Athenian.

text: And that this is no mere boast thrown out for the occasion, but plain matter of fact, the power of the state acquired by these habits proves.

And that this is no

text: For Athens alone of her contemporaries is found when tested to be greater than her reputation, and alone gives no occasion to her assailants to blush at the antagonist by whom they have been worsted, or to her subjects to question her title by merit to rule.

text: That panegyric is now in a great measure complete; for the Athens that I have celebrated is only what the heroism of these and their like have made her, men whose fame, unlike that of most Hellenes, will be found to be only commensurate with their deserts.

No, holding that

text: Thus choosing to die resisting, rather than to live submitting, they fled only from dishonour, but met danger face to face, and after one brief moment, while at the summit of their fortune, escaped, not from their fear, but from their glory. “So died these men as became Athenians.

text: You, their survivors, must determine to have as unfaltering a resolution in the field, though you may pray that it may have a happier issue.

text: And not contented with ideas derived only from words of the advantages which are bound up with the defence of your country, though these would furnish a valuable text to a speaker even before an audience so alive to them as the present, you must yourselves realize the power of Athens, and feed your eyes upon her from day to day, till love of her fills your hearts; and then, when all her greatness shall break upon you, you must reflect that it was by courage, sense of duty, and a keen feeling of honour in action that men were enabled to win all this, and that no personal failure in an enterprise could make them consent to deprive their country of their valour, but they laid it at her feet as the most glorious contribution that they could offer.
text_raw:

text: For it is not the miserable that would most justly be unsparing of their lives; these have nothing to hope for: it is rather they to whom continued life may bring reverses as yet unknown, and to whom a fall, if it came, would be most tremendous in its consequences.

text: And surely, to a man of spirit, the degradation of cowardice must be immeasurably more grievous than the unfelt death which strikes him in the midst of his strength and patriotism! “Comfort, therefore, not condolence, is what I have to offer to the parents of the dead who may be here.

text: Numberless are the chances to which, as they know, the life of man is subject; but fortunate indeed are they who draw for their lot a death so glorious as that which has caused your mourning, and to whom life has been so exactly measured as to terminate in the happiness in which it has been passed.

text: Still I know that this is a hard saying, especially when those are in question of whom you will constantly be reminded by seeing in the homes of others blessings of which once you also boasted: for grief is felt not so much for the want of what we have never known, as for the loss of that to which we have been long accustomed.

text: As a rule, however, there was no ostensible cause; but people in good health were all of a sudden attacked by violent heats in the head, and redness and inflammation in the eyes, the inward parts, such as the throat or tongue, becoming bloody and emitting an unnatural and fetid breath.

In

text: Externally the body was not very hot to the touch, nor pale in its appearance, but reddish, livid, and breaking out into small pustules and ulcers.

text: The body meanwhile did not waste away so long as the distemper was at its height, but held out to a marvel against its ravages; so that when they succumbed, as in most cases, on the seventh or eighth day to the internal inflammation, they had still some strength in them.

text: For the disorder first settled in the head, ran its course from thence through the whole of the body, and, even where it did not prove mortal, it still left its mark on the extremities; for it settled in the privy parts, the fingers and the toes, and many escaped with the loss of these, some too with that of their eyes.

text: Others again were seized with an entire loss of memory on their first recovery, and did not know either themselves or their friends.
text_raw:
Others again were seized with an entire loss of memory on their

text: But while the nature of the distemper was such as to baffle all description, and its attacks almost too grievous for human nature to endure, it was still in the following circumstance that its difference from all ordinary disorders was most clearly shown.
text_raw:

text: All the birds and beasts that prey upon human bodies, either abstained from touching them (though there were many lying unburied), or died after tasting them.
text_raw:
All the birds and

text: In proof of this, it was noticed that birds of this kind actually disappeared; they were not about the bodies, or indeed to be seen at all.

In proof of this, it was noticed that

text: But of course the effects which I have mentioned could best be studied in a domestic animal like the dog.

But of course the effects which I have mentioned could best be studied in a

text: Such then, if we pass over the varieties of particular cases which were many and peculiar, were the general features of the distemper.
text_raw:

text: Meanwhile the town enjoyed an immunity from all the ordinary disorders; or if any case occurred, it ended in this.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the town enjoyed an

text: Some died in neglect, others in the midst of every attention.
text_raw:
Some

text: No remedy was found that could be used as a specific; for what did good in one case, did harm in another.
text_raw:
No remedy was found that could be
used as a specific; for what did good in one case, did harm in another.

text: Strong and weak constitutions proved equally incapable of resistance, all alike being swept away, although dieted with the utmost precaution.
text_raw:
Strong and weak
constitutions proved equally incapable of resistance, all alike being swept away, although

text: By far the most terrible feature in the malady was the dejection which ensued when any one felt himself sickening, for the despair into which they instantly fell took away their power of resistance, and left them a much easier prey to the disorder; besides which, there was the awful spectacle of men dying like sheep, through having caught the infection in nursing each other.
text_raw:
By far the most terrible feature in the malady was the
dejection which ensued when any one felt himself sickening, for the despair into which

the disorder; besides which, there was the awful spectacle of men dying like sheep,

text: This caused the greatest mortality.
text_raw:
This caused the greatest
mortality.

text: On the one hand, if they were afraid to visit each other, they perished from neglect; indeed many houses were emptied of their inmates for want of a nurse: on the other, if they ventured to do so, death was the consequence.
text_raw:
On the one hand, if they were afraid to visit each other, they perished from
neglect; indeed many houses were emptied of their inmates for want of a nurse: on the
other, if they ventured to do so, death was the consequence.

text: This was especially the case with such as made any pretensions to goodness: honour made them unsparing of themselves in their attendance in their friends’ houses, where even the members of the family were at last worn out by the moans of the dying, and succumbed to the force of the disaster.
text_raw:
This was especially the case
with such as made any pretensions to goodness: honour made them unsparing of
themselves in their attendance in their friends’ houses, where even the members of the

text: Yet it was with those who had recovered from the disease that the sick and the dying found most compassion.
text_raw:
Yet it was with those who had recovered from the disease that the sick and the

text: These knew what it was from experience, and had now no fear for themselves; for the same man was never attacked twice—never at least fatally.
text_raw:
These knew what it was from experience, and had now no
fear for themselves; for the same man was never attacked twice—never at least fatally.

text: And such persons not only received the congratulations of others, but themselves also, in the elation of the moment, half entertained the vain hope that they were for the future safe from any disease whatsoever.
text_raw:
And such persons not only received the congratulations of others, but themselves also, in

text: An aggravation of the existing calamity was the influx from the country into the city, and this was especially felt by the new arrivals.
text_raw:
An aggravation of the existing calamity was the influx from the country into the city, and
this was especially felt by the new arrivals.

text: As there were no houses to receive them, they had to be lodged at the hot season of the year in stifling cabins, where the mortality raged without restraint.
text_raw:
As there were no houses to receive them, they
had to be lodged at the hot season of the year in stifling cabins, where the mortality raged

text: The bodies of dying men lay one upon another, and half-dead creatures reeled about the streets and gathered round all the fountains in their longing for water.
text_raw:
The bodies of dying men lay one upon another, and half-dead creatures
reeled about the streets and gathered round all the fountains in their longing for water.

text: The sacred places also in which they had quartered themselves were full of corpses of persons that had died there, just as they were; for as the disaster passed all bounds, men, not knowing what was to become of them, became utterly careless of everything, whether sacred or profane.
text_raw:
The
sacred places also in which they had quartered themselves were full of corpses of persons
that had died there, just as they were; for as the disaster passed all bounds, men, not
knowing what was to become of them, became utterly careless of everything, whether
sacred or profane.

text: All the burial rites before in use were entirely upset, and they buried the bodies as best they could.
text_raw:
All the burial rites before in use were entirely upset, and they buried the
bodies as best they could.

text: Many from want of the proper appliances, through so many of their friends having died already, had recourse to the most shameless sepultures: sometimes getting the start of those who had raised a pile, they threw their own dead body upon the stranger’s pyre and ignited it; sometimes they tossed the corpse which they were carrying on the top of another that was burning, and so went off.
text_raw:
Many from want of the proper appliances, through so many of
their friends having died already, had recourse to the most shameless sepultures:

text: Nor was this the only form of lawless extravagance which owed its origin to the plague.
text_raw: Nor was this the only form of lawless extravagance which owed its origin to the plague.

text: Men now coolly ventured on what they had formerly done in a corner, and not just as they pleased, seeing the rapid transitions produced by persons in prosperity suddenly dying and those who before had nothing succeeding to their property.
text_raw:
Men now coolly ventured on what they had formerly done in a corner, and not just as they

text: So they resolved to spend quickly and enjoy themselves, regarding their lives and riches as alike things of a day.
text_raw:
So they resolved to spend
quickly and enjoy themselves, regarding their lives and riches as alike things of a day.

text: Perseverance in what men called honour was popular with none, it was so uncertain whether they would be spared to attain the object; but it was settled that present enjoyment, and all that contributed to it, was both honourable and useful.
text_raw:
Perseverance in what men called honour was popular with none, it was so uncertain

text: Fear of gods or law of man there was none to restrain them.
text_raw:
Fear of gods or

text: As for the first, they judged it to be just the same whether they worshipped them or not, as they saw all alike perishing; and for the last, no one expected to live to be brought to trial for his offences, but each felt that a far severer sentence had been already passed upon them all and hung ever over their heads, and before this fell it was only reasonable to enjoy life a little.
text_raw:

text: Such was the nature of the calamity, and heavily did it weigh on the Athenians; death raging within the city and devastation without.
text_raw:
Such was the nature of the calamity, and heavily did it weigh on the Athenians; death

text: Among other things which they remembered in their distress was, very naturally, the following verse which the old men said had long ago been uttered:

Among other things which they

text: So a dispute arose as to whether dearth and not death had not been the word in the verse; but at the present juncture, it was of course decided in favour of the latter; for the people made their recollection fit in with their sufferings.
I fancy, however, that if another Dorian war should ever afterwards come upon us, and a dearth should happen to accompany it, the verse will probably be read accordingly.

I fancy, however, that if another Dorian

text: The same summer Hagnon, son of Nicias, and Cleopompus, son of Clinias, the colleagues of Pericles, took the armament of which he had lately made use, and went off upon an expedition against the Chalcidians in the direction of Thrace and Potidaea, which was still under siege.

text: I am of opinion that national greatness is more for the advantage of private citizens, than any individual well-being coupled with public humiliation.

I am of opinion that national greatness is more for the advantage of

text: A man may be personally ever so well off, and yet if his country be ruined he must be ruined with it; whereas a flourishing commonwealth always affords chances of salvation to unfortunate individuals.

text: Since then a state can support the misfortunes of private citizens, while they cannot support hers, it is surely the duty of every one to be forward in her defence, and not like you to be so confounded with your domestic afflictions as to give up all thoughts of the common safety, and to blame me for having counselled war and yourselves for having voted it.

Since then a state can support the misfortunes of private citizens,
while they cannot support hers, it is surely the duty of every one to be forward in her

text: And yet if you are angry with me, it is with one who, as I believe, is second to no man either in knowledge of the proper policy, or in the ability to expound it, and who is moreover not only a patriot but an honest one.

text: Born, however, as you are, citizens of a great state, and brought up, as you have been, with habits equal to your birth, you should be ready to face the greatest disasters and still to keep unimpaired the lustre of your name.

text: For the judgment of mankind is as relentless to the weakness that falls short of a recognized renown, as it is jealous of the arrogance that aspires higher than its due.

the weakness that falls short of a recognized renown, as it is jealous of the arrogance that
aspires higher than its due.

text: If those are not enough, I will now reveal an advantage arising from the greatness of your dominion, which I think has never yet suggested itself to you, which I never mentioned in my previous speeches, and which has so bold a sound that I should scarce adventure it now, were it not for the unnatural depression which I see around me.

If those are not enough, I
will now reveal an advantage arising from the greatness of your dominion, which I think
has never yet suggested itself to you, which I never mentioned in my previous speeches,

text: You perhaps think that your empire extends only over your allies;
text_raw:
You perhaps think that your empire extends
only over your allies;

text: I will declare to you the truth.
text_raw: I will declare to you the truth.

text: The visible field of action has two parts, land and sea.
text_raw:
The visible field of action has two
parts, land and sea.

text: In the whole of one of these you are completely supreme, not merely as far as you use it at present, but also to what further extent you may think fit: in fine, your naval resources are such that your vessels may go where they please, without the King or any other nation on earth being able to stop them.
text_raw:
In the whole of one of these you are completely supreme, not merely
as far as you use it at present, but also to what further extent you may think fit: in fine,
your naval resources are such that your vessels may go where they please, without the
King or any other nation on earth being able to stop them.

text: So that although you may think it a great privation to lose the use of your land and houses, still you must see that this power is something widely different; and instead of fretting on their account, you should really regard them in the light of the gardens and other accessories that embellish a great fortune, and as, in comparison, of little moment.
text_raw:
So that although you may think
it a great privation to lose the use of your land and houses, still you must see that this
power is something widely different; and instead of fretting on their account, you should
really regard them in the light of the gardens and other accessories that embellish a great
fortune, and as, in comparison, of little moment.

text: You should know too that liberty preserved by your efforts will easily recover for us what we have lost, while, the knee once bowed, even what you have will pass from you.
text_raw:
You should know too that liberty
preserved by your efforts will easily recover for us what we have lost, while, the knee
once bowed, even what you have will pass from you.

text: Your fathers receiving these possessions not from others, but from themselves, did not let slip what their labour had acquired, but delivered them safe to you; and in this respect at least you must prove yourselves their equals, remembering that to lose what one has got is more disgraceful than to be balked in getting, and you must confront your enemies not merely with spirit but with disdain.
text_raw:
Your fathers receiving these
possessions not from others, but from themselves, did not let slip what their labour had
acquired, but delivered them safe to you; and in this respect at least you must prove
yourselves their equals, remembering that to lose what one has got is more disgraceful
than to be balked in getting, and you must confront your enemies not merely with spirit
but with disdain.

text: Confidence indeed a blissful ignorance can impart, ay, even to a coward’s breast, but disdain is the privilege of those who, like us, have been assured by reflection of their superiority to their adversary.
text_raw:
Confidence indeed a blissful ignorance can impart, ay, even to a
coward’s breast, but disdain is the privilege of those who, like us, have been assured by

text: And where the chances are the same, knowledge fortifies courage by the contempt which is its consequence, its trust being placed, not in hope, which is the prop of the desperate, but in a judgment grounded upon existing resources, whose anticipations are more to be depended upon. “Again, your country has a right to your services in sustaining the glories of her position.
text_raw:
And where the chances are the same,
knowledge fortifies courage by the contempt which is its consequence, its trust being
placed, not in hope, which is the prop of the desperate, but in a judgment grounded upon
existing resources, whose anticipations are more to be depended upon.
“Again, your country has a right to your services in sustaining the glories of her position.

text: These are a common source of pride to you all, and you cannot decline the burdens of empire and still expect to share its honours.
text_raw:
These are a common source of pride to you all, and you cannot decline the burdens of
empire and still expect to share its honours.

text: You should remember also that what you are fighting against is not merely slavery as an exchange for independence, but also loss of empire and danger from the animosities incurred in its exercise.
text_raw:
You should remember also that what you are
fighting against is not merely slavery as an exchange for independence, but also loss of
empire and danger from the animosities incurred in its exercise.

text: Besides, to recede is no longer possible, if indeed any of you in the alarm of the moment has become enamoured of the honesty of such an unambitious part.
text_raw:
Besides, to recede is no
longer possible, if indeed any of you in the alarm of the moment has become enamoured
of the honesty of such an unambitious part.

text: For what you hold is, to speak somewhat plainly, a tyranny; to take it perhaps was wrong, but to let it go is unsafe.
text_raw:
For what you hold is, to speak somewhat
plainly, a tyranny; to take it perhaps was wrong, but to let it go is unsafe.

text: And men of these retiring views, making converts of others, would quickly ruin a state; indeed the result would be the same if they could live independent by themselves; for the retiring and unambitious are never secure without vigorous protectors at their side; in fine, such qualities are useless to an imperial city, though they may help a dependency to an unmolested servitude. “But you must not be seduced by citizens like these or angry with me—who, if I voted for war, only did as you did yourselves—in spite of the enemy having invaded your country and done what you could be certain that he would do, if you refused to comply with his demands; and although besides what we counted for, the plague has come upon us —the only point indeed at which our calculation has been at fault.
text_raw:
And men of
these retiring views, making converts of others, would quickly ruin a state; indeed the
result would be the same if they could live independent by themselves; for the retiring and
unambitious are never secure without vigorous protectors at their side; in fine, such
qualities are useless to an imperial city, though they may help a dependency to an

“But you must not be seduced by citizens like these or angry with me—who, if I voted
for war, only did as you did yourselves—in spite of the enemy having invaded your
country and done what you could be certain that he would do, if you refused to comply

text: It is this, I know, that
text_raw: It is this, I know, that

text: has had a large share in making me more unpopular than I should otherwise have been— quite undeservedly, unless you are also prepared to give me the credit of any success with which chance may present you.

has had a large share in making me more unpopular than I should otherwise have been—
