For some seventy days they thus lived all
together, after which all, except the Athenians and any Siceliots or Italiots who had joined
in the expedition, were sold.

text: The total number of prisoners taken it would be difficult to state exactly, but it could not have been less than seven thousand.
text_raw:
The total number of prisoners taken it would be difficult to
state exactly, but it could not have been less than seven thousand.

text: This was the greatest Hellenic achievement of any in thig war, or, in my opinion, in Hellenic history; at once most glorious to the victors, and most calamitous to the conquered.
text_raw:
This was the greatest Hellenic achievement of any in thig war, or, in my opinion, in
Hellenic history; at once most glorious to the victors, and most calamitous to the
conquered.

text: They were beaten at all points and altogether; all that they suffered was great; they were destroyed, as the saying is, with a total destruction, their fleet, their army, everything was destroyed, and few out of many returned home.
Such were the events in Sicily.
text_raw:
Such were the events in
Sicily.

text: Nineteenth and Twentieth Years of the War—Revolt of Ionia— Intervention of Persia— The War in Ionia When the news was brought to Athens, for a long while they disbelieved even the most respectable of the soldiers who had themselves escaped from the scene of action and clearly reported the matter, a destruction so complete not being thought credible.
text_raw:
Nineteenth and Twentieth Years of the War—Revolt of Ionia— Intervention of Persia—
The War in Ionia
When the news was brought to Athens, for a long while they disbelieved even the most
respectable of the soldiers who had themselves escaped from the scene of action and
clearly reported the matter, a destruction so complete not being thought credible.

text: When the conviction was forced upon them, they were angry with the orators who had joined in promoting the expedition, just as if they had not themselves voted it, and were enraged also with the reciters of oracles and soothsayers, and all other omen-mongers of the time who had encouraged them to hope that they should conquer Sicily.
text_raw:
When
the conviction was forced upon them, they were angry with the orators who had joined in
promoting the expedition, just as if they had not themselves voted it, and were enraged
also with the reciters of oracles and soothsayers, and all other omen-mongers of the time
who had encouraged them to hope that they should conquer Sicily.

text: Already distressed at all points and in all quarters, after what had now happened, they were seized by a fear and consternation quite without example.
text_raw:
Already distressed at
all points and in all quarters, after what had now happened, they were seized by a fear and
consternation quite without example.

text: It was grievous enough for the state and for every man in his proper person to lose so many heavy infantry, cavalry, and able-bodied troops, and to see none left to replace them; but when they saw, also, that they had not sufficient ships in their docks, or money in the treasury, or crews for the ships, they began to despair of salvation.
text_raw:
It was grievous enough for the state and for every
man in his proper person to lose so many heavy infantry, cavalry, and able-bodied troops,
and to see none left to replace them; but when they saw, also, that they had not sufficient
ships in their docks, or money in the treasury, or crews for the ships, they began to despair
of salvation.

text: They thought that their enemies in Sicily would immediately sail with their fleet against Piraeus, inflamed by so signal a victory; while their adversaries at home, redoubling all their preparations, would vigorously attack them by sea and land at once, aided by their own revolted confederates.
text_raw:
They thought that their enemies in Sicily would immediately sail with their
fleet against Piraeus, inflamed by so signal a victory; while their adversaries at home,
redoubling all their preparations, would vigorously attack them by sea and land at once,
aided by their own revolted confederates.

text: Nevertheless, with such means as they had, it was determined to resist to the last, and to provide timber and money, and to equip a fleet as they best could, to take steps to secure their confederates and above all Euboea, to reform things in the city upon a more economical footing, and to elect a board of elders to advise upon the state of affairs as occasion should arise.
text_raw:
Nevertheless, with such means as they had, it
was determined to resist to the last, and to provide timber and money, and to equip a fleet
as they best could, to take steps to secure their confederates and above all Euboea, to
reform things in the city upon a more economical footing, and to elect a board of elders to
advise upon the state of affairs as occasion should arise.

text: In short, as is the way of a democracy, in the panic of the moment they were ready to be as prudent as possible.
text_raw:
In short, as is the way of a
democracy, in the panic of the moment they were ready to be as prudent as possible.

text: These resolves were at once carried into effect.
text_raw: These resolves were at once carried into effect.

text: Summer was now over.
text_raw: Summer was now over.

text: The winter ensuing saw all Hellas stirring under the impression of the great Athenian disaster in Sicily.
text_raw:
The winter
ensuing saw all Hellas stirring under the impression of the great Athenian disaster in
Sicily.

text: Neutrals now felt that even if uninvited they ought no longer to stand aloof from the war, but should volunteer to march against the Athenians, who, as they severally reflected, would probably have come against them if the Sicilian campaign had succeeded.
text_raw:
Neutrals now felt that even if uninvited they ought no longer to stand aloof from
the war, but should volunteer to march against the Athenians, who, as they severally
reflected, would probably have come against them if the Sicilian campaign had succeeded.

text: Besides, they considered that the war would now be short, and that it would be creditable for them to take part in it.
text_raw:
Besides, they considered that the war would now be short, and that it would be creditable
for them to take part in it.

text: Meanwhile the allies of the Lacedaemonians felt all more anxious than ever to see a speedy end to their heavy labours.
text_raw:
Meanwhile the allies of the Lacedaemonians felt all more
anxious than ever to see a speedy end to their heavy labours.

text: But above all, the subjects of the Athenians showed a readiness to revolt even beyond their ability, judging the circumstances with passion, and refusing even to hear of the Athenians being able to last out the coming summer.
text_raw:
But above all, the subjects of
the Athenians showed a readiness to revolt even beyond their ability, judging the
circumstances with passion, and refusing even to hear of the Athenians being able to last
out the coming summer.

text: Beyond all this, Lacedaemon was encouraged by the near prospect of being joined in great force in the spring by her allies in Sicily, lately forced by events to acquire their navy.
text_raw:
Beyond all this, Lacedaemon was encouraged by the near
prospect of being joined in great force in the spring by her allies in Sicily, lately forced by
events to acquire their navy.

text: With these reasons for confidence in every quarter, the Lacedaemonians now resolved to throw themselves without reserve into the war, considering that, once it was happily terminated, they would be finally delivered from such dangers as that which would have threatened them from Athens, if she had become mistress of Sicily, and that the overthrow of the Athenians would leave them in quiet enjoyment of the supremacy over all Hellas.
text_raw:
With these reasons for confidence in every quarter, the
Lacedaemonians now resolved to throw themselves without reserve into the war,
considering that, once it was happily terminated, they would be finally delivered from
such dangers as that which would have threatened them from Athens, if she had become
mistress of Sicily, and that the overthrow of the Athenians would leave them in quiet
enjoyment of the supremacy over all Hellas.

text: Their king, Agis, accordingly set out at once during this winter with some troops from Decelea, and levied from the allies contributions for the fleet, and turning towards the Malian Gulf exacted a sum of money from the Oetaeans by carrying off most of their cattle in reprisal for their old hostility, and, in spite of the protests and opposition of the Thessalians, forced the Achaeans of Phthiotis and the other subjects of the Thessalians in those parts to give him money and hostages, and deposited the hostages at Corinth, and tried to bring their countrymen into the confederacy.
text_raw:
Their king, Agis, accordingly set out at once during this winter with some troops from
Decelea, and levied from the allies contributions for the fleet, and turning towards the
Malian Gulf exacted a sum of money from the Oetaeans by carrying off most of their
cattle in reprisal for their old hostility, and, in spite of the protests and opposition of the
Thessalians, forced the Achaeans of Phthiotis and the other subjects of the Thessalians in
those parts to give him money and hostages, and deposited the hostages at Corinth, and
tried to bring their countrymen into the confederacy.

text: The Lacedaemonians now issued a requisition to the cities for building a hundred ships, fixing their own quota and that of the Boeotians at twenty-five each; that of the Phocians and Locrians together at fifteen; that of the Corinthians at fifteen; that of the Arcadians, Pellenians, and Sicyonians together at ten; and that of the Megarians, Troezenians, Epidaurians, and Hermionians together at ten also; and meanwhile made every other preparation for commencing hostilities by the spring.
In the meantime the Athenians were not idle.
text_raw: In the meantime the Athenians were not idle.

text: During this same winter, as they had determined, they contributed timber and pushed on their ship-building, and fortified Sunium to enable their corn-ships to round it in safety, and evacuated the fort in Laconia which they had built on their way to Sicily; while they also, for economy, cut down any other expenses that seemed unnecessary, and above all kept a careful look-out against the revolt of their confederates.
text_raw:
During this same winter, as they had
determined, they contributed timber and pushed on their ship-building, and fortified
Sunium to enable their corn-ships to round it in safety, and evacuated the fort in Laconia
which they had built on their way to Sicily; while they also, for economy, cut down any
other expenses that seemed unnecessary, and above all kept a careful look-out against the
revolt of their confederates.

text: While both parties were thus engaged, and were as intent upon preparing for the war as they had been at the outset, the Euboeans first of all sent envoys during this winter to Agis to treat of their revolting from Athens.
text_raw:
While both parties were thus engaged, and were as intent upon preparing for the war as
they had been at the outset, the Euboeans first of all sent envoys during this winter to Agis
to treat of their revolting from Athens.

text: Agis accepted their proposals, and sent for Alcamenes, son of Sthenelaidas, and Melanthus from Lacedaemon, to take the command in Euboea.
text_raw:
Agis accepted their proposals, and sent for
Alcamenes, son of Sthenelaidas, and Melanthus from Lacedaemon, to take the command
in Euboea.

text: These accordingly arrived with some three hundred Neodamodes, and Agis began to arrange for their crossing over.
text_raw:
These accordingly arrived with some three hundred Neodamodes, and Agis
began to arrange for their crossing over.

text: But in the meanwhile arrived some Lesbians, who also wished to revolt; and these being supported by the Boeotians, Agis was persuaded to defer acting in the matter of Euboea, and made arrangements for the revolt of the Lesbians, giving them Alcamenes, who was to have sailed to Euboea, as governor, and himself promising them ten ships, and the Boeotians the same number.
text_raw:
But in the meanwhile arrived some Lesbians, who
also wished to revolt; and these being supported by the Boeotians, Agis was persuaded to
defer acting in the matter of Euboea, and made arrangements for the revolt of the
Lesbians, giving them Alcamenes, who was to have sailed to Euboea, as governor, and
himself promising them ten ships, and the Boeotians the same number.

text: All this was done without instructions from home, as Agis while at Decelea with the army that he commanded had power to send troops to whatever quarter he pleased, and to levy men and money.
text_raw:
All this was done
without instructions from home, as Agis while at Decelea with the army that he
commanded had power to send troops to whatever quarter he pleased, and to levy men and
money.

text: During this period, one might say, the allies obeyed him much more than they did the Lacedaemonians in the city, as the force he had with him made him feared at once wherever he went.
text_raw:
During this period, one might say, the allies obeyed him much more than they did
the Lacedaemonians in the city, as the force he had with him made him feared at once
wherever he went.

text: While Agis was engaged with the Lesbians, the Chians and Erythraeans, who were also ready to revolt, applied, not to him but at Lacedaemon; where they arrived accompanied by an ambassador from Tissaphernes, the commander of King Darius, son of Artaxerxes, in the maritime districts, who invited the Peloponnesians to come over, and promised to maintain their army.
text_raw:
While Agis was engaged with the Lesbians, the Chians and
Erythraeans, who were also ready to revolt, applied, not to him but at Lacedaemon; where
they arrived accompanied by an ambassador from Tissaphernes, the commander of King
Darius, son of Artaxerxes, in the maritime districts, who invited the Peloponnesians to
come over, and promised to maintain their army.

text: The King had lately called upon him for the tribute from his government, for which he was in arrears, being unable to raise it from the Hellenic towns by reason of the Athenians; and he therefore calculated that by weakening the Athenians he should get the tribute better paid, and should also draw the Lacedaemonians into alliance with the King; and by this means, as the King had commanded him, take alive or dead Amorges, the bastard son of Pissuthnes, who was in rebellion on the coast of Caria.
text_raw:
The King had lately called upon him for
the tribute from his government, for which he was in arrears, being unable to raise it from
the Hellenic towns by reason of the Athenians; and he therefore calculated that by
weakening the Athenians he should get the tribute better paid, and should also draw the
Lacedaemonians into alliance with the King; and by this means, as the King had
commanded him, take alive or dead Amorges, the bastard son of Pissuthnes, who was in
rebellion on the coast of Caria.

text: While the Chians and Tissaphernes thus joined to effect the same object, about the same time Calligeitus, son of Laophon, a Megarian, and Timagoras, son of Athenagoras, a Cyzicene, both of them exiles from their country and living at the court of Pharnabazus, son of Pharnaces, arrived at Lacedaemon upon a mission from Pharnabazus, to procure a fleet for the Hellespont; by means of which, if possible, he might himself effect the object of Tissaphernes’ ambition and cause the cities in his government to revolt from the Athenians, and so get the tribute, and by his own agency obtain for the King the alliance of the Lacedaemonians.
text_raw:
While the Chians and Tissaphernes thus joined to effect the same object, about the same
time Calligeitus, son of Laophon, a Megarian, and Timagoras, son of Athenagoras, a
Cyzicene, both of them exiles from their country and living at the court of Pharnabazus,
son of Pharnaces, arrived at Lacedaemon upon a mission from Pharnabazus, to procure a
fleet for the Hellespont; by means of which, if possible, he might himself effect the object
of Tissaphernes’ ambition and cause the cities in his government to revolt from the
Athenians, and so get the tribute, and by his own agency obtain for the King the alliance
of the Lacedaemonians.

text: The emissaries of Pharnabazus and Tissaphernes treating apart, a keen competition now ensued at Lacedaemon as to whether a fleet and army should be sent first to Ionia and Chios, or to the Hellespont.
text_raw:
The emissaries of Pharnabazus and Tissaphernes treating apart, a keen competition now
ensued at Lacedaemon as to whether a fleet and army should be sent first to Ionia and
Chios, or to the Hellespont.

text: The Lacedaemonians, however, decidedly favoured the Chians and Tissaphernes, who were seconded by Alcibiades, the family friend of Endius, one of the ephors for that year.
text_raw:
The Lacedaemonians, however, decidedly favoured the
Chians and Tissaphernes, who were seconded by Alcibiades, the family friend of Endius,
one of the ephors for that year.

text: Indeed, this is how their house got its Laconic name, Alcibiades being the family name of Endius.
text_raw:
Indeed, this is how their house got its Laconic name,
Alcibiades being the family name of Endius.

text: Nevertheless the Lacedaemonians first sent to Chios Phrynis, one of the Perioeci, to see whether they had as many ships as they said, and whether their city generally was as great as was reported; and upon his bringing word that they had been told the truth, immediately entered into alliance with the Chians and Erythraeans, and voted to send them forty ships, there being already, according to the statement of the Chians, not less than sixty in the island.
text_raw:
Nevertheless the Lacedaemonians first sent
to Chios Phrynis, one of the Perioeci, to see whether they had as many ships as they said,
and whether their city generally was as great as was reported; and upon his bringing word
that they had been told the truth, immediately entered into alliance with the Chians and
Erythraeans, and voted to send them forty ships, there being already, according to the
statement of the Chians, not less than sixty in the island.

text: At first the Lacedaemonians meant to send ten of these forty themselves, with Melanchridas their admiral; but afterwards, an earthquake having occurred, they sent Chalcideus instead of Melanchridas, and instead of the ten ships equipped only five in Laconia.
text_raw:
At first the Lacedaemonians
meant to send ten of these forty themselves, with Melanchridas their admiral; but
afterwards, an earthquake having occurred, they sent Chalcideus instead of Melanchridas,
and instead of the ten ships equipped only five in Laconia.

text: And the winter ended, and with it ended also the nineteenth year of this war of which Thucydides is the historian.
text_raw:
And the winter ended, and with
it ended also the nineteenth year of this war of which Thucydides is the historian.

text: At the beginning of the next summer the Chians were urging that the fleet should be sent off, being afraid that the Athenians, from whom all these embassies were kept a secret, might find out what was going on, and the Lacedaemonians at once sent three Spartans to Corinth to haul the ships as quickly as possible across the Isthmus from the other sea to that on the side of Athens, and to order them all to sail to Chios, those which Agis was equipping for Lesbos not excepted.
text_raw:
At the beginning of the next summer the Chians were urging that the fleet should be sent
off, being afraid that the Athenians, from whom all these embassies were kept a secret,
might find out what was going on, and the Lacedaemonians at once sent three Spartans to
Corinth to haul the ships as quickly as possible across the Isthmus from the other sea to
that on the side of Athens, and to order them all to sail to Chios, those which Agis was
equipping for Lesbos not excepted.

text: The number of ships from the allied states was thirty- nine in all.
text_raw:
The number of ships from the allied states was thirty-
nine in all.

text: Meanwhile Calligeitus and Timagoras did not join on behalf of Pharnabazus in the expedition to Chios or give the money—twenty-five talents—which they had brought with them to help in dispatching a force, but determined to sail afterwards with another force by themselves.
text_raw:
Meanwhile Calligeitus and Timagoras did not join on behalf of Pharnabazus in the
expedition to Chios or give the money—twenty-five talents—which they had brought with
them to help in dispatching a force, but determined to sail afterwards with another force
by themselves.

text: Agis, on the other hand, seeing the Lacedaemonians bent upon going to Chios first, himself came in to their views; and the allies assembled at Corinth and held a council, in which they decided to sail first to Chios under the command of Chalcideus, who was equipping the five vessels in Laconia, then to Lesbos, under the command of Alcamenes, the same whom Agis had fixed upon, and lastly to go to the Hellespont, where the command was given to Clearchus, son of Ramphias.
text_raw:
Agis, on the other hand, seeing the Lacedaemonians bent upon going to
Chios first, himself came in to their views; and the allies assembled at Corinth and held a
council, in which they decided to sail first to Chios under the command of Chalcideus,
who was equipping the five vessels in Laconia, then to Lesbos, under the command of
Alcamenes, the same whom Agis had fixed upon, and lastly to go to the Hellespont, where
the command was given to Clearchus, son of Ramphias.

text: Meanwhile they would take only half the ships across the Isthmus first, and let those sail off at once, in order that the Athenians might attend less to the departing squadron than to those to be taken across afterwards, as no care had been taken to keep this voyage secret through contempt of the impotence of the Athenians, who had as yet no fleet of any account upon the sea.
text_raw:
Meanwhile they would take only
half the ships across the Isthmus first, and let those sail off at once, in order that the
Athenians might attend less to the departing squadron than to those to be taken across
afterwards, as no care had been taken to keep this voyage secret through contempt of the
impotence of the Athenians, who had as yet no fleet of any account upon the sea.

text: Agreeably to this determination, twenty-one vessels were at once conveyed across the Isthmus.
text_raw:
Agreeably to this determination, twenty-one vessels were at once conveyed across the
Isthmus.

text: They were now impatient to set sail, but the Corinthians were not willing to accompany them until they had celebrated the Isthmian festival, which fell at that time.
text_raw:
They were now impatient to set sail, but the Corinthians were not willing to accompany
them until they had celebrated the Isthmian festival, which fell at that time.

text: Upon this Agis proposed to them to save their scruples about breaking the Isthmian truce by taking the expedition upon himself.
text_raw:
Upon this Agis
proposed to them to save their scruples about breaking the Isthmian truce by taking the
expedition upon himself.

text: The Corinthians not consenting to this, a delay ensued, during which the Athenians conceived suspicions of what was preparing at Chios, and sent Aristocrates, one of their generals, and charged them with the fact, and, upon the denial of the Chians, ordered them to send with them a contingent of ships, as faithful confederates.
text_raw:
The Corinthians not consenting to this, a delay ensued, during
which the Athenians conceived suspicions of what was preparing at Chios, and sent
Aristocrates, one of their generals, and charged them with the fact, and, upon the denial of
the Chians, ordered them to send with them a contingent of ships, as faithful confederates.

text: Seven were sent accordingly.
text_raw: Seven were sent accordingly.

text: The reason of the dispatch of the ships lay in the fact that the mass of the Chians were not privy to the negotiations, while the few who were in the secret did not wish to break with the multitude until they had something positive to lean upon, and no longer expected the Peloponnesians to arrive by reason of their delay.
text_raw:
The reason of the dispatch of the ships lay in the fact that the
mass of the Chians were not privy to the negotiations, while the few who were in the
secret did not wish to break with the multitude until they had something positive to lean
upon, and no longer expected the Peloponnesians to arrive by reason of their delay.

text: In the meantime the Isthmian games took place, and the Athenians, who had been also invited, went to attend them, and now seeing more clearly into the designs of the Chians, as soon as they returned to Athens took measures to prevent the fleet putting out from Cenchreae without their knowledge.
text_raw:
In the meantime the Isthmian games took place, and the Athenians, who had been also
invited, went to attend them, and now seeing more clearly into the designs of the Chians,
as soon as they returned to Athens took measures to prevent the fleet putting out from
Cenchreae without their knowledge.

text: After the festival the Peloponnesians set sail with twenty-one ships for Chios, under the command of Alcamenes.
text_raw:
After the festival the Peloponnesians set sail with
twenty-one ships for Chios, under the command of Alcamenes.

text: The Athenians first sailed against them with an equal number, drawing off towards the open sea.
text_raw:
The Athenians first sailed
against them with an equal number, drawing off towards the open sea.

text: The enemy, however, turning back before he had followed them far, the Athenians returned also, not trusting the seven Chian ships which formed part of their number, and afterwards manned thirty-seven vessels in all and chased him on his passage alongshore into Spiraeum, a desert Corinthian port on the edge of the Epidaurian frontier.
text_raw:
The enemy,
however, turning back before he had followed them far, the Athenians returned also, not
trusting the seven Chian ships which formed part of their number, and afterwards manned
thirty-seven vessels in all and chased him on his passage alongshore into Spiraeum, a
desert Corinthian port on the edge of the Epidaurian frontier.

text: After losing one ship out at sea, the Peloponnesians got the rest together and brought them to anchor.
text_raw:
After losing one ship out at
sea, the Peloponnesians got the rest together and brought them to anchor.

text: The Athenians now attacked not only from the sea with their fleet, but also disembarked upon the coast; and a melee ensued of the most confused and violent kind, in which the Athenians disabled most of the enemy’s vessels and killed Alcamenes their commander, losing also a few of their own men.
text_raw:
The Athenians
now attacked not only from the sea with their fleet, but also disembarked upon the coast;
and a melee ensued of the most confused and violent kind, in which the Athenians
disabled most of the enemy’s vessels and killed Alcamenes their commander, losing also a
few of their own men.

text: After this they separated, and the Athenians, detaching a sufficient number of ships to blockade those of the enemy, anchored with the rest at the islet adjacent, upon which they proceeded to encamp, and sent to Athens for reinforcements; the Peloponnesians having been joined on the day after the battle by the Corinthians, who came to help the ships, and by the other inhabitants in the vicinity not long afterwards.
text_raw:
After this they separated, and the Athenians, detaching a sufficient number of ships to
blockade those of the enemy, anchored with the rest at the islet adjacent, upon which they
proceeded to encamp, and sent to Athens for reinforcements; the Peloponnesians having
been joined on the day after the battle by the Corinthians, who came to help the ships, and
by the other inhabitants in the vicinity not long afterwards.

text: These saw the difficulty of keeping guard in a desert place, and in their perplexity at first thought of burning the ships, but finally resolved to haul them up on shore and sit down and guard them with their land forces until a convenient opportunity for escaping should present itself.
text_raw:
These saw the difficulty of
keeping guard in a desert place, and in their perplexity at first thought of burning the
ships, but finally resolved to haul them up on shore and sit down and guard them with
their land forces until a convenient opportunity for escaping should present itself.

text: Agis also, on being informed of the disaster, sent them a Spartan of the name of Thermon.
text_raw:
Agis
also, on being informed of the disaster, sent them a Spartan of the name of Thermon.

text: The Lacedaemonians first received the news of the fleet having put out from the Isthmus, Alcamenes having been ordered by the ephors to send off a horseman when this took place, and immediately resolved to dispatch their own five vessels under Chalcideus, and Alcibiades with him.
text_raw:
The
Lacedaemonians first received the news of the fleet having put out from the Isthmus,
Alcamenes having been ordered by the ephors to send off a horseman when this took
place, and immediately resolved to dispatch their own five vessels under Chalcideus, and
Alcibiades with him.

text: But while they were full of this resolution came the second news of the fleet having taken refuge in Spiraeum; and disheartened at their first step in the Ionian war proving a failure, they laid aside the idea of sending the ships from their own country,
text_raw:
But while they were full of this resolution came the second news of
the fleet having taken refuge in Spiraeum; and disheartened at their first step in the Ionian
war proving a failure, they laid aside the idea of sending the ships from their own country,

text: and even wished to recall some that had already sailed.
text_raw: and even wished to recall some that had already sailed.

text: Perceiving this, Alcibiades again persuaded Endius and the other ephors to persevere in the expedition, saying that the voyage would be made before the Chians heard of the fleet’s misfortune, and that as soon as he set foot in Ionia, he should, by assuring them of the weakness of the Athenians and the zeal of Lacedaemon, have no difficulty in persuading the cities to revolt, as they would readily believe his testimony.
text_raw:
Perceiving this, Alcibiades again persuaded Endius and the other ephors to persevere in
the expedition, saying that the voyage would be made before the Chians heard of the
fleet’s misfortune, and that as soon as he set foot in Ionia, he should, by assuring them of
the weakness of the Athenians and the zeal of Lacedaemon, have no difficulty in
persuading the cities to revolt, as they would readily believe his testimony.

text: He also represented to Endius himself in private that it would be glorious for him to be the means of making Ionia revolt and the King become the ally of Lacedaemon, instead of that honour being left to Agis (Agis, it must be remembered, was the enemy of Alcibiades); and Endius and his colleagues thus persuaded, he put to sea with the five ships and the Lacedaemonian Chalcideus, and made all haste upon the voyage.
text_raw:
He also
represented to Endius himself in private that it would be glorious for him to be the means
of making Ionia revolt and the King become the ally of Lacedaemon, instead of that
honour being left to Agis (Agis, it must be remembered, was the enemy of Alcibiades);
and Endius and his colleagues thus persuaded, he put to sea with the five ships and the
Lacedaemonian Chalcideus, and made all haste upon the voyage.

text: About this time the sixteen Peloponnesian ships from Sicily, which had served through the war with Gylippus, were caught on their return off Leucadia and roughly handled by the twenty-seven Athenian vessels under Hippocles, son of Menippus, on the lookout for the ships from Sicily.
text_raw:
About this time the sixteen Peloponnesian ships from Sicily, which had served through
the war with Gylippus, were caught on their return off Leucadia and roughly handled by
the twenty-seven Athenian vessels under Hippocles, son of Menippus, on the lookout for
the ships from Sicily.

text: After losing one of their number, the rest escaped from the Athenians and sailed into Corinth.
text_raw:
After losing one of their number, the rest escaped from the
Athenians and sailed into Corinth.

text: Meanwhile Chalcideus and Alcibiades seized all they met with on their voyage, to prevent news of their coming, and let them go at Corycus, the first point which they touched at in the continent.
text_raw:
Meanwhile Chalcideus and Alcibiades seized all they met with on their voyage, to
prevent news of their coming, and let them go at Corycus, the first point which they
touched at in the continent.

text: Here they were visited by some of their Chian correspondents and, being urged by them to sail up to the town without announcing their coming, arrived suddenly before Chios.
text_raw:
Here they were visited by some of their Chian correspondents
and, being urged by them to sail up to the town without announcing their coming, arrived
suddenly before Chios.

text: The many were amazed and confounded, while the few had so arranged that the council should be sitting at the time; and after speeches from Chalcideus and Alcibiades stating that many more ships were sailing up, but saying nothing of the fleet being blockaded in Spiraeum, the Chians revolted from the Athenians, and the Erythraeans immediately afterwards.
text_raw:
The many were amazed and confounded, while the few had so
arranged that the council should be sitting at the time; and after speeches from Chalcideus
and Alcibiades stating that many more ships were sailing up, but saying nothing of the
fleet being blockaded in Spiraeum, the Chians revolted from the Athenians, and the
Erythraeans immediately afterwards.

text: After this three vessels sailed over to Clazomenae, and made that city revolt also; and the Clazomenians immediately crossed over to the mainland and began to fortify Polichna, in order to retreat there, in case of necessity, from the island where they dwelt.
text_raw:
After this three vessels sailed over to Clazomenae,
and made that city revolt also; and the Clazomenians immediately crossed over to the
mainland and began to fortify Polichna, in order to retreat there, in case of necessity, from
the island where they dwelt.

text: While the revolted places were all engaged in fortifying and preparing for the war, news of Chios speedily reached Athens.
text_raw:
While the revolted places were all engaged in fortifying and preparing for the war, news
of Chios speedily reached Athens.

text: The Athenians thought the danger by which they were now menaced great and unmistakable, and that the rest of their allies would not consent to keep quiet after the secession of the greatest of their number.
text_raw:
The Athenians thought the danger by which they were
now menaced great and unmistakable, and that the rest of their allies would not consent to
keep quiet after the secession of the greatest of their number.

text: In the consternation of the moment they at once took off the penalty attaching to whoever proposed or put to the vote a proposal for using the thousand talents which they had jealously avoided touching throughout the whole war, and voted to employ them to man a large number of ships, and to send off at once under Strombichides, son of Diotimus, the eight vessels, forming part of the blockading fleet at Spiraeum, which had left the blockade and had returned after pursuing and failing to overtake the vessels with Chalcideus.
text_raw:
In the consternation of the
moment they at once took off the penalty attaching to whoever proposed or put to the vote
a proposal for using the thousand talents which they had jealously avoided touching
throughout the whole war, and voted to employ them to man a large number of ships, and
to send off at once under Strombichides, son of Diotimus, the eight vessels, forming part
of the blockading fleet at Spiraeum, which had left the blockade and had returned after
pursuing and failing to overtake the vessels with Chalcideus.

text: These were to be followed shortly afterwards by twelve more under Thrasycles, also taken from the blockade.
text_raw:
These were to be followed
shortly afterwards by twelve more under Thrasycles, also taken from the blockade.

text: They also recalled the seven Chian vessels, forming part of their squadron blockading the fleet in Spiraeum, and giving the slaves on board their liberty, put the freemen in confinement, and speedily manned and sent out ten fresh ships to blockade the Peloponnesians in the place of all those that had departed, and decided to man thirty more.
text_raw:
They
also recalled the seven Chian vessels, forming part of their squadron blockading the fleet
in Spiraeum, and giving the slaves on board their liberty, put the freemen in confinement,
and speedily manned and sent out ten fresh ships to blockade the Peloponnesians in the
place of all those that had departed, and decided to man thirty more.

text: Zeal was not wanting,
text_raw: Zeal was not wanting,

text: and no effort was spared to send relief to Chios.
text_raw: and no effort was spared to send relief to Chios.

text: In the meantime Strombichides with his eight ships arrived at Samos, and, taking one Samian vessel, sailed to Teos and required them to remain quiet.
text_raw:
In the meantime Strombichides with his eight ships arrived at Samos, and, taking one
Samian vessel, sailed to Teos and required them to remain quiet.

text: Chalcideus also set sail with twenty-three ships for Teos from Chios, the land forces of the Clazomenians and Erythraeans moving alongshore to support him.
text_raw:
Chalcideus also set sail
with twenty-three ships for Teos from Chios, the land forces of the Clazomenians and
Erythraeans moving alongshore to support him.

text: Informed of this in time, Strombichides put out from Teos before their arrival, and while out at sea, seeing the number of the ships from Chios, fled towards Samos, chased by the enemy.
text_raw:
Informed of this in time, Strombichides
put out from Teos before their arrival, and while out at sea, seeing the number of the ships
from Chios, fled towards Samos, chased by the enemy.

text: The Teians at first would not receive the land forces, but upon the flight of the Athenians took them into the town.
text_raw:
The Teians at first would not
receive the land forces, but upon the flight of the Athenians took them into the town.

text: There they waited for some time for Chalcideus to return from the pursuit, and as time went on without his appearing, began themselves to demolish the wall which the Athenians had built on the land side of the city of the Teians, being assisted by a few of the barbarians who had come up under the command of Stages, the lieutenant of Tissaphernes.
text_raw:
There they waited for some time for Chalcideus to return from the pursuit, and as time
went on without his appearing, began themselves to demolish the wall which the
Athenians had built on the land side of the city of the Teians, being assisted by a few of
the barbarians who had come up under the command of Stages, the lieutenant of
Tissaphernes.

text: Meanwhile Chalcideus and Alcibiades, after chasing Strombichides into Samos, armed the crews of the ships from Peloponnese and left them at Chios, and filling their places with substitutes from Chios and manning twenty others, sailed off to effect the revolt of Miletus.
text_raw:
Meanwhile Chalcideus and Alcibiades, after chasing Strombichides into Samos, armed
the crews of the ships from Peloponnese and left them at Chios, and filling their places
with substitutes from Chios and manning twenty others, sailed off to effect the revolt of
Miletus.

text: The wish of Alcibiades, who had friends among the leading men of the Milesians, was to bring over the town before the arrival of the ships from Peloponnese, and thus, by causing the revolt of as many cities as possible with the help of the Chian power and of Chalcideus, to secure the honour for the Chians and himself and Chalcideus, and, as he had promised, for Endius who had sent them out.
text_raw:
The wish of Alcibiades, who had friends among the leading men of the Milesians,
was to bring over the town before the arrival of the ships from Peloponnese, and thus, by
causing the revolt of as many cities as possible with the help of the Chian power and of
Chalcideus, to secure the honour for the Chians and himself and Chalcideus, and, as he
had promised, for Endius who had sent them out.

text: Not discovered until their voyage was nearly completed, they arrived a little before Strombichides and Thrasycles (who had just come with twelve ships from Athens, and had joined Strombichides in pursuing them), and occasioned the revolt of Miletus.
text_raw:
Not discovered until their voyage was
nearly completed, they arrived a little before Strombichides and Thrasycles (who had just
come with twelve ships from Athens, and had joined Strombichides in pursuing them),
and occasioned the revolt of Miletus.

text: The Athenians sailing up close on their heels with nineteen ships found Miletus closed against them, and took up their station at the adjacent island of Lade.
text_raw:
The Athenians sailing up close on their heels with
nineteen ships found Miletus closed against them, and took up their station at the adjacent
island of Lade.

text: The first alliance between the King and the Lacedaemonians was now concluded immediately upon the revolt of the Milesians, by Tissaphernes and Chalcideus, and was as follows:
text_raw:
The first alliance between the King and the Lacedaemonians was now
concluded immediately upon the revolt of the Milesians, by Tissaphernes and Chalcideus,
and was as follows:

text: The Lacedaemonians and their allies made a treaty with the King and Tissaphernes upon the terms following:
text_raw:
The Lacedaemonians and their allies made a treaty with the King and Tissaphernes upon
the terms following:

text: Whatever country or cities the King has, or the King’s ancestors had, shall be the king’s: and whatever came in to the Athenians from these cities, either money or any other thing, the King and the Lacedaemonians and their allies shall jointly hinder the Athenians from receiving either money or any other thing.
text_raw:
Whatever country or cities the King has, or the King’s ancestors had, shall be the
king’s: and whatever came in to the Athenians from these cities, either money or any other
thing, the King and the Lacedaemonians and their allies shall jointly hinder the Athenians
from receiving either money or any other thing.

text: The war with the Athenians shall be carried on jointly by the King and by the Lacedaemonians and their allies: and it shall not be lawful to make peace with the Athenians except both agree, the King on his side and the Lacedaemonians and their allies on theirs.
text_raw:
The war with the Athenians shall be carried on jointly by the King and by the
Lacedaemonians and their allies: and it shall not be lawful to make peace with the
Athenians except both agree, the King on his side and the Lacedaemonians and their allies
on theirs.

text: If any revolt from the King, they shall be the enemies of the Lacedaemonians and their allies.
text_raw:
If any revolt from the King, they shall be the enemies of the Lacedaemonians and their
allies.

text: And if any revolt from the Lacedaemonians and their allies, they shall be the enemies of the King in like manner.
text_raw:
And if any revolt from the Lacedaemonians and their allies, they shall be the
enemies of the King in like manner.

text: This was the alliance.
text_raw: This was the alliance.

text: After this the Chians immediately manned ten more vessels and
text_raw: After this the Chians immediately manned ten more vessels and

text: sailed for Anaia, in order to gain intelligence of those in Miletus, and also to make the cities revolt.
text_raw:
sailed for Anaia, in order to gain intelligence of those in Miletus, and also to make the
cities revolt.

text: A message, however, reaching them from Chalcideus to tell them to go back again, and that Amorges was at hand with an army by land, they sailed to the temple of Zeus, and there sighting ten more ships sailing up with which Diomedon had started from Athens after Thrasycles, fled, one ship to Ephesus, the rest to Teos.
text_raw:
A message, however, reaching them from Chalcideus to tell them to go back
again, and that Amorges was at hand with an army by land, they sailed to the temple of
Zeus, and there sighting ten more ships sailing up with which Diomedon had started from
Athens after Thrasycles, fled, one ship to Ephesus, the rest to Teos.

text: The Athenians took four of their ships empty, the men finding time to escape ashore; the rest took refuge in the city of the Teians; after which the Athenians sailed off to Samos, while the Chians put to sea with their remaining vessels, accompanied by the land forces, and caused Lebedos to revolt, and after it Erae.
text_raw:
The Athenians took
four of their ships empty, the men finding time to escape ashore; the rest took refuge in the
city of the Teians; after which the Athenians sailed off to Samos, while the Chians put to
sea with their remaining vessels, accompanied by the land forces, and caused Lebedos to
revolt, and after it Erae.

text: After this they both returned home, the fleet and the army.
text_raw: After this they both returned home, the fleet and the army.

text: About the same time the twenty ships of the Peloponnesians in Spiraeum, which we left chased to land and blockaded by an equal number of Athenians, suddenly sallied out and defeated the blockading squadron, took four of their ships, and, sailing back to Cenchreae, prepared again for the voyage to Chios and Ionia.
text_raw:
About the same time the twenty ships of the Peloponnesians in Spiraeum, which we left
chased to land and blockaded by an equal number of Athenians, suddenly sallied out and
defeated the blockading squadron, took four of their ships, and, sailing back to Cenchreae,
prepared again for the voyage to Chios and Ionia.

text: Here they were joined by Astyochus as high admiral from Lacedaemon, henceforth invested with the supreme command at sea.
text_raw:
Here they were joined by Astyochus as
high admiral from Lacedaemon, henceforth invested with the supreme command at sea.

text: The land forces now withdrawing from Teos, Tissaphernes repaired thither in person with an army and completed the demolition of anything that was left of the wall, and so departed.
text_raw:
The land forces now withdrawing from Teos, Tissaphernes repaired thither in person with
an army and completed the demolition of anything that was left of the wall, and so
departed.

text: Not long after his departure Diomedon arrived with ten Athenian ships, and, having made a convention by which the Teians admitted him as they had the enemy, coasted along to Erae, and, failing in an attempt upon the town, sailed back again.
text_raw:
Not long after his departure Diomedon arrived with ten Athenian ships, and,
having made a convention by which the Teians admitted him as they had the enemy,
coasted along to Erae, and, failing in an attempt upon the town, sailed back again.

text: About this time took place the rising of the commons at Samos against the upper classes, in concert with some Athenians, who were there in three vessels.
text_raw:
About this time took place the rising of the commons at Samos against the upper classes,
in concert with some Athenians, who were there in three vessels.

text: The Samian commons put to death some two hundred in all of the upper classes, and banished four hundred more, and themselves took their land and houses; after which the Athenians decreed their independence, being now sure of their fidelity, and the commons henceforth governed the city, excluding the landholders from all share in affairs, and forbidding any of the commons to give his daughter in marriage to them or to take a wife from them in future.
text_raw:
The Samian commons
put to death some two hundred in all of the upper classes, and banished four hundred
more, and themselves took their land and houses; after which the Athenians decreed their
independence, being now sure of their fidelity, and the commons henceforth governed the
city, excluding the landholders from all share in affairs, and forbidding any of the
commons to give his daughter in marriage to them or to take a wife from them in future.

text: After this, during the same summer, the Chians, whose zeal continued as active as ever, and who even without the Peloponnesians found themselves in sufficient force to effect the revolt of the cities and also wished to have as many companions in peril as possible, made an expedition with thirteen ships of their own to Lesbos; the instructions from Lacedaemon being to go to that island next, and from thence to the Hellespont.
text_raw:
After this, during the same summer, the Chians, whose zeal continued as active as ever,
and who even without the Peloponnesians found themselves in sufficient force to effect
the revolt of the cities and also wished to have as many companions in peril as possible,
made an expedition with thirteen ships of their own to Lesbos; the instructions from
Lacedaemon being to go to that island next, and from thence to the Hellespont.

text: Meanwhile the land forces of the Peloponnesians who were with the Chians and of the allies on the spot, moved alongshore for Clazomenae and Cuma, under the command of Eualas, a Spartan; while the fleet under Diniadas, one of the Perioeci, first sailed up to Methymna and caused it to revolt, and, leaving four ships there, with the rest procured the revolt of Mitylene.
text_raw:
Meanwhile
the land forces of the Peloponnesians who were with the Chians and of the allies on the
spot, moved alongshore for Clazomenae and Cuma, under the command of Eualas, a
Spartan; while the fleet under Diniadas, one of the Perioeci, first sailed up to Methymna
and caused it to revolt, and, leaving four ships there, with the rest procured the revolt of
Mitylene.

text: In the meantime Astyochus, the Lacedaemonian admiral, set sail from Cenchreae with four ships, as he had intended, and arrived at Chios.
text_raw:
In the meantime Astyochus, the Lacedaemonian admiral, set sail from Cenchreae with
four ships, as he had intended, and arrived at Chios.

text: On the third day after his arrival, the Athenian ships, twenty-five in number, sailed to Lesbos under Diomedon and Leon, who had lately arrived with a reinforcement of ten ships from Athens.
text_raw:
On the third day after his arrival, the
Athenian ships, twenty-five in number, sailed to Lesbos under Diomedon and Leon, who
had lately arrived with a reinforcement of ten ships from Athens.

text: Late in the same day Astyochus put to sea, and taking one Chian vessel with him sailed to Lesbos to render what assistance he could.
text_raw:
Late in the same day
Astyochus put to sea, and taking one Chian vessel with him sailed to Lesbos to render
what assistance he could.

text: Arrived at Pyrrha, and from thence the next day at Eresus, he there learned that Mitylene had been taken, almost without a blow, by the Athenians, who
text_raw:
Arrived at Pyrrha, and from thence the next day at Eresus, he
there learned that Mitylene had been taken, almost without a blow, by the Athenians, who

text: had sailed up and unexpectedly put into the harbour, had beaten the Chian ships, and landing and defeating the troops opposed to them had become masters of the city.
text_raw:
had sailed up and unexpectedly put into the harbour, had beaten the Chian ships, and
landing and defeating the troops opposed to them had become masters of the city.

text: Informed of this by the Eresians and the Chian ships, which had been left with Eubulus at Methymna, and had fled upon the capture of Mitylene, and three of which he now fell in with, one having been taken by the Athenians, Astyochus did not go on to Mitylene, but raised and armed Eresus, and, sending the heavy infantry from his own ships by land under Eteonicus to Antissa and Methymna, himself proceeded alongshore thither with the ships which he had with him and with the three Chians, in the hope that the Methymnians upon seeing them would be encouraged to persevere in their revolt.
text_raw:
Informed of this by the Eresians and the Chian ships, which had been left with Eubulus at
Methymna, and had fled upon the capture of Mitylene, and three of which he now fell in
with, one having been taken by the Athenians, Astyochus did not go on to Mitylene, but
raised and armed Eresus, and, sending the heavy infantry from his own ships by land
under Eteonicus to Antissa and Methymna, himself proceeded alongshore thither with the
ships which he had with him and with the three Chians, in the hope that the Methymnians
upon seeing them would be encouraged to persevere in their revolt.

text: As, however, everything went against him in Lesbos, he took up his own force and sailed back to Chios; the land forces on board, which were to have gone to the Hellespont, being also conveyed back to their different cities.
text_raw:
As, however,
everything went against him in Lesbos, he took up his own force and sailed back to Chios;
the land forces on board, which were to have gone to the Hellespont, being also conveyed
back to their different cities.

text: After this six of the allied Peloponnesian ships at Cenchreae joined the forces at Chios.
text_raw:
After this six of the allied Peloponnesian ships at Cenchreae
joined the forces at Chios.

text: The Athenians, after restoring matters to their old state in Lesbos, set sail from thence and took Polichna, the place that the Clazomenians were fortifying on the continent, and carried the inhabitants back to their town upon the island, except the authors of the revolt, who withdrew to Daphnus; and thus Clazomenae became once more Athenian.
text_raw:
The Athenians, after restoring matters to their old state in
Lesbos, set sail from thence and took Polichna, the place that the Clazomenians were
fortifying on the continent, and carried the inhabitants back to their town upon the island,
except the authors of the revolt, who withdrew to Daphnus; and thus Clazomenae became
once more Athenian.

text: The same summer the Athenians in the twenty ships at Lade, blockading Miletus, made a descent at Panormus in the Milesian territory, and killed Chalcideus the Lacedaemonian commander, who had come with a few men against them, and the third day after sailed over and set up a trophy, which, as they were not masters of the country, was however pulled down by the Milesians.
text_raw:
The same summer the Athenians in the twenty ships at Lade, blockading Miletus, made a
descent at Panormus in the Milesian territory, and killed Chalcideus the Lacedaemonian
commander, who had come with a few men against them, and the third day after sailed
over and set up a trophy, which, as they were not masters of the country, was however
pulled down by the Milesians.

text: Meanwhile Leon and Diomedon with the Athenian fleet from Lesbos issuing from the Oenussae, the isles off Chios, and from their forts of Sidussa and Pteleum in the Erythraeid, and from Lesbos, carried on the war against the Chians from the ships, having on board heavy infantry from the rolls pressed to serve as marines.
text_raw:
Meanwhile Leon and Diomedon with the Athenian fleet
from Lesbos issuing from the Oenussae, the isles off Chios, and from their forts of Sidussa
and Pteleum in the Erythraeid, and from Lesbos, carried on the war against the Chians
from the ships, having on board heavy infantry from the rolls pressed to serve as marines.

text: Landing in Cardamyle and in Bolissus they defeated with heavy loss the Chians that took the field against them and, laying desolate the places in that neighbourhood, defeated the Chians again in another battle at Phanae, and in a third at Leuconium.
text_raw:
Landing in Cardamyle and in Bolissus they defeated with heavy loss the Chians that took
the field against them and, laying desolate the places in that neighbourhood, defeated the
Chians again in another battle at Phanae, and in a third at Leuconium.

text: After this the Chians ceased to meet them in the field, while the Athenians devastated the country, which was beautifully stocked and had remained uninjured ever since the Median wars.
text_raw:
After this the
Chians ceased to meet them in the field, while the Athenians devastated the country,
which was beautifully stocked and had remained uninjured ever since the Median wars.

text: Indeed, after the Lacedaemonians, the Chians are the only people that I have known who knew how to be wise in prosperity, and who ordered their city the more securely the greater it grew.
text_raw:
Indeed, after the Lacedaemonians, the Chians are the only people that I have known who
knew how to be wise in prosperity, and who ordered their city the more securely the
greater it grew.

text: Nor was this revolt, in which they might seem to have erred on the side of rashness, ventured upon until they had numerous and gallant allies to share the danger with them, and until they perceived the Athenians after the Sicilian disaster themselves no longer denying the thoroughly desperate state of their affairs.
text_raw:
Nor was this revolt, in which they might seem to have erred on the side of
rashness, ventured upon until they had numerous and gallant allies to share the danger
with them, and until they perceived the Athenians after the Sicilian disaster themselves no
longer denying the thoroughly desperate state of their affairs.

text: And if they were thrown out by one of the surprises which upset human calculations, they found out their mistake in company with many others who believed, like them, in the speedy collapse of the Athenian power.
text_raw:
And if they were thrown out
by one of the surprises which upset human calculations, they found out their mistake in
company with many others who believed, like them, in the speedy collapse of the
Athenian power.

text: While they were thus blockaded from the sea and plundered by land, some of the citizens undertook to bring the city over to the Athenians.
text_raw:
While they were thus blockaded from the sea and plundered by land,
some of the citizens undertook to bring the city over to the Athenians.

text: Apprised of this the authorities took no action themselves, but brought Astyochus, the admiral, from Erythrae, with four ships that he had with him, and considered how they could most quietly, either by taking hostages or by some other means, put an end to the conspiracy.
text_raw:
Apprised of this the
authorities took no action themselves, but brought Astyochus, the admiral, from Erythrae,
with four ships that he had with him, and considered how they could most quietly, either
by taking hostages or by some other means, put an end to the conspiracy.

text: While the Chians were thus engaged, a thousand Athenian heavy infantry and fifteen
text_raw: While the Chians were thus engaged, a thousand Athenian heavy infantry and fifteen

text: hundred Argives (five hundred of whom were light troops furnished with armour by the Athenians), and one thousand of the allies, towards the close of the same summer sailed from Athens in forty-eight ships, some of which were transports, under the command of Phrynichus, Onomacles, and Scironides, and putting into Samos crossed over and encamped at Miletus.
text_raw:
hundred Argives (five hundred of whom were light troops furnished with armour by the
Athenians), and one thousand of the allies, towards the close of the same summer sailed
from Athens in forty-eight ships, some of which were transports, under the command of
Phrynichus, Onomacles, and Scironides, and putting into Samos crossed over and
encamped at Miletus.

text: Upon this the Milesians came out to the number of eight hundred heavy infantry, with the Peloponnesians who had come with Chalcideus, and some foreign mercenaries of Tissaphernes, Tissaphernes himself and his cavalry, and engaged the Athenians and their allies.
text_raw:
Upon this the Milesians came out to the number of eight hundred
heavy infantry, with the Peloponnesians who had come with Chalcideus, and some foreign
mercenaries of Tissaphernes, Tissaphernes himself and his cavalry, and engaged the
Athenians and their allies.

text: While the Argives rushed forward on their own wing with the careless disdain of men advancing against Ionians who would never stand their charge, and were defeated by the Milesians with a loss little short of three hundred men, the Athenians first defeated the Peloponnesians, and driving before them the barbarians and the ruck of the army, without engaging the Milesians, who after the rout of the Argives retreated into the town upon seeing their comrades worsted, crowned their victory by grounding their arms under the very walls of Miletus.
text_raw:
While the Argives rushed forward on their own wing with the
careless disdain of men advancing against Ionians who would never stand their charge,
and were defeated by the Milesians with a loss little short of three hundred men, the
Athenians first defeated the Peloponnesians, and driving before them the barbarians and
the ruck of the army, without engaging the Milesians, who after the rout of the Argives
retreated into the town upon seeing their comrades worsted, crowned their victory by
grounding their arms under the very walls of Miletus.

text: Thus, in this battle, the Ionians on both sides overcame the Dorians, the Athenians defeating the Peloponnesians opposed to them, and the Milesians the Argives.
text_raw:
Thus, in this battle, the Ionians on
both sides overcame the Dorians, the Athenians defeating the Peloponnesians opposed to
them, and the Milesians the Argives.

text: After setting up a trophy, the Athenians prepared to draw a wall round the place, which stood upon an isthmus; thinking that, if they could gain Miletus, the other towns also would easily come over to them.
text_raw:
After setting up a trophy, the Athenians prepared to
draw a wall round the place, which stood upon an isthmus; thinking that, if they could
gain Miletus, the other towns also would easily come over to them.

text: Meanwhile about dusk tidings reached them that the fifty-five ships from Peloponnese and Sicily might be instantly expected.
text_raw:
Meanwhile about dusk tidings reached them that the fifty-five ships from Peloponnese
and Sicily might be instantly expected.

text: Of these the Siceliots, urged principally by the Syracusan Hermocrates to join in giving the finishing blow to the power of Athens, furnished twenty-two—twenty from Syracuse, and two from Silenus; and the ships that we left preparing in Peloponnese being now ready, both squadrons had been entrusted to Therimenes, a Lacedaemonian, to take to Astyochus, the admiral.
text_raw:
Of these the Siceliots, urged principally by the
Syracusan Hermocrates to join in giving the finishing blow to the power of Athens,
furnished twenty-two—twenty from Syracuse, and two from Silenus; and the ships that we
left preparing in Peloponnese being now ready, both squadrons had been entrusted to
Therimenes, a Lacedaemonian, to take to Astyochus, the admiral.

text: They now put in first at Leros the island off Miletus, and from thence, discovering that the Athenians were before the town, sailed into the Iasic Gulf, in order to learn how matters stood at Miletus.
text_raw:
They now put in first at
Leros the island off Miletus, and from thence, discovering that the Athenians were before
the town, sailed into the Iasic Gulf, in order to learn how matters stood at Miletus.

text: Meanwhile Alcibiades came on horseback to Teichiussa in the Milesian territory, the point of the gulf at which they had put in for the night, and told them of the battle in which he had fought in person by the side of the Milesians and Tissaphernes, and advised them, if they did not wish to sacrifice Ionia and their cause, to fly to the relief of Miletus and hinder its investment.
text_raw:
Meanwhile Alcibiades came on horseback to Teichiussa in the Milesian territory, the point
of the gulf at which they had put in for the night, and told them of the battle in which he
had fought in person by the side of the Milesians and Tissaphernes, and advised them, if
they did not wish to sacrifice Ionia and their cause, to fly to the relief of Miletus and
hinder its investment.

text: Accordingly they resolved to relieve it the next morning.
text_raw: Accordingly they resolved to relieve it the next morning.

text: Meanwhile Phrynichus, the Athenian commander, had received precise intelligence of the fleet from Leros, and when his colleagues expressed a wish to keep the sea and fight it out, flatly refused either to stay himself or to let them or any one else do so if he could help it.
text_raw:
Meanwhile Phrynichus, the
Athenian commander, had received precise intelligence of the fleet from Leros, and when
his colleagues expressed a wish to keep the sea and fight it out, flatly refused either to stay
himself or to let them or any one else do so if he could help it.

text: Where they could hereafter contend, after full and undisturbed preparation, with an exact knowledge of the number of the enemy’s fleet and of the force which they could oppose to him, he would never allow the reproach of disgrace to drive him into a risk that was unreasonable.
text_raw:
Where they could hereafter
contend, after full and undisturbed preparation, with an exact knowledge of the number of
the enemy’s fleet and of the force which they could oppose to him, he would never allow
the reproach of disgrace to drive him into a risk that was unreasonable.

text: It was no disgrace for an Athenian fleet to retreat when it suited them: put it as they would, it would be more disgraceful to be beaten, and to expose the city not only to disgrace, but to the most serious danger.
text_raw:
It was no disgrace
for an Athenian fleet to retreat when it suited them: put it as they would, it would be more
disgraceful to be beaten, and to expose the city not only to disgrace, but to the most
serious danger.

text: After its late misfortunes it could hardly be justified in voluntarily taking the offensive even with the strongest force, except in a case of absolute necessity: much less then without compulsion could it rush upon peril of its own seeking.
text_raw:
After its late misfortunes it could hardly be justified in voluntarily taking
the offensive even with the strongest force, except in a case of absolute necessity: much
less then without compulsion could it rush upon peril of its own seeking.

text: He told them to take up their wounded as quickly as they could and the troops and stores which they had
text_raw:
He told them to
take up their wounded as quickly as they could and the troops and stores which they had

text: brought with them, and leaving behind what they had taken from the enemy’s country, in order to lighten the ships, to sail off to Samos, and there concentrating all their ships to attack as opportunity served.
text_raw:
brought with them, and leaving behind what they had taken from the enemy’s country, in
order to lighten the ships, to sail off to Samos, and there concentrating all their ships to
attack as opportunity served.

text: As he spoke so he acted; and thus not now more than afterwards, nor in this alone but in all that he had to do with, did Phrynichus show himself a man of sense.
text_raw:
As he spoke so he acted; and thus not now more than
afterwards, nor in this alone but in all that he had to do with, did Phrynichus show himself
a man of sense.

text: In this way that very evening the Athenians broke up from before Miletus, leaving their victory unfinished, and the Argives, mortified at their disaster, promptly sailed off home from Samos.
text_raw:
In this way that very evening the Athenians broke up from before Miletus,
leaving their victory unfinished, and the Argives, mortified at their disaster, promptly
sailed off home from Samos.

text: As soon as it was morning the Peloponnesians weighed from Teichiussa and put into Miletus after the departure of the Athenians; they stayed one day, and on the next took with them the Chian vessels originally chased into port with Chalcideus, and resolved to sail back for the tackle which they had put on shore at Teichiussa.
text_raw:
As soon as it was morning the Peloponnesians weighed from Teichiussa and put into
Miletus after the departure of the Athenians; they stayed one day, and on the next took
with them the Chian vessels originally chased into port with Chalcideus, and resolved to
sail back for the tackle which they had put on shore at Teichiussa.

text: Upon their arrival Tissaphernes came to them with his land forces and induced them to sail to Iasus, which was held by his enemy Amorges.
text_raw:
Upon their arrival
Tissaphernes came to them with his land forces and induced them to sail to Iasus, which
was held by his enemy Amorges.

text: Accordingly they suddenly attacked and took Iasus, whose inhabitants never imagined that the ships could be other than Athenian.
text_raw:
Accordingly they suddenly attacked and took Iasus,
whose inhabitants never imagined that the ships could be other than Athenian.

text: The Syracusans distinguished themselves most in the action.
text_raw:
The
Syracusans distinguished themselves most in the action.

text: Amorges, a bastard of Pissuthnes and a rebel from the King, was taken alive and handed over to Tissaphernes, to carry to the King, if he chose, according to his orders:
text_raw:
Amorges, a bastard of Pissuthnes
and a rebel from the King, was taken alive and handed over to Tissaphernes, to carry to
the King, if he chose, according to his orders:

text: Iasus was sacked by the army, who found a very great booty there, the place being wealthy from ancient date.
text_raw:
Iasus was sacked by the army, who found a
very great booty there, the place being wealthy from ancient date.

text: The mercenaries serving with Amorges the Peloponnesians received and enrolled in their army without doing them any harm, since most of them came from Peloponnese, and handed over the town to Tissaphernes with all the captives, bond or free, at the stipulated price of one Doric stater a head; after which they returned to Miletus.
text_raw:
The mercenaries serving
with Amorges the Peloponnesians received and enrolled in their army without doing them
any harm, since most of them came from Peloponnese, and handed over the town to
Tissaphernes with all the captives, bond or free, at the stipulated price of one Doric stater a
head; after which they returned to Miletus.

text: Pedaritus, son of Leon, who had been sent by the Lacedaemonians to take the command at Chios, they dispatched by land as far as Erythrae with the mercenaries taken from Amorges; appointing Philip to remain as governor of Miletus.
text_raw:
Pedaritus, son of Leon, who had been sent by
the Lacedaemonians to take the command at Chios, they dispatched by land as far as
Erythrae with the mercenaries taken from Amorges; appointing Philip to remain as
governor of Miletus.

text: Summer was now over.
text_raw: Summer was now over.

text: The winter following, Tissaphernes put Iasus in a state of defence, and passing on to Miletus distributed a month’s pay to all the ships as he had promised at Lacedaemon, at the rate of an Attic drachma a day for each man.
text_raw:
The winter following, Tissaphernes put Iasus in a state of
defence, and passing on to Miletus distributed a month’s pay to all the ships as he had
promised at Lacedaemon, at the rate of an Attic drachma a day for each man.

text: In future, however, he was resolved not to give more than three obols, until he had consulted the King; when if the King should so order he would give, he said, the full drachma.
text_raw:
In future,
however, he was resolved not to give more than three obols, until he had consulted the
King; when if the King should so order he would give, he said, the full drachma.

text: However, upon the protest of the Syracusan general Hermocrates (for as Therimenes was not admiral, but only accompanied them in order to hand over the ships to Astyochus, he made little difficulty about the pay), it was agreed that the amount of five ships’ pay should be given over and above the three obols a day for each man;
text_raw:
However,
upon the protest of the Syracusan general Hermocrates (for as Therimenes was not
admiral, but only accompanied them in order to hand over the ships to Astyochus, he
made little difficulty about the pay), it was agreed that the amount of five ships’ pay
should be given over and above the three obols a day for each man;

text: Tissaphernes paying thirty talents a month for fifty-five ships, and to the rest, for as many ships as they had beyond that number, at the same rate.
text_raw:
Tissaphernes paying
thirty talents a month for fifty-five ships, and to the rest, for as many ships as they had
beyond that number, at the same rate.

text: The same winter the Athenians in Samos, having been joined by thirty-five more vessels from home under Charminus, Strombichides, and Euctemon, called in their squadron at Chios and all the rest, intending to blockade Miletus with their navy, and to send a fleet and an army against Chios; drawing lots for the respective services.
text_raw:
The same winter the Athenians in Samos, having been joined by thirty-five more vessels
from home under Charminus, Strombichides, and Euctemon, called in their squadron at
Chios and all the rest, intending to blockade Miletus with their navy, and to send a fleet
and an army against Chios; drawing lots for the respective services.

text: This intention they carried into effect;
text_raw:
This intention they
carried into effect;

text: Strombichides, Onamacles, and Euctemon sailing against Chios, which fell to their lot, with thirty ships and a part of the thousand heavy infantry, who had been to Miletus, in transports; while the rest remained masters of the sea with seventy-four
text_raw:
Strombichides, Onamacles, and Euctemon sailing against Chios, which
fell to their lot, with thirty ships and a part of the thousand heavy infantry, who had been
to Miletus, in transports; while the rest remained masters of the sea with seventy-four

text: ships at Samos, and advanced upon Miletus.
text_raw: ships at Samos, and advanced upon Miletus.

text: Meanwhile Astyochus, whom we left at Chios collecting the hostages required in consequence of the conspiracy, stopped upon learning that the fleet with Therimenes had arrived, and that the affairs of the league were in a more flourishing condition, and putting out to sea with ten Peloponnesian and as many Chian vessels, after a futile attack upon Pteleum, coasted on to Clazomenae, and ordered the Athenian party to remove inland to Daphnus, and to join the Peloponnesians, an order in which also joined Tamos the king’s lieutenant in Ionia.
text_raw:
Meanwhile Astyochus, whom we left at Chios collecting the hostages required in
consequence of the conspiracy, stopped upon learning that the fleet with Therimenes had
arrived, and that the affairs of the league were in a more flourishing condition, and putting
out to sea with ten Peloponnesian and as many Chian vessels, after a futile attack upon
Pteleum, coasted on to Clazomenae, and ordered the Athenian party to remove inland to
Daphnus, and to join the Peloponnesians, an order in which also joined Tamos the king’s
lieutenant in Ionia.

text: This order being disregarded, Astyochus made an attack upon the town, which was unwalled, and having failed to take it was himself carried off by a strong gale to Phocaea and Cuma, while the rest of the ships put in at the islands adjacent to Clazomenae—Marathussa, Pele, and Drymussa.
text_raw:
This order being disregarded, Astyochus made an attack upon the
town, which was unwalled, and having failed to take it was himself carried off by a strong
gale to Phocaea and Cuma, while the rest of the ships put in at the islands adjacent to
Clazomenae—Marathussa, Pele, and Drymussa.

text: Here they were detained eight days by the winds, and, plundering and consuming all the property of the Clazomenians there deposited, put the rest on shipboard and sailed off to Phocaea and Cuma to join Astyochus.
text_raw:
Here they were detained eight days by the
winds, and, plundering and consuming all the property of the Clazomenians there
deposited, put the rest on shipboard and sailed off to Phocaea and Cuma to join
Astyochus.

text: While he was there, envoys arrived from the Lesbians who wished to revolt again.
text_raw: While he was there, envoys arrived from the Lesbians who wished to revolt again.

text: With Astyochus they were successful; but the Corinthians and the other allies being averse to it by reason of their former failure, he weighed anchor and set sail for Chios, where they eventually arrived from different quarters, the fleet having been scattered by a storm.
text_raw:
With
Astyochus they were successful; but the Corinthians and the other allies being averse to it
by reason of their former failure, he weighed anchor and set sail for Chios, where they
eventually arrived from different quarters, the fleet having been scattered by a storm.

text: After this Pedaritus, whom we left marching along the coast from Miletus, arrived at Erythrae, and thence crossed over with his army to Chios, where he found also about five hundred soldiers who had been left there by Chalcideus from the five ships with their arms.
text_raw:
After
this Pedaritus, whom we left marching along the coast from Miletus, arrived at Erythrae,
and thence crossed over with his army to Chios, where he found also about five hundred
soldiers who had been left there by Chalcideus from the five ships with their arms.

text: Meanwhile some Lesbians making offers to revolt, Astyochus urged upon Pedaritus and the Chians that they ought to go with their ships and effect the revolt of Lesbos, and so increase the number of their allies, or, if not successful, at all events harm the Athenians.
text_raw:
Meanwhile some Lesbians making offers to revolt, Astyochus urged upon Pedaritus and
the Chians that they ought to go with their ships and effect the revolt of Lesbos, and so
increase the number of their allies, or, if not successful, at all events harm the Athenians.

text: The Chians, however, turned a deaf ear to this, and Pedaritus flatly refused to give up to him the Chian vessels.
text_raw:
The Chians, however, turned a deaf ear to this, and Pedaritus flatly refused to give up to
him the Chian vessels.

text: Upon this Astyochus took five Corinthian and one Megarian vessel, with another from Hermione, and the ships which had come with him from Laconia, and set sail for Miletus to assume his command as admiral; after telling the Chians with many threats that he would certainly not come and help them if they should be in need.
text_raw:
Upon this Astyochus took five Corinthian and one Megarian vessel, with another from
